title: 3.2.0.1 Overview
text:
ChipStack TUI (Terminal User Interface) is a terminal-based interface that enables interaction with
ChipStack artifacts and agents. It provides a set of specialized modes designed to support different
engineering tasks, including design, dynamic verification, formal verification, debug, and RTL Signoff.
Each mode is optimized for its respective workflow, offering targeted tools and capabilities to improve
efficiency and focus.
Run the following commands to discover the modes

ChipStack Interfaces--3.2 Chipstack TUI

Run the following commands to discover the modes
chipstack tui --help
To invoke ChipStack TUI run the command:
chipstack tui --config <config_file_path>
The TUI displays the available modes. Use the
up
and
down
arrows to navigate to the desired mode,
then press Enter to invoke it.
To open the TUI in a certain mode, run the command:
chipstack tui --mode <mode>
#example:
chipstack tui --mode formal
The mode is presented at the bottom toolbar of the TUI

ChipStack Interfaces--3.2 Chipstack TUI

Chipstack Web UI
)

To
copy

data
from the TUI to the clipboard, select the desired text. The text will be copied to the
clipboard, and a notification will appear in the lower-right corner of the TUI.

title: 3.2.0.4 Save and restore a session
text:
ChipStack lets you save and restore TUI sessions. Restored sessions preserve the conversation state,
allowing you to stop and restart a session without losing context.
There are two ways to restore a previous session:
Use a named session
– Named sessions allow you to save and resume a session by name,
making it easy to return to a specific workflow.
Select a previously saved session
– When no session name is provided, the TUI displays a list
of available sessions and lets you choose which one to resume.
To start a new named session:
chipstack tui --session-name my_design_review --mode mental-model
To resume an existing named session
chipstack tui --session-name my_design_review
When resuming, omit --mode, the session already has its mode saved.
Sessions are stored at:
chipstack_artifacts/tui/sessions/<session-name>.json

ChipStack Interfaces--3.2 Chipstack TUI

exists

→
session is loaded and conversation history is restored
If the name
does not exist

→
a new session is created with that name
Session names can be any string (e.g. fifo_rtl_check, axi_review_june)
When no session name is provided, the TUI presents the previously saved sessions and lets you
choose which session to resume.

Chipstack Agents Artifacts
Chipstack agents follow a unified structure for storing their generated artifacts. This facilitates sharing
data across agents and serves as memory in the agentic flow.
The agents write their outputs under a single root directory named
chipstack_artifacts
, located directly
under your work area.
Key Conventions
Root selection
: chipstack_artifacts is created in the current working directory.
Design root
: `chipstack_artifacts/<top_design_name>/` is the canonical home for all artifacts for
one DUT. If no top-design name is known, agents write directly under chipstack_artifacts.
Per-agent subfolder
: each agent (e.g. `uvm_agent`, `formal_agent`, etc.) gets its own subdirectory
under the design root.
Reserved names
- (not treated as design roots): `Archive`, `tui_sessions`, `app_state`, `cli_logs`,
`.symphony_logs`, `tui`, `tmp`, `compile_n_fix`, `semantic_cache`.
Auto Discovery
- agents walk up from your current path to find the enclosing design root, so
shared artifacts (e.g. the mental model) are picked up automatically.
Archive
– holds snapshots of old design roots
Run results
– per each agent, keep execution results of cadence tools.
Note, the UVM agent artifacts are sibling to the design related artifacts as the UVM is not part of the
design

chapter: 7.2 Integration to coding agents through Command Line (CLI)
section: 7.2 Integration to coding agents through Command Line (CLI)
title: 7.2 Integration to coding agents through Command Line (CLI)
text:
ChipStack exposes its agents as plain CLI commands (`chipstack mental-model generate`, `chipstack
dv-debug-agent auto-debug`, etc.). The corresponding SKILL.md files describe how to invoke these
shell commands, required flags, argument discovery steps, and example invocations. The head agent
runs these as shell subprocesses and reads stdout/stderr in real time.
Use the following Chipstack command-line to install the skills for CLI integration:
Chipstack install-skills <coding agent name>
Example:
# Install CLI skill files for Claude Code
chipstack install-skills claude-code # installs to ~/.claude/skills/
chipstack install-skills claude-code --project # installs to .claude/skills/
# Install for Gemini CLI
chipstack install-skills gemini-cli
The skills are installed in the related directory of the coding agent
/home/<user>/.claude/skills
/home/<user>/.copilot/skills
/home/<user>/.gemini/skills

ChipStack Integration into Coding Agents--7.2 Integration to coding agents through Command Line (CLI)

chapter: 7.3 Integration to coding agents through MCP
section: 7.3 Integration to coding agents through MCP
title: 7.3 Integration to coding agents through MCP
text:
ChipStack operates a local MCP server (chipstack mcp run) that exposes its agents as structured tool
interfaces. Head agents such as Claude Code or Gemini CLI connect to this server and invoke
capabilities—e.g., generate_mental_model, run_formal_agent, or run_dv_debug_agent—
directly,
without requiring shell execution.
Use the following Chipstack command line to install the skills for MCP integration:
Chipstack mcp install-skills <coding agent name>
Example:
# 1. Install the SKILL.md files so Claude Code
chipstack mcp install-skills claude-code # all

modes
chipstack mcp install-skills claude-code --mode dv_debug --mode formal #

specific modes

Chipstack VSCODE Extension
Chipstack provides you with vscode extension (VSIX) for efficiency and quality. The extension offers
capabilities powered by Cadence Tools – Superlint and Jasper Language Server.
The following capabilities are supported:
Language Support & Syntax Highlighting

Registers Verilog (.v, .vh) and SystemVerilog (.sv, .svh) as
first-class languages in VS Code — no external tooling required:
Syntax highlighting with theme-aware coloring.
Bracket matching for HDL constructs.
Comment toggling, auto-closing pairs, and code folding via //region markers.
Jasper Language Server (LSP)

Powered by Jasper built-in language server. When enabled:
Auto-complete — completion suggestions while typing.
Go-to-definition — jump to symbol definitions.
Hover tooltips — type and documentation on hover.
Real-time diagnostics — compilation and syntax errors surfaced as red marks in the Problems
panel. Configured by (standard VS Code settings)
"jasper.lsp": true
"cad.formal.toolPath": "/path/to/jasper"
Real-Time Linting (Jasper Superlint)
- On each file-save, Superlint runs and results appear in a
dedicated Jasper Superlint panel:
Violations organized as a tree: file
→
violation item (tag + message)
Click any violation to jump to the exact source location.
Severity levels: error, warning, info, hint — each with themed icons
Violation count badge on the panel header.
Results also pushed to VS Code's Problems panel (source: jasper-superlint)

Chipstack VSCODE Extension

Configured by Configured by (standard VS Code settings):
"jasper.superlint.realtime.enabled": true

Diagnostics & Problems Panel Integration
Two named diagnostic sources, both appear as inline
marks in the editor and in the standard VS Code Problems panel :
jasper-superlint — lint violations
jasper-lsp — language server compilation errors
Use the VSIX extension that is provided as part of the release

9.1
Chipstack Mental Model Agent
The Mental Model Agent is the cognitive backbone of the ChipStack platform. It derives a mental model
from the design specification and RTL, capturing design intent, functional behavior, interface protocols,
and boundary conditions. When needed, agents use the Mental Model as a common semantic
foundation, enabling design and verification tasks to remain tightly aligned. As the model evolves,

chapter: 7.3 Integration to coding agents through MCP
section: 7.3 Integration to coding agents through MCP
title: 7.3 Integration to coding agents through MCP
text:
uring design intent, functional behavior, interface protocols,
and boundary conditions. When needed, agents use the Mental Model as a common semantic
foundation, enabling design and verification tasks to remain tightly aligned. As the model evolves,
agents can reason consistently across domains—for example, propagating design changes into
verification updates or identifying verification gaps resulting from design modifications. Once artifacts
are generated for the mental model, you can
review
them,
chat
, and ask for
changes
using the CLI or
TUI.
As part of its functionality, the Mental Model Agent checks
consistency between the RTL to the Spec
.
The agent uses a balanced reasoning approach to find high confidence inconsistencies while keeping
a low false positive rate. The agent will report on
CONFIRMED — rtl and spec agree.

ChipStack Agents--9.1 Chipstack Mental Model Agent

CONTRADICTED — explicit conflict
INCOMPLETE_SPEC — feature exists in rtl but spec is missing or insufficient.
INCOMPLETE — specs describe
something
the rtl doesn't fully implement.
Note
It is recommended to use a spec for better context and higher quality downstream agents.
Spec only input is currently not supported.
It is recommended to create the mental model from the design directory for using relative paths.
9.1.1
Mental Model Agent Configuration
The following configurations are related to the Mental Model Agent:
force_mental_model_inconsistency_check: false # Auto-run RTL/spec consistency

check during mental model generation
use_rag_for_spec_files: true # Use RAG/vector DB for spec files;

false = convert binary specs to markdown + read directly
mental_model_continue_on_parse_failure: true # Continue generation even if

design parsing fails/has errors
9.1.2
Mental Model Agent – Generated Artifacts
The main generated artifact of the Mental Model Agent is the mental model itself, which is generated in
three formats: PDF, Markdown, and JSON.
mental_model_backup.* are created automatically on update runs and are not copied to the
archive.
inconsistency_report.json and
inconsistency_summary.md
are only present when generate
inconsistency-analysis was run (or force_mental_model_inconsistency_check: true is set in
config).
parsed_design/ contains intermediate Verific parse output consumed by the agent — not intended
for direct user consumption.

Chipstack Formal Agent
The Formal Verification Agent automates the entire formal verification workflow within ChipStack, from
design comprehension to coverage analysis. It orchestrates multiple verification stages to generate,
execute, and evaluate formal test benches with minimal manual effort.
The formal verification flow consists of the following stages:
Mental Model Generation

9.3
Chipstack Coverage Agent
The Functional Coverage Agent automates the creation of a functional coverage model for dynamic
verification. It generates System Verilog coverGroups from RTL and specifications, ensuring that the
coverage model reflects design intent. By leveraging formal analysis, the agent prunes unreachable
coverage points and delivers a clean model.
Note
: Only DUT external ports are used. No internal signals or hierarchical references. The Agent flow
consists of the following stages:
Mental Model
The flow invokes the Mental Model Agent to analyze the RTL and specification files. It
extracts key structural and functional design features, forming an internal representation
(mental model) of the design.
Test Plan Generation
Based on the mental model, the agent enumerates functional scenarios and coverage
intents derived from the specification. It constructs a functional coverage test plan that
defines required Coverage space by means of CoverGroups, CoverPoints and Bins
Testbench Generation
Using the functional coverage test plan, the agent automatically generates optimized System
Verilog coverGroups. The generated coverage testbench includes all required coverPoints
and crosses, structured for reuse. It is packaged so it can be directly integrated into a
simulation regression environment.
Run Verification
The agent runs the Formal Verification Engine (Jasper) to analyze the generated
coverGroups. Unreachable coverPoints are automatically identified and excluded from the
coverage model.

9.8
Chipstack RTL Coding Agent – Upgrade RTL
The agent upgrades a given RTL according to a provided
RTL change request
that outlines the
requested RTL modifications. A change request can range from a simple code-change description to a
detailed RTL design-change document or specification. The agent generates RTL across multiple
modules with dependencies. The agent can run as a full end-to-end flow or step by step using the pre-
generated artifacts of previous stages.
The agent consists of the following steps
Mental Model
The agent analyzes the RTL and associated specifications, building a structured model of
the design (ports, clocks, resets, pipelines, and functional intent) before upgrading the RTL
uArch Spec
Based on the mental model, the agent generates a micro architecture specification
document describing the change
Upgrade RTL

Based on the uArch specification for the change and the mental model, the agent upgrades
the RTL, compiles and fixes errors with a dedicated agent, and yields production-ready RTL
for integration or implementation
The mental model is upgraded and aligned with the upgraded RTL
Note: for minor changes, the agent may decide to skip generation of the mental model and uArch spec
from the change request.
9.8.1
Upgrade RTL Agent Configuration
The following configuration is needed for the RTL Agent
# Compile-n-fix tool path (matches --cnf-mode)
formal_bin_path: jaspergold # for --cnf-mode formal (default)
sim_bin_path: xrun # for --cnf-mode dv
# EDA tool timeout
eda_tool_timeout: 600 # seconds before tool is killed
# Mental Model generation quality vs. speed
use_mental_model_lite_steps: true # 7-step pipeline, recommended
use_mental_model_very_lite: false # single-shot, faster but lower quality
# Artifact reuse between runs
reuse_runid: true

9.9
Chipstack DV Debug Agent
The DV Debug Agent fixes simulation failures. The agent executes the entire debug cycle using the
following steps.
RCA (Root-cause-analysis)
The agent leverages the power of LLM combined with Cadence Tools, Tools' Agents and AI
Apps (e.g. Verisium Debug RCA Agent) to get a root cause of the failure and to explore the
design and testbench / failure data. The agent generates a summary report that includes
simulation failure, the observed root-cause, the supporting evidence, recommendations, and
next steps.
Auto Fix
The agent understands the failure and affected logic and extracts key signals, conditions,
and context. It deploys Chipstack RTL and UVM agents to apply the fix for the failure. The
Agent verifies the fix by running simulation.
9.9.1
DV Debug Agent – Configuration and Setting
Set the following setting in the config file
verisium_debug_root: /path/to/verisium/installation
simulation_bin_path: xrun # must be on PATH; used to compile/re-run after

applying a fix

Chipstack Workflows Overview

title: 10.2.0.1 Workflows overview
text:
A workflow is a fully automated, multi-step verification or design task that runs end-to-end and allows
user interaction and feedback on predefined criteria. The key idea is that workflows are
spec-driven
:
rather than expressing your intent in a prompt, you encode it in one or more
workflow

title: 10.2.0.1 Workflows overview
text: Spec

title: 10.2.0.1 Workflows overview
text:
YAML files
that are resolved before the agent starts. The workflow infrastructure consumes the YAML files and auto-
generates an agentic 'executable workflow' from a workflow spec. The workflow YAML is a graph
definition file that describes the workflow as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of nodes and edges. It is the
authoritative specification of what the workflow does, in what order, and which decisions are made
between steps.

session
state: # Python class holding shared state across nodes

source_file: state.py

marks terminal nodes
documentation:

control flow between nodes

- from_node: node_c

title: 10.2.0.3 Workflows Web UI
text:
When a workflow is launched, ChipStack starts a standalone web application called
workflow_designer_webui — a pre-built executable bundled with the ChipStack installation. It runs as a
persistent background server (survives across workflow runs) and serves a React-based single-page
application at a local URL like
http://localhost:<port>/<session_id
>.
The web UI is a
live dashboard
for a running workflow session. It is structured around several panels:
Left Toolbar
– displays all opened TUI sessions and all running workflows. Select for viewing the
data related to the TUI or the workflow
Graph
- The Graph Tab displays the workflow graph (driven from YMAL) and highlights the current
executed node.
State
– The State tab contains information on the current shared state object (key/value pairs
written by nodes)
Node status
– each node shows its status – running , finished, pending input, error
Execution steps
– the key steps done by the agent
Logs
– messages print by each step of the agent

Overview
This document describes the applicability of different debug capabilities in the following
sections:
• Using Debug Options
• Options Supported by -debug_access
• Options Supported by -debug_region

Using Debug Options
The following table describes the applicability of different debug capabilities:
Table-1: Debug Options
Option Description
-debug_access(+option) Use the -debug_access option at compile time to have more
granular control over debug capabilities in a simulation.
The -debug_access option enables the dumping of the VPD
and FSDB files for post-processing debug, and reduces debug
capabilities when compared to the -debug_pp option.
You can specify additional options with the -debug_access
option to selectively enable the required debug capabilities.
You can optimize simulation performance by enabling only the
required debug capabilities.
Following is the use model of the -debug_access option:
-debug_access(+<option_name>)*
For more information, see “Options Supported by
-debug_access ” section.
-debug_region Use the -debug_region option to have better control over
the performance of -debug_access. The -debug_region
option enables you to apply debugging capabilities to the
desired portion of a design [DUT, cell, testbench, and standard
package (OVM, UVM, VMM, and RAL), or encrypted instances
(modules, programs, packages, and interfaces)].
You must use the -debug_region option along with the
-debug_access option at compile time. Following is the syntax
of -debug_region:
-debug_access(+<option>)* -
debug_region(option_name)(option_name)*
For more information, see “Options Supported by
-debug_region” section.

Options Supported by -debug_access
The following table describes the options supported by -debug_access:
Table 1 Supported Options of -debug_access
Option Name Description
r This option enables the read capability for the entire design. This enables PLI
access to get value, and enables the UCLI get command. This is the minimum
debug option to invoke the Verdi interactive mode.
w This option applies write (deposit) capability to the registers and variables for the
entire design.
wn This option applies write (deposit) capability to the nets for the entire design.
fn This option applies force capability to the nets for the entire design. This option is
equivalent to -debug_access+r+fn.
fwn This option applies write (deposit) and force capability to all nets in the design. This
option is equivalent to -debug_access+r+wn+fn.
f This option enables the following:
• Read capability on registers, variables, and nets
• Write (deposit) capability on registers and variables
• Force capability on registers, variables, and nets
This option is equivalent to -debug_access+r+w+fn+f.
drivers
drivers This option enables driver debugging capability. This option is equivalent to
-debug_access+r+drivers.
line
line This option enables line debugging. It allows you to use the commands
for step/next and line breakpoints. This option is equivalent to
-debug_access+r+line.
cbk
cbk This option enables dumping of SystemVerilog string type signals and PLI-based
callbacks on nets, registers, and variables. This option is equivalent to
-debug_access+r+cbk.
cbkd
cbkd This option enables both dumping and PLI-based callbacks on dynamic nets,
registers, and variables defined in classes. Class object debugging is also enabled.
This option is equivalent to -debug_access+r+line+cbkd.

Chapter 3: Options Supported by -debug_access

Table 1 Supported Options of -debug_access (Continued)
Option Name Description
thread
thread This option enables the debugging of the SystemVerilog threads. This option is
equivalent to -debug_access+r+thread.
class
class This option enables debugging of the SystemVerilog classes and class
objects, but the capability is also applied to the remaining portion of the
design as specified by the -debug_region option. This option is equivalent
to:-debug_access+r+w+thread+line+cbk+cbkd.
pp
pp This option enables write capability on registers and variables, callbacks for the
entire design, driver capability, and assertion debug capability.

debugging
This option is equivalent to: -debug_access+line+r+w+wn+cbk

You can use the -debug_access+designer option for debugging design and

Options Supported by -debug_region
The following table describes the options supported by -debug_region.
Table-3: The -debug_region Options
Option
Name
Description
+cell Applies debug capabilities to both real cell modules and the ports of real cell
modules.
+cellports Applies debug capabilities only to the ports of real cell modules.
-lib The -debug_region-lib option removes debug capabilities from libraries (files
passed to VCS with the preceding -v/-y compiler options).
+encrypt Applies debug capabilities to the fully-encrypted instances (modules, programs,
packages, and interfaces).
=sv The -debug_region=sv option applies debug capabilities only to the program,
package, interface or module containing SystemVerilog constructs, and to
SystemC.
Debug capabilities are applied to SystemVerilog code inside cells and fully
encrypted blocks only when the +cell option is also used.
Debug capabilities are applied to the Verilog code inside fully encrypted modules
only when the +encrypt option is also used.
=verilog The -debug_region=verilog option applies debug capabilities to all Verilog code
and to SystemC.
Debug capabilities are applied to the Verilog code inside cells only when the +cell
option is also used.
Debug capabilities are applied to the Verilog code inside fully encrypted modules
only when the +encrypt option is also used.
=vhdl The -debug_region=vhdloption applies debug capabilities to the VHDL code and
to SystemC.

Controlling SystemVerilog Assertions and
Reporting Disabled Assertions
The document explains how to control assertions and report disabled assertions. The
document includes the following sections:
• Controlling SystemVerilog Assertions and Reporting Disabled Assertions
• Generating an Assertion Report
VCS provides various options to control or monitor assertions. If you are using more than
one of these assertion control options, you need to know their precedence when used
together. The order of precedence from highest to lowest is as follows:
• Precedence 1:
• Controlling assertions globally using the following compile-time options:
◦ %vcs -assert disable <other compile-time options>
◦ %vcs -assert disable_assert <other compile-time options>
◦ %vcs -assert disable_cover <other compile-time options>
• Precedence 2:
• Controlling assertions using Configuration based control using the
hier=<configuration_filename> compile-time option:
◦ %vcs -assert hier=<configuration_filename> <other compile-time
options>
• Precedence 3:
• Controlling assertions using Configuration based control using the
hier=<configuration_filename> runtime option:
• You must pass the -assert enable_hier option at compile time to enable assertion
control at runtime.

◦ %vcs -assert enable_hier <other compile-time options>
◦ %simv -assert hier=<configuration_filename> <other runtime options>
◦ Runtime time 0 statically disabled
• Precedence 4:
• Dynamically enable/disable assertions:
◦ $asserton/$assertoff/$assertkill using source code
◦ $asserton/$assertoff/$assertkill using call command in UCLI
◦ assertion [on/off] {-r} [-module/-scope/-assert] [<pattern>]
• Precedence 5:
• Enabling or disabling assertions dynamically with force
◦ assertion [on/off] {-force} {-r} [-module/-scope/-assert]
[<pattern>]
◦ -force is passed to override the Control

Generating an Assertion Report
Generating an Assertion Report
You can use the -assert report=file_name runtime option to generate a report file with
the specified name.
Use Model
Use the -assert report=file_name runtime option to generate assertion report that are
fired, as shown in the following command:
% vcs <assertion_options>
% simv -assert report=<path/file_name>
If you do not specify the file_name argument, the assert.report report is generated (by
default).
VCS/VCS MX generates the following two assertion reports:
• assert.report.disablelog or file_name.disablelog
The section of the report contains list of assertions that are disabled. If you do not specify
the file_name argument, the assert.report.disablelog report is generated by default.
It also contains generates a report of assertions which are disabled using any of the
following mechanisms.
• Disabled Module Assertions (at compile time)
The section of the report contains assertions that are disabled at the module level through
configuration file using the -assert hier option (including those selected by wildcards)
are captured.
For example:
% vcs -assert hier=<assert.cfg>
% simv -assert report=report3
The configuration file assert.cfg contains -tree top . The report3.disablelog report
contains assertions for the disabled module assertions and its hierarchies at compile time.
The other sections of the report remain empty.
• Assertions disabled using the -assert hier option
The section of the report contains assertions that are disabled by runtime - assert hier
option (including those selected by wildcards).
For example:
% vcs -assert -enable_hier < other_compile_time_options

Generating an Assertion Report
% simv -assert hier=<assert.cfg> -assert report=report4
The configuration file assert.cfg contains -tree top . The report4.disablelog
report contains assertions that are disabled by runtime - assert hier option and its
hierarchies. The other sections of the report remain empty.
• Assertions disabled by dynamic assertion controls
The section of the report contains list of system task ($asserton/off/kills) calls with
time, arguments and source file information that are controlled in the source code or
through UCLI.
• Dynamically disabled assertions at end-of-simulation
The section of the report contains assertions that are disabled using the $assertoff/
kill system task at the end of simulation.
Note:
The -assert disable or -assert disable_assert or -assert
disable_cover that are used at compile time to disable everything are not
dumped in the runtime assertion report file.

Cross-Module References From Verilog to VHDL
and Vice Versa
For MX designs, you might need to access Verilog signals in VHDL scope or VHDL signals
in Verilog scope. To access VHDL signals in Verilog scope, you can use the regular Verilog
language Cross-Module Reference (XMR), whereas to access Verilog signals in VHDL
scope, you need to use the hdl_xmr procedures and tasks.
VCS MX provides the hdl_xmr procedure and $hdl_xmr system task to access Verilog
signals in VHDL scope.
This document briefly describes how to access or traverse cross-module references in MX
designs. The document includes the following sections:
• Using hdl_xmr and $hdl_xmr
• Examples
Using hdl_xmr and $hdl_xmr
The syntax of the hdl_xmr procedure or the $hdl_xmr system task is as follows:
hdl_xmr("source_object", "destination_object", [verbosity]); or
$hdl_xmr("source_object" , "destination_object", [verbosity]);
Here,
source_object is a VHDL signal or Verilog register or net.
destination_object is a VHDL signal or a Verilog register.
verbosity refers to the optional verbosity index, which can be 0 or 1.
For more information, see Chapter “Elaborating the Design” in the VCS/VCS MX User
Guide.

in Verilog scope

entity ent1 is
end entity ent1;

architecture arch of ent1 is
signal count : std_logic_vector(3 downto 0);
signal clk,rst : bit;
process(clk,rst)
if(rst='1') then
count <= (others => '0');
elsif(clk'event and clk='1') then
count <= count + 1;

else
clk <= not clk; wait for 5 ns;
end if;
end process clk_gen;
stimulus : process
rst <= '1';
wait for 2 ns;
rst <= '0';
wait for 30 ns;
wait;

The document explains how to debug conflicting issues or errors in constraints. The
document includes the following sections:
• Introduction
• Reproducing the Conflicting Issue
• Fixing the Conflicting Issues
• Debugging Conflict Using the Interactive Testbench Feature
Introduction
While running a constraint test case, VCS MX or Constraint Solver generates random
stimulus by meeting or by honoring all the given constraint conditions in the test case. In
case if there are no feasible solutions to honor the given constraint conditions, then solver
generates an error message and prints the given problem definition with a minimal set of
constraint conditions that have no solution.
Consider the following test case:
program automatic test;
class cls;
rand bit [7:0] x1, x2, x3;
constraint cons1 {x1 inside {[10:20]};}
constraint cons2 {x2 inside {[100:200]};}
constraint cons3 {(x1 % 2) -> {x3 < 200;}}
constraint cons4 {x2 < 100;}
endclass

initial begin
cls obj = new;
obj.randomize();
end
endprogram

Reproducing the Conflicting Issue
When you compile and run the above test case, VCS MX generates the following conflict
error message:
Among the given four constraint conditions in the test case, solver automatically identifies
the above two conditions (minimal set of conditions) that are having conflict conditions and
prints them in the log.
Reproducing the Conflicting Issue
In these cases of conflicting errors, apart from printing the minimal set of conditions
that cause the conflicting issues, VCS MX also creates or extracts a handy test case
automatically, such as simv.cst/testcases/extracted_r_1_p_2.sv, with a minimal

Reproducing the Conflicting Issue
set of constraints to reproduce the issue in standalone mode to better understand the
conflicting conditions, as shown:
The naming convention for the above message is as follows:
simv.cst/testcases/ // 'simv' is the default binary name;
extracted_r_1_p_2.sv // r_1 represents the first serial randomize
call;
// p_2 represents the partition number that VCS
creates internally
Now, compiling and running the extracted test case reproduces the issue in the standalone
mode. Based on the observed conflicting issues, you need to fix the test case. Once
the extracted test case passes, you can port the changes into the original test case
accordingly.

Fixing the Conflicting Issues
Fixing the Conflicting Issues
Typically, most of the conflicting errors are due to the following test case issues:
• In case of conflicts with rand variables that are connected with multiple conditions,
resolve the conflicting conditions.
• In case of conflicts due to combination of state (non-rand) and rand variables, check
whether the values associated with the state variables are correct (lying in the legal
solution space).
• In case of conflict issues due to state variables only, check the values associated with
state variables as per the given conditions.
In case of complex test case that involves multiple rand variables and complex constraints,
the constraint interactive debugging feature helps to understand the issue more effectively.
For that, you can compile and run the test case with required debug capabilities as follows:
% vcs -sverilog -debug_access+all -kdb -lca
% simv -gui=Verdi
Once simv is loaded into the GUI, create a breakpoint to stop the simulation when the
solver fails due to the conflicting issue.
1. Create a breakpoint to stop the simulation when the solver fails
To create a breakpoint, perform the following steps:
a. In the command prompt, type the following command:

In the Breakpoint Manager window, perform the following steps:

c. In the Class Name field, type *.
d. Choose the Inconsistency as the solver condition (When you select this condition,
the breakpoint is hit when the inconsistent constraints are detected during
randomization).

e. Click Create.

On running the simulation, the following warning message is displayed due to the

3. Click OK.
The Constraint_Dbg window opens with all the required details:
This solver pane or window represents the given constraint problem definition in terms
of partitions (clusters or independent blocks). In case of a conflict, solver automatically
identifies the smaller set of constraints or the particular partition that cause the
conflicting issues and lists all the details under the Inconsistent node. This contains
the list of the variables and the connected constraints that cause the conflicting issue.
From the given example test case, you can notice that the conflict is due to the rand
variable x2 that is connected by two constraint conditions that conflict or contradict
each other.

4. Double-click these constraints to view them directly in the source code (see the figure
below), as shown:
5. To fix the conflicting issue, in general you might need to edit the test case as follows:
a. For conflicting constraints, you need to change or disable them.
b. For rand variables, check and modify the rand_mode property, if required.
c. For state variables, check and change or force the correct value associated with
them.
For these changes, VCS MX provides an Interactive Debug feature that allows you to
modify the constraint problem and proceed with the simulation without any recompilation.
Enabling or Disabling Conflicting Constraints
You can enable or disable the conflicting constraints. For example, you can disable the
inconsistent constraint cons4.
To enable or disable conflicting constraint, perform the following steps:
1. In the Solver pane, select the randomize call.
2. Right-click and select Show in Local View.
3. In the Local pane, select the inconsistent constraint, such as cons4.
4. Right-click and select Set Constraint Mode.
5. Select Off to disable the constraint.

Enabling or Disabling Randomization of Random Variables
You can enable or disable the randomization of the random variables by setting the
rand_mode property On or Off.
To set the rand_mode property, perform the following steps:
1. In the Solver pane, select the randomize call.
2. Right-click and select Show in Local View.
3. In the Local pane, select the random variable.
4. Right-click and select Set Rand Mode.
5. Select the mode as On or Off to enable or disable the randomization variable,
respectively.

Re-Doing the Randomization
When the simulation is already in Constraint Debug mode, you can re-randomize
the modified problem definition and step in the constraint solver mode. After the re-
randomization is complete, the simulation enters the Constraint Debug mode and stop
before the post-randomize call. In addition to the previously observed tabs, another set
of Solver and Relation tabs, namely Solver_R and Relation_R tab are added in the
Constraint_Dbg window to display the re-randomized solved results.
To redo the randomization, perform the following steps:
1. Click the
button to redo the randomization, as shown:
2. You can re-randomize the results in the Split -> Solver pane, where the constraint
cons4 is in gray color (as it is disabled), as shown:
With this by disabling one of the conflicting constraint at runtime itself, you can see or
confirm that the conflicting issue got resolved. From this interactive debug analysis, port
the changes to the original test case to fix the conflicting issue. Thus, constraint interactive
debug analysis helps you to narrow down the issue quickly from solver pane.

Introduction
The following sections describe debugging of simulation failures and mismatches using
Verdi:
• Debugging Simulation Failures
• Debugging Simulation Mismatches

Debugging Simulation Failures
The following sections introduce how to quickly debug simulation failures using some of
the key features of Verdi:
• Trace Drivers and Loads
• Trace Connectivity
• Active Annotation
• Trace the Active Driver
• Trace to Root Cause Automatically
• Demo Videos
Trace Drivers and Loads
The Trace > Driver and Trace > Load options (or their equivalent toolbar icons) allow
you to trace all of the drivers and loads, respectively, that are associated with a selected
signal. These commands can also be accessed by right-clicking a signal in the Source
Code pane.
Trace Connectivity
The Trace > Connectivity option traces the drivers and loads simultaneously. To trace the
connectivity of a signal, highlight a signal, and choose the Trace > Connectivity option
from the main menu or the right-click option.

Chapter 2: Debugging Simulation Failures
Active Annotation
The results of the trace are displayed in the Trace tab of the Message pane in the nTrace
main window.
The Show Next and the Show Previous toolbar icons or the Trace > Show Next and
Trace > Show Previous options allow you to locate the next load and the previous load/
driver respectively, that are associated with a selected signal.
Active Annotation
Active annotation allows you to view simulation results under the corresponding
variable in the Source Code pane. Before using active annotation, you must first load a set
of simulation results in the form of the FSDB file.
Select the Source > Active Annotation option to enable active annotation. The values
associated with each signal (at time 0) are displayed under the signals.
In the nSchema window, use the Schematic > Active Annotation command to enable
active annotation. You can add line coloring annotation using the Schematic > Annotate
in Color option.
After an FSDB file containing the dumped force information is loaded in Verdi, you can
also view the force values in the nSchema window. The forced values are annotated with
the caret "^" character.
In the nWave window, select a signal and use the Search Forward icon on the toolbar to
step through value changes. You can also search backward using the Search Backward
icon.
Parameter Annotation
To view values of parameters as annotation in the nTrace window, select Source >
Parameter Annotation option.
Function Annotation
The signal value in a function can be seen by its source annotation, but to calculate
the values at function calling statement, function annotation can be enabled by clicking
Source > Function Annotation.

Chapter 2: Debugging Simulation Failures
Trace the Active Driver
Trace the Active Driver
You can use the Active Trace right-click option to locate the active driver in the Source
Code pane for the selected signal. Active trace can be performed multiple times until the
cause is located.
To trace the active driver of a signal, right-click the signal and choose the Active Trace
option from the menu. The source code displays the changes to the active driving unit, and
the signal in the driving statement is highlighted. You can continue Active Trace until you
locate the source of a value.
Trace to Root Cause Automatically
In the nTrace window, the root cause of an issue can be traced automatically with one
of these options: Trace This Value or Trace Active X. Select a signal in the Source
Code pane and click the Auto Trace toolbar icon. The Temporal Flow View opens and
automatically performs the trace as per the following commands:
• Trace This Value
: For the current time, if the current value is known.
• Trace Active X
: For the current time, if the current value is unknown.

Debugging Simulation Mismatches
Using Verdi, you can locate the cause of the simulation mismatch using the nCompare
window. The nCompare window compares the simulation results stored in FSDB dump
files using flexible, user-specified comparison criteria. The nCompare window provides the
following features:
• Compares all the selected signals by time sequence, therefore finding the design error
with minimum comparison time.
• Displays the mismatch results in the nCompare window. Sorts the mismatch results in
the nCompare window by simulation time or design hierarchy.
• The nCompare window is tightly integrated with the nWave window for easy viewing of
the mismatch results in the nWavewindow.
In the nWave window, choose the Tools > nCompare option to open the nCompare
window. To start the waveform comparison, choose the Comparison > Run option or click
the Run icon on the toolbar of the nCompare window to start the waveform comparison.
After the waveform comparison is completed, the nCompare window displays the
mismatches on the result window. To view the mismatches by time sequence, choose the
View > View By Time option.
You can use the debug features mentioned in the Debugging Simulation Failures section
to debug simulation mismatches.

Overview
This document describes the various switches, options, or utilities available with VCS that
can be used to extract a test case from an existing environment. Based on your scenario
and requirement, you can select any of the available utilities to generate a list of source
files, environment variables, command-line options, testbench, and so on appropriately.

Prerequisites
An existing DUT environment and a VCS-licensed tool.

Use Model
The following sections describe the various switches, options, or utilities available with
VCS that can be used to extract a test case from an existing environment:
• Generating a List of Source Files
• Generating a List of Environment Variables
• Generating a List of Command-Line Options
• Capturing a Verilog Design to a File
Generating a List of Source Files
To generate a file that contains a list of absolute path names to the source files of all the
module definitions in a design or an IP block, use the following option:
-bom top-level_module -bfl filename
Note that the -bom option must be accompanied by the -bfl option.
The argument for the -bom option is the module name of the top-level module in the
design or the IP block.
The argument for the -bfl option is the filename that contains the list. VCS MX adds the
.bflextension to the filename you specify.
If the module definition is in a Verilog source file in a Verilog library directory, the name of
the directory and the source file is included in the path names.
If the module definition is in a Verilog library file, the path name of the library file is
included in the list.
Following is an example of the output pathname file:
/file_system/design_group/LIBDIR/dev.v
/file_system/user_name/design1/top.v
/file_system/design_group/libfile

Chapter 3: Use Model
Generating a List of Environment Variables
Generating a List of Environment Variables
To dump all the environment variables that are set in the terminal before starting the
compilation and the simulation process into a log file, use the -diag env option. This log
file can be used to debug the environment related issues when the verification setup is
complex and multiple nested scripts are used.
To dump all the environment variables, use the -diag env option with vlogan/vcs
command line or simv command line.
Syntax
Following is the syntax for -diag env option:
• % vlogan -diag env
It dumps all the environment variables in the vlogan_env_diag_<pid>.log log file that
is generated in the AN.DB directory.
• % vcs -diag env
It dumps all the environment variables in the vcs_env_diag_<pid>.log log file that is
generated in the simv.daidirdirectory.
• % simv -diag env
It dumps all the environment variables in the simv_env_diag_<pid>.log log file that is
generated in the current working directory.
Generating a List of Command-Line Options
To log or record the VCS command-line options, you can use one of the following options:
• The -E echo simulation switch
This switch displays all the user specified compilation options with other default
compilation options used when simv executable file is created.
For example:
% vcs -sverilog -l comp.log test.v -o test.simv
% test.simv -E echo > vcs_switches.log
% cat vcs_switches.log
-Mcfl= -pipe -m32 -O -I

This switch does not run the simulation and other simulation options cannot be used with
it. With the UUM flow, this switch displays the VCS elaboration command-line only and the
analysis steps vlogan and vhdlan switches are not reflected.
• The -l <filename> compilation switch
This switch stores the VCS compilation messages in a log file with all the vcs
compilation options at the top of the specified file name. If -R option is also used, it
runs the simulation in one step, that is, runs the simv executable after linking and
-loption captures the compilation and simulation options in the same log file.
For example:
% vcs -sverilog -l comp.log test.v -o test.simv -R
% cat comp.log
Command: vcs -sverilog -l comp.log test.v -o test.simv -R
Parsing design file 'test.v'
Top Level Modules:
test
No TimeScale specified
Starting vcs inline pass
../test.simv up to date
Command: ./test.simv -a comp.log
In this example, the lines followed by Command are the VCS command-line options used for
compiling and simulating the design.
Capturing a Verilog Design to a File
The-Xman=28 or the -Xmangle=28 compilation switch can be used to capture an entire
Verilog design into a file. It produces a jumbled version of the input source files by
changing the variable names to words from the list and generates the tokens.v output
file. The tokens.v file contains original source file names and line numbers appended
to each module header along with a comprehensive statistics about the contents of the
original source. The tokens.v file can be used as an aid to debug compilation issues and
simulation issues encountered in the design.

Overview
This document describes the differences between post-processing debug and interactive
debug in the following sections:
• Post-Processing Debug
• Interactive Debug
Post-Processing Debug Versus Interactive Debug
Y-2026.03-SP2

Post-Processing Debug
Post-processing debug mode allows you to debug the design using a database. In post-
processing mode, Fast Signal Data Base (FSDB) design database file is created during
the simulation, and all the instance/signal values are dumped into this file. Post-processing
debug is recommended for debugging DUTs. In post-processing debug mode, you can use
Verdi to:
• View design hierarchy
• Debug source code
• View waveforms
• Compare waveforms
• Trace drivers and loads
• View schematic and path schematic
Post-Processing Debug Versus Interactive Debug
Y-2026.03-SP2

Interactive Debug
Interactive debug mode allows you to setup and run the simulation interactively in real-
time using a compiled Verilog, VHDL, or mixed design. In this mode, you can use various
commands to control the simulation interactively. Interactive debug is recommended for
Testbench debug. In interactive debug mode, you can use Verdi to:
• Control the simulation using the following breakpoints:
◦ Line breakpoint
◦ Event breakpoint
◦ Constraint breakpoint
◦ Method breakpoint
◦ Thread breakpoint
• Advance the simulation further using the following features:
◦ Step
◦ Next
◦ Step by thread
◦ Step by testbench
◦ Step into Solver
• Perform reverse debug using the following features:
◦ Debug with running the simulation backwards
• View design hierarchy
• Debug source code
• View waveforms
• Execute Tcl commands
• Trace drivers and loads
• View schematics and path schematics

1. VCS Two-Step Flow or Three-Step Flow 4
Introduction 4
Deciding on Two-Step Flow or Three-Step Flow 5

VCS Two-Step Flow or Three-Step Flow
The document explains the simulation flows supported by VCS MX. The document
includes the following sections:
• Introduction
• Deciding on Two-Step Flow or Three-Step Flow
Introduction
VCS/VCS MX supports the following two major flows:
• Two-step flow is supported for Verilog or SystemVerilog users. The two-step flow
involves the following two steps:
◦ Compilation – This is the first step to simulate your design. In this step, VCS/VCS
MX builds the instance hierarchy and generates a simv binary executable. This
binary executable is later used for simulation.
◦ Simulation – In this step, VCS/VCS MX runs the simulation using the simv binary
executable generated during compilation step.
Note:
For information on these steps, refer to the VCS User Guide.
• Three-step flow can be used for mixed-language. VHDL users and even Verilog users
can opt for this flow. The three-step flow is also known as Unified Use Model (UUM)
flow. Simulating a design using the three-step flow involves the following three steps:
• Analysis – This is the first step to simulate your design. In this step, you analyze your
VHDL, Verilog using vhdlan or vlogan commands accordingly.
• Elaboration – In this step, using the intermediate files generated during analysis, VCS
MX builds the instance hierarchy and generates a binary executable simv.
• Simulation – In this step, VCS/VCS MX runs the simulation using the simv binary
executable generated during compilation step.
VCS Two-Step Flow or Three-Step Flow
Y-2026.03-SP2

Chapter 1: VCS Two-Step Flow or Three-Step Flow
Deciding on Two-Step Flow or Three-Step Flow
Note:
For information on these steps, refer to the VCS User Guide.
Deciding on Two-Step Flow or Three-Step Flow
The following are the guidelines based on the topologies that help you to decide whether
two-step flow is suitable or three-step flow is suitable:
• The two-step flow has easy use model to adapt and can be used by Verilog or
SystemVerilog users. User just need to write one compilation command to compile the
design and one simulation command to simulate using VCS only.
• The three-step flow can be used for MX designs (with VHDL, Verilog/SystemVerilog
units), or Pure Verilog designs, or Pure VHDL designs.
• When you analyze a design, VCS MX stores the intermediate files in a design library,
also called as a logical library. This logical library is pointed to a physical library and the
mapping is present in the synopsys_sim.setup file. The three-step flow allows you to
use multiple logical libraries for your design when you want to create multiple $unit
compilation scope.

Binding a Verilog Module in MX Designs 5

The bind construct can be used to specify one or more instances of a module without
modifying the code of the target. This bind construct can also be used for interfaces,
program or checker modules. For more details, see IEEE SystemVerilog LRM Std.
1800™-2012.
The bind directive can be specified in any of the following:
• A module
• An interface
• A compilation unit
This document briefly describes how to bind your Verilog and VHDL design. You can bind
a Verilog module either in pure Verilog designs or in MX designs.
The document includes the following sections:
• Binding a Verilog Module in Pure Verilog Designs
• Binding a Verilog Module in MX Designs
Binding a Verilog Module in Pure Verilog Designs
For pure Verilog design, the bind construct for Verilog targets can be used anywhere
within your Verilog source file as shown in the following example. In this example, the bind
construct creates an inst instance inside top.dut.
File: test.v
module top;
dut dut_inst();
bind dut child inst(); //child instantiated in DUT using bind
construct

1. Overview 4
VCS Unreachability Analysis (UNR) 4
Use Model 5
VC Formal Coverage Analyzer (VCF FCA) 9

Overview
You can either use VCS UNR or VCF FCA based on the capabilities that each tool offers.
This document provides you an overview of the capabilities supported by VCS UNR and
VCF FCA. You can choose to use either UNR or FCA based on your requirements.
This section consists of the following subsections:
• VCS Unreachability Analysis (UNR)
• VC Formal Coverage Analyzer (VCF FCA)
VCS Unreachability Analysis (UNR)
The unreachability analysis (UNR) flow of VCS focuses on finding the unreachable code
in a design using formal techniques. You can use this flow to complement the simulation-
based code coverage driven verification technique. The UNR flow of VCS provides the
ability to:
• Import a simulation coverage database.
• Perform formal checks on the uncovered items from the coverage database. Determine
if there are any coverage targets that are impossible to reach with any set of input
vectors.
• Save the unreachable items in the form of an exclusion file. You can use this exclusion
file in conjunction with the simulation coverage database to generate the final coverage
report.
You can also run VCS UNR without importing a simulation coverage database. In this
case, the analysis is performed on the coverage goals extracted for the entire DUT.
However, since the technology underneath is formal verification, which is performance
intensive, it is recommended to execute with a simulation coverage database.
The main advantage of VCS UNR flow is that, you can invoke UNR using the simulation
coverage command line with additional switches and requires minimal setup time. This
method helps you find the dead code in the design without knowing the formal verification
techniques.

Chapter 1: Overview
VC Formal Coverage Analyzer (VCF FCA)
For VHDL designs, UNR supports the following coverage metrics:
• Line
• Condition
VC Formal Coverage Analyzer (VCF FCA)
The VC Formal Coverage Analyzer (VCF FCA) is an application of the VC Formal platform
that finds coverage properties in a design and automatically tests them for reachability.
VCS UNR uses VCF FCA in the background to perform unreachability analysis. However,
the benefits that VCS UNR provides is that, it is not required to be aware of the formal
technology. You can simply use the -unr option as a plug-in solution to automatically find
dead code in your design.
VCF FCA can work on its own, without VCS. When used this way, you can work with
the Formal tool and use formal debugging methods. These include complexity analysis,
interactive snip points, setting constraints, and viewing traces for goals that are covered.
The VCF FCA GUI makes it simple to use these debugging tools.

Conclusion 8

The document explains how to debug constraints and distribution issues. The document
includes the following sections:
• Introduction
• Constraints Distribution Analysis
• Conclusion
Introduction
To meet functional coverage goals, you must generate the stimulus with all possible
combinations. Sometimes, it might be important to generate a specific random stimulus
with more weightage than compared to the entire solution space. Sometimes, there might
be a discrepancy between users’ expectations and solver results. This document helps
you to debug constraints and distribution issues.
Constraints Distribution Analysis
The Distribution and Histogram feature of constraint testbench interactive debug helps
you to visualize the random value distribution from histogram diagrams. This helps you to
understand the generated distribution pattern quickly. It also allows you to provide hooks to
change constraints to get the desired distribution easily, if required.
For example, consider the following code snippet:
class cls;
rand bit enable;
rand bit [7:0] addr;
constraint cons1 {addr inside {10, [21:25]};}
endclass
Here, the rand variable addr selects any one of the value from the given range with equal
probability. You can see the random variable distribution in the GUI debugging.

Chapter 1: Viewing the Random Variable Distribution
Constraints Distribution Analysis
Compile the test case with the required debug capability and load simv into the GUI as
follows:
% vcs -sverilog test.v -debug_access+all -kdb -lca
% simv -gui=Verdi
Once simv is loaded into the GUI, step into the constraint solver.
To perform distribution re-randomization, perform the following steps:
1. Make sure that there are no conflict issues in the test case, click to step into the
solver pane as shown:
The Constraints Solver pane opens as shown:
In the Solver pane window, you could observe the initial value range specified for the
random variable (addr). From the static analysis, the solver computes the feasible
solution space available for the random variable and displays next to the initial value.
2. To observe the random value distribution, click , as shown:

Chapter 1: Viewing the Random Variable Distribution
Constraints Distribution Analysis
The Distribution Randomize window opens, as shown:
3. In the distribution randomize box, specify the number of re-randomizations. The default
value is 100 and the valid number must be between 2 to 99999.
4. Select the Accumulate Mode option to accumulate the results of the previous
randomization data. This option is enabled by default.
5. Click the OK button to perform the distribution re-randomization.
The randomization is performed for the specified number of times and then the
simulation is stopped in the Solver pane. The Constraint_Dbg window displays the
Dist_R and Histogram_R tabs, as shown:
6. To check the distribution of a particular variable, select the variable and right-click it to
select the Show Histogram option.
The distribution of values for the variable is drawn as a histogram in the Histogram_R
tab. The count on the bar shows the number of times the particular value got generated.
The value of 0 means that either there is no hit or that the value is not part of the solution
space.

Chapter 1: Viewing the Random Variable Distribution
Constraints Distribution Analysis
Modifying the Distribution by Adding a New Constraint
For instance, if you are looking for a different distribution pattern, such as 50% of the

1. Analyzing Constraints Timeout Issues 4
Introduction 4
Reproducing the Timeout Issue 4
Analyzing the Timeout Issue 5

This document help you to understand how to reproduce or analyze the timeout issues.
This document includes the following sections:
• Introduction
• Reproducing the Timeout Issue
• Analyzing the Timeout Issue
Introduction
When running a constraint test case, VCS or Constraint Solver generates random stimulus
by honoring all the given constraint conditions that are specified in the test case. In case
of very complex or huge number of conditions, sometimes the solver results in a timeout
failure.
Reproducing the Timeout Issue
In case of timeout, VCS creates or extracts a handy test case automatically, such as
simv.cst/testcases/extracted_r_1_p_1_timeout.sv with the set of constraints that
reproduces the timeout issue to better understand the issue in a standalone test case.
Y-2026.03-SP2

Chapter 1: Analyzing Constraints Timeout Issues
Analyzing the Timeout Issue
The naming convention for the test case is as follows:
simv.cst/ // simv is the default binary file
created
extracted_r_1_p_1_timeout.sv // r_1 represents the first serial
randomize call
// p_1 represents the partition number
that VCS creates internally
You should be able to reproduce the timeout issue locally in the standalone environment
by running this extracted test case.
If the automatically extracted test case does not reproduce the timeout behavior, perform
the following:
1. Comment out the use of static seed in the extracted test case as shown:
2. Run the test case with multiple random seeds as follows:
% simv +ntb_random_seed_automatic
Sometimes, this helps you to reproduce the timeout issue.
Analyzing the Timeout Issue
Sometimes due to complex constraints, solver might result into timeout issues with a
specific random seed. In such cases, you can change the random seed to pass the test
case. A random seed is an input to the solver that might change the solver execution path
or flow. This might help you to get the random stimulus and avoid the timeout issues.
You should run the test case by changing the seed automatically or by changing it
manually as follows:
% simv +ntb_random_seed_automatic // sets the seed automatically;
% simv +ntb_random_seed=123456 // set the seed manually;
Y-2026.03-SP2

Chapter 1: Analyzing Constraints Timeout Issues
Analyzing the Timeout Issue
If you continue to see the timeout issue, as mentioned in the above timeout log, either
run the extracted test case or run the original test case using the following runtime solver
diagnostic options to get more details regarding the timeout behavior:
• +ntb_enable_solver_diagnostics=1 or
• +ntb_enable_solver_diagnostics=2
The +ntb_enable_solver_diagnostics=1 option helps you to understand the variables
that cause most of the slowdown or the timeout behavior, as shown:
The +ntb_enable_solver_diagnostics=2 option helps you to understand the operators
or constraint in the given problem definition that results in timeout issues, as shown:
For example, you might see these messages due to the use of complex constraints with
non-linear arithmetic operators or due to the use of heavy bit-selects or bit-wise operations
on the rand variable that might cause this timeout behavior.
By following these key messages from the diagnostic logs and by slightly changing the test
case, you can avoid these timeout issues. Even after making these changes if the issue
persists, contact vcs_support@synopsys.com for further assistance.

1. Controlling VCS Error Messages 4
2. Controlling Error Messages Using Compile-Time Options 5
3. Controlling Error Messages Using a Configuration File 6
4. Upgrading Lint and Warning Messages to Error Messages 7
5. Downgrading Error Messages to Warning Messages 8

You can control error, warning, and lint messages in VCS MX in the following two ways:
• Using the -error, -suppress, +lint, and +warn compile-time options.
• Using a configuration file.
This document explains how to control the error and warning messages in VCS MX. It
also explains how to upgrade and downgrade the messages. The document includes the
following sections:
• Controlling Error Messages Using Compile-Time Options
• Controlling Error Messages Using a Configuration File
• Upgrading Lint and Warning Messages to Error Messages
• Downgrading Error Messages to Warning Messages

Controlling Error Messages Using Compile-Time
Options
The -error, -suppress, +lint, and +warn options control the error, warning and lint
messages. Using these options, you can perform the following:
• Disable the display of any error, warning, or lint messages.
• Disable the display of specific messages.
• Limit the display of specific messages to a maximum number that you specify.
To control the display of specific messages, you need the message IDs. A message ID is
the character string in a message between the square brackets [ ]. For example, consider
the following:
Here, the message ID is MFACF.
The new compile-time options for controlling the messages and their syntax are as follows:
-error=[no]message_ID[:max_number],|none|all
-error=all,noWarn_ID|noLint_ID
+warn=[no]message_ID[:max_number],|none|all
+lint=[no]message_ID[:max_number],|none|all
-suppress[=message_ID,]
Note:
The -error option is also a simulation option.

Controlling Error Messages Using a
Configuration File
Using a configuration file, you can control the lint, warning, and error messages that VCS
displays by specifying the following entities:
• Source file name
• Module name
• Design subhierarchy
You can control these messages with entries in a configuration file that you can specify
with the following compile-time option:
-msg_config=message_configuration_file_name
In the message configuration file, the basic rule is as follows:
Each configuration entry is enclosed in braces or curly brackets { }.
For example:
{ +warn=noTFIPC;
+file=$VCS_HOME/vmm.sv;
}
This entry disables the warning message with the TFIPC message ID in the vmm.sv source
file for the VCS installation.

Upgrading Lint and Warning Messages to Error
Messages
To upgrade lint and warning messages to error messages, use the -error=arguments
message operation command in the configuration entry. The arguments that you can enter
are as follows:
+lint=all -error=all
Upgrades all the lint and warning messages to error messages. You must specify the
commands in the same order specified in the following example:
% vlogan -sverilog test.sv +lint=all -error=all
-error=ID1,ID2
A comma separated list of lint and warning message IDs that upgrades the warning
messages to error messages.
For example:
-error=CDUB,MFACF
Here, the list of IDs upgrades the lint message with the CDUB ID and the warning message
with the MFACF ID to error messages.

Downgrading Error Messages to Warning
Messages
To downgrade error messages to warning messages, you can use a message operation
command in the configuration entry that begins with the following:
-error=noID1,noID2
Here, the comma-separated list is the list of error message IDs preceded by the keyword
no.
For example:
-error=noURMI,noETMFCB

Introduction
The Coverage Technology Reference Manual contains list of coverage commands that
you can use for your reference while using VCS to collect your coverage data. This
manual is not a comprehensive guide for coverage technology and should be used in
conjunction with the Coverage Technology User Guide.
If you are using the VCS Online Documentation, click this link Coverage Technology User
Guide to view in the HTML interface. If you are using the PDF interface, see cov_ug.pdf to
view the PDF document.
The chapter contains the following sections:
• Operations When You Compile or Simulate
• Merging VCS Results for Regressions

Operations When You Compile or Simulate
There are many operations related to generating coverage metrics that you can perform
while compiling or simulating your design. These include specifying coverage for libraries
and cells, naming intermediate data files, using glitch suppression, and so on.
You can also control the scope of the coverage compilation using either pragmas or a
-cm_hier configuration file.
Using Coverage Metrics Files and Directories
When you use the -cm compile-time option, VCS creates the

Operations When You Compile or Simulate
During compilation, VCS writes data files about the design in the snps/coverage/
db/design directory (for Verilog and VHDL).
During simulation, VCS writes intermediate data files (also called test files) that record the
coverage results from the simulation in the snps/coverage/db/testdata directory (for
Verilog and for VHDL).
Each directory under testdata contains all the coverage data for the test. The base name
of the test is the name of the directory.
To see how to select names for the coverage data files, see Naming Intermediate Data
Files. You might want to do so if you plan multiple simulations with different stimuli and you
want to see the coverage results from the different simulations.
Also during simulation, VCS writes design information into the simv.vdb/snps/
coverage/db/ directory. These files are compatible with all the supported platforms.
For example, if you have VCS compile and monitor for coverage using the Solaris
platform, you can display coverage information using the RHEL32 platform.
See the release notes (available through the online HTML documentation system) for a list
of supported platforms.
The simv.vdb directory is named after the simv executable file. If you name the simulation
executable file something else with the -o compile-time option, VCS names the coverage
metrics database directory after the name you assigned to the simulation executable.
For example, if you name the executable, mysimv, as follows:
% vcs source.v -cm fsm -o mysimv
VCS creates the mysimv.vdb directory instead of the simv.vdb directory.

Operations When You Compile or Simulate
When you use the -cm_dir option at compile time, the name and location of this directory
is hard-coded into the simv executable, so there is no need to use the option at runtime to
specify this directory.
Using the -cm_dir option at runtime specifies a different location for the test files that VCS
writes at runtime.
If you specify a different location for the intermediate data files at runtime, you must
specify that directory's location using the -dir option to URG when generating reports, all
of the directories can be listed as well with one -dir option. For example, -dir db1.vdb
db2.vdb.
To summarize when to use -cm_dir and for what purpose:
• At compile-time, to specify a different name or location for the coverage database
directory (simv.vdb) that is created during compilation.
• If you move the coverage database directory or the binary executable to a new location
after VCS creates it during compilation, use the -cm_dir option at runtime, to specify
the path for the coverage database directory .
• If you invoke your binary executable from a different location, then use the -cm_dir
option at runtime to specify the path for the coverage database directory.
The following command lines illustrate these different possibilities:
% vcs -cm line -cm_dir /net/design1/my_cov_info source.v

Operations When You Compile or Simulate
If you want to specify both arguments, include the plus delimiter (+) between the two

Naming Intermediate Data Files
By default, when VCS monitors for any type of coverage, it records the results in
intermediate
data filesnaming
intermediate data files named “test” with various extensions, as follows:
test filesnaming
•
test.line file
line.verilog.data.xml for line coverage
•
test.fsm file
fsm.verilog.data.xml for FSM coverage
•
test.cond file
cond.verilog.data.xml for condition coverage
•
test.tgl file
tgl.verilog.data.xml for toggle coverage
•
test.path filetest.branch file
branch.verilog.data.xml for branch coverage
By default, VCS writes these files in the./simv.vdb/snps/coverage/db/testdata
directory. URG reads these files to show coverage results.
If you store the results of multiple simulations in the same directory, you will want to have a
different name for these intermediate data files directory.
For example, you might want to apply different stimuli in different simulations and have
intermediate data files with different names so that you can compare coverage results
using URG.
To specify a different name for the intermediate data files, you can do either of the
following:
• Include the
-cm_name-cm_name[-]
-cm_name option at compile-time. For example:
% vcs source.v -cm line -cm_name testm
This command line compiles into the executable the name that the executable will
use when it writes the intermediate data files. After simulation, the simv.vdb/snps/
coverage/db/testm directory contains the line.verilog.data.xml file.
• Include the -cm_name option at runtime, for example:
% simv -cm line -cm_name testm
You can override the directory name (testm) that you have provided during compilation
by providing a different directory name with the simv command line options (say testn).
You cannot use the option -cm_name to specify a different location for these files. Use the
-cm_dir option instead to have simv place the generated files in a different directory.

Merging VCS Results for Regressions
Merging VCS Results for Regressions
URG automatically merges the results from the intermediate data files that VCS writes
during more than one simulation of your design.
This section describes four methods for VCS for running the regressions to produce
merged coverage results. In most of these methods, you only need to compile for
coverage once and then run multiple simulations, either sequentially or in parallel.
You can use either different names for intermediate data files in the same directory or
create different directories for these intermediate data files and then inform URG where to
look for them.
Method 1: Build the simv executable once, then simulate three times sequentially
using the same testbench, but different inputs.
There are a number of ways to use the same testbench in different simulations with
different input stimulus values. One common way is to use the $readmemb system task to
read values from a file into the elements of a memory.
Then for each simulation, you change the contents of the data file specified in the system
task. VCS reads this data at runtime and you make no changes to the system task.
Therefore, you only need to compile for coverage one time.
The values in the memory elements control the execution of your design and exercise
different parts of the design during the different simulations.
When the simulations are over, you can see the total and merged coverage from all three
simulations.
This procedure is as follows:
1. Compile for coverage:
% vcs -cm coverage_arguments \
additional_options_and_source_files
This command line instructs VCS to compile for the selected types of coverage. VCS
creates the simv.vdb directory in the current directory. In this directory, it creates the
snps/coverage/db directory.
2. Start the first simulation, specifying a name for the intermediate data files that
associates them with the first simulation:
% simv -cm_name test1 -cm coverage_arguments \
During simulation, VCS writes the line.verilog.data.xml, fsm.verilog.data.xml
intermediate data files in the ./simv.vdb/snps/coverage/db/testdata/test1
directory.

execute different $readmemb system tasks depending on the runtime option you use for
each parallel simulation.

Merging VCS Results for Regressions
The +one, +two, and +three options are used for the $test$plusargs system tasks in
the testbench.
3. Run URG once again specifying the name of the directory and the name of the report
files.
% urg -dir /net/design1/oursimv.vdb -dbname \
mergedir/merged
Method 4: Build three different simv executables and simulate sequentially or in
parallel.
To simulate sequentially, the procedure is as follows:
1. Compile three times for coverage using different testbenches, specifying an alternative
name for the simv executable. By doing this, you are also specifying an alternative
name for the simv.vdb coverage metrics database:
% vcs -o simv1 test.v -cm coverage_arguments \
additional_options_and_source_files

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
% vcs -o simv2 test.v -cm coverage_arguments \
additional_options_and_source_files

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
% vcs -o simv3 test.v -cm coverage_arguments \
additional_options_and_source_files
When VCS does these compilations for coverage, it creates three coverage metrics
directories in the current directory: simv1.vdb, simv2.vdb, and simv3.vdb.
In step 1, all three tests use different stimulus. However, they all use the
same source files from the same directories:
◦ Identical hierarchy
◦ No differences with +define or `include
◦ Source files are passed identically
If some source files are passed as a library in one design and not in the other, then
use cm_libs.
2. Simulate the executables either sequentially or in parallel.

SystemVerilog Support for Code Coverage
3. Run URG telling it the name and location of the three directories that you created and
the name of the report files:
% urg -dir simv1.vdb simv2.vdb simv3.vdb -dbname \
mergedir/merged
The report files are generated in the urgReport directory.
Merging Multiple Coverage Databases
The preferred method to merge different coverage databases is to provide the coverage
database, which contains code coverage, as the first one to URG.
For example, assuming that the design is not changed between the multiple runs:
1. First run (compile+simulation) contains the assert coverage alone.
2. Second run (compile+simulation) contains the Code coverage alone.
Use the following URG command to merge multiple coverage databases:
% urg -dir ./codeCov/simv.vdb -dir ./assert/simv.vdb \
-dbname merged

-cm line|cond|fsm|tgl|branch|assert
Specifies compiling for the specified type or types of coverage. The arguments specifies
the types of coverage:
line — Compile for line or statement coverage.
cond — Compile for condition coverage.
fsm — Compile for FSM coverage.

tgl — Compile for toggle coverage.
branch — Compile for branch coverage.
assert — Compile for SystemVerilog assertion coverage.
If you want VCS to compile for more than one type of coverage, use the plus (+) character
as a delimiter between arguments, for example:
-cm line+cond+fsm+tgl-cm_assert_hier-cm_assert_hier[cm_assert_hier]
-cm_assert_hier filename
Limits assertion coverage to the module instances specified in filename. This option
applies to assertion coverage only that is when you use -cm assert option. If this option
is not used, coverage is implemented on the whole design. You can either enable or
disable:
• Assertions in a module or in a hierarchy
• An individual assertion
You should use the -cm_dir or -cm_name options for renaming the coverage database.
The option -cm_assert_hier is not supported for mixed language
simulations.
The <filename> can be a text file and you can specify the file name for
the <filename>.

-assert <assertion_name> or -assert <assertion_hierarchical_name>
If assertion_name is provided, VCS disables the assertions based on wildcard matching
of the name in the full design. If assertion_hierarchical_name is provided, VCS disables
the assertions based on wildcard matching of the name in the particular hierarchy given.
-assert my_assert
Disables all assertions with name my_assert in the full design.
-assert A*
Disables all assertions whose name starts with A in the full design.
-assert *
Disables all assertions in the full design.

-assert top.INST2.A
Disables all assertions whose names start with A in the hierarchy top.INST2. If assertions
whose name starts with A exists in inner scopes under top.INST2, they are not disabled.
This command has affect on assertions only in scope top.INST2.
+assert <assertion_name> or +assert <assertion_hierarchical_name>
If assertion_name is provided, VCS enables the assertions based on wildcard matching
of the name in the full design. If assertion_hierarchical_name is provided, then VCS
enables the assertions based on wildcard matching of the name in the given hierarchy.
+assert my_assert
Enables all assertions with name my_assert in the full design.
+assert A*
Enables all assertions whose name starts with A in the full design.
+assert *
Enables all assertions in the full design.
+assert top.INST2.A
Enables assertion A in the hierarchy top.INST2.
+tree <module_instance_name> or +tree<assertion_hierarchical_name>
If module_instance_name is provided, VCS enables assertions in the specified
module instance and all module instances hierarchically under that instance. If
assertion_hierarchical_name is provided, VCS enables the specified SystemVerilog
assertion. Wildcard characters can also be used for specifying the hierarchy.
+tree top.inst1
Enables the assertions in module instance top.inst1 and all the assertions in the module
instances under this instance.
+tree top.INST*
Enables all assertions from all the instances whose names start with INST under module
top.
