Specifying Stable Names for Conditions in a Design
Code coverage automatically finds conditions in a design and monitors whether they are
covered in simulation runs. These objects are identified in an ad hoc manner, depending
on the type of object. For example, signals in toggle coverage and machines in finite state
machine (FSM) coverage can be identified by signal names. Statements, branches, and
conditions are identified by line numbers. Conditions are identified by a sequence number
within a given module (for example, 1st, 2nd, and 3rd).

The following are the two categories of conditions:
• Conditions with stable names — An object name is stable, if it is not sensitive to
unrelated changes. For example, the name of a signal for toggle or FSM coverage is
stable. The condition name can be changed by changing the signal name itself.

title: 0.00 1 100 test::cg_def::SHAPE{abm=2} (for cgd1, cgd3 and cgd5)
text:
ns:
• Conditions with stable names — An object name is stable, if it is not sensitive to
unrelated changes. For example, the name of a signal for toggle or FSM coverage is
stable. The condition name can be changed by changing the signal name itself.
• Conditions with unstable names — Object names that are sensitive to unrelated
changes in the design are unstable. For example, any condition whose name depends
on a source line number has an unstable name, since even adding a comment can
change the name.
This feature allows you to specify stable names for conditions, whose names are unstable,
by default.
Naming a Condition in a Module
You can use the coverage name <condition name> pragma to name a condition in a
module. For example:
//coverage name a1
if (a || (b && c))
In the example, the condition name a1 is assigned to the statement if (a || (b && c)) .
Any conditions found in the statement can be addressed starting with a1, rather than with
a sequence number in the module or source line number. The pragma should be inserted
immediately before the condition.
Note that the naming convention for the coverage name pragma is restricted to the
following:
• All lower and uppercase characters
• All digits
• Underscore
• Dollar symbol
• Square brackets [ ]
• Dot
Advantages of Assigning Stable Names for Conditions
Assigning stable names for conditions is useful for excluding continuous conditions
and FSvectors specified in exclusion files (el files) for condition coverage, see section
Generating El File for Condition Coverage for more information on el files.
You can exclude conditions and vectors using the condids given in el file, which is
generated by Verdi. However, the names of conditions and vectors in that file are

sequence numbers generated by an incrementing counter. For example, condition 1,
condition 2, and so on.
An issue in this approach is that if a new condition is added, then all the sequence
numbers for conditions below the addition are invalidated. Where you once had conditions
with IDs 5, 6, 7, the IDs are now 6, 7, and 8. Any file that contains a condition to ‘exclude
condition 6’ is now excluding the incorrect one.
If you assign a stable name to a condition, then that name will be shown in any coverage
reports (and available through UCAPI).
Assigning stable names for conditions is accomplished by providing tags in the source and
generating an .el file using Verdi for condition coverage metric. This metric will contain the
stable names and excluded vectors in the generated file.
Generating El File for Condition Coverage
If you use Verdi to generate the el file, the dumped file contains the stable name for
tagged conditions instead of the Integer IDs.
While applying the el file to your design, if the module or instance checksum has
changed, then only the conditions with given stable names are considered for exclusion.
The remaining non-stable IDs are ignored in URG and are under review in Verdi.
The auto_stablefile.el file is generated when you specify the -cond ids option in
the urg command line. In this el file, all the condition exclusions are commented. You can
uncomment any condition exclusion as required.
Specifying Tags in the Source
This section explains how tags are specified in the source and how condition names are
derived from these tags.
Condition and Sub-condition
//coverage name a1
if (a || (b && c)) {
…
}
The top-level condition is a || (b && c) . It is broken down by code coverage into two
terms. Its name is a1:
a || (b && c) Condition a1

There is also a sub-condition with two terms, named a1.1:
b && c Condition a1.1
Specifying Multiple Conditions in a Statement
A statement might contain more than one independent condition.
//coverage name mycond
x <= (a || (b && c)) ? ( (d && (e || f)) ? 1'b1 : 1'b0 ) : 1'b1;
There are two conditions, (a || (b && c)) and (d && (e || f)) in the example. Both
the conditions are part of the same statement, but there is only one name pragma.
VCS assigns names based on the name. The first condition is named as mycond:
a || (b && c) Condition mycond
b && c Condition mycond.1
The second condition is named as mycond.2:
d && (e || f) Condition mycond.2
e || f Condition mycond.3
If there were additional conditions, then they would be named as mycond.<serial
number of condition on the line> . For example, mycond.2, mycond.3, and so on.
This additional naming is valid only for one statement.
Specifying Multiple Statements in a Line
If a single source line contains multiple statements, then only the first statement is named
by a preceding pragma. For example:
//coverage name a2
x <= (a || b) ? 1'b0 : 1'b1; y = (c && d) ? 1'b0 : 1'b1;
a || b Condition a2

There is no name for the second condition c && d , since it occurs in another statement
that has no pragma preceding it. If you want to assign a name to c && d , then you must
place the statement on a separate line:
//coverage name a2
x <= (a || b) ? 1'b0 : 1'b1;
//coverage name a3
y = (c && d) ? 1'b0 : 1'b1;
a || b Condition a2
c && d Condition a3

In the URG reports, condition ID numbers are shown if the -cond ids option is specified.
These appear inlined with the condition coverage reports. For example, in URG, you can
view the following:

You can use the covdb_get_annotation(condObj, "id") to get the stable name from
the condition ID handle.
Limitations With Stable Names for Conditions
The following are the limitations of this functionality:
• The support for stable names is not available for VHDL conditions. It is available only
for Verilog conditions.
• There should be no other lines (even blank lines) between the condition statement line
and the pragma line.
The stable name for condition cannot have a period (.) character in it; it is reserved for
condition coverage naming scheme for sub- conditions.
You do not need to compile the entire design hierarchy for code coverage. Instead, you
can limit the scope of coverage metrics by doing either of the following:
• Use the -cm_hier compile-time option and its configuration file to specify the module
definitions, instances and subhierarchies, and source files that you want VCS either to
exclude from coverage or exclusively compile for coverage (see Using a Configuration
File and Enhancements to the -cm_hier and -hier Switches).
• Use the -cm_hier_enable_moduletree_vhdl switch with the -cm_hier option at
compile time to include or exclude coverage metrics for all instances of a specified
VHDL module tree and for all module instances in the hierarchy below the specified
VHDL module tree. For Verilog, VCS provides support to include or exclude coverage
metrics for all instances of a specified Verilog module tree, by default. For more details,
see Module Tree Support for Verilog and VHDL.
• Use the -cm_report noinitial compile-time option to disable the monitoring of
the contents of
initial blocksdisable
initial blocks for line, condition, and branch metrics (see Disabling the
Monitoring of Initial Blocks).
• Use pragmas in your Verilog source code to exclude lines, source files, and module
instances from coverage (see Using Pragmas to Limit Line Coverage).
• Use pragmas in your VHDL source code to exclude lines from coverage (see Using
Pragmas to Limit VHDL Lines From Coverage).
Using a Configuration File
Statements in the configuration file begin with a plus (+) or minus (-) sign. If a statement
begins with a plus sign (+), it specifies what VCS should compile for coverage. If a

statement begins with a minus sign (-), it specifies what VCS should not compile for
Special Behavior of the First Rule in 'cm_hier' and 'hier' Files
The first rule in a cm_hier or hier file has a special behavior:
• If the first rule is a +, it implicitly excludes everything except what is included by that
rule.
• If the first rule is a -, it implicitly includes everything except what is excluded by that
rule.
Subsequent rules then work on the coverage space left by the rules before them.
In the example below, the +tree directive has no effect because the -moduletree rule
before it has already automatically included the whole design (except for module trees
rooted at MEMS).
-moduletree MEMS_*
begin tgl +tree tb_top 2 end
• URG has an option, -hier, that accepts a subset of the controls that can be used in
the compile-time -cm_hier file. The files are the same other than the differences noted
below.
• Coverage metrics also has another type of configuration file Using an FSM
Configuration File for specifying FSMs in a design.
• VCS Coverage supports -cm_hier on multiple configuration files via a plus (+) sign.
-cm_hier my.cover1.cfg+my.cover2.cfg
You can use the following statements in the configuration file:
+tree instance_name [level_number] VCS compile only the specified instance and
the instances under it for coverage. These instances can be Verilog module or VHDL
entity instances. VCS exclude all other instances from coverage.
A level number of 0 (or no level number) specifies the entire subhierarchy, 1 specifies only
this instance, 2 specifies this instance and those instances directly under this instance,

-cm_hier my.cover1.cfg+my.cover2.cfg
You can use the following statements in the configuration file:
+tree instance_name [level_number] VCS compile only the specified instance and
the instances under it for coverage. These instances can be Verilog module or VHDL
entity instances. VCS exclude all other instances from coverage.
A level number of 0 (or no level number) specifies the entire subhierarchy, 1 specifies only
this instance, 2 specifies this instance and those instances directly under this instance,

below the specified instance. There is no limit to the integer you specify as the level
number.

If the subhierarchy includes instances in the other HDL, VCS does not include these
instances.
-tree instance_name [level_number] VCS exclude this instance from coverage and
other instances under it. These instances can be Verilog module or VHDL entity instances.
VCS include all other instances in coverage.
A level number of 0 (or no level number) specifies the entire subhierarchy, 1 specifies only
this instance, 2 specifies this instance and those instances directly under this instance,
and so on.
If the subhierarchy includes instances in the other HDL, VCS does not exclude these
instances.
+module module_name | entity_name
VCS compiles all instances of the specified Verilog module or VHDL entity definition, and
excludes all other definitions under it, for coverage.
-module module_name | entity_name
VCS does not compile all instances of the specified Verilog module or VHDL entity
definition, and includes all other definitions under it, for coverage.
+file file_name
VCS compile for coverage only the code in this file. If the file is not in the current directory,
specify the path name of the file.
-file file_name
VCS excludes the code in this file from coverage. If the file is not in the current directory,
specify the path name of the file.
Limitation
The -/+file is supposed to work at the module and instance levels which are defined
in the file specified in the directive. They do not work on signals or even when part of a
module is inside the specified file. The starting line of the module definition should be in
the file for it to be considered for the -/+file directive for cm_hier. With -/+file, it is not
supported to reference a Verilog Include file that has just part of the internals of a Verilog
module.
+filelist file_name
VCS compile for coverage only the source files listed in the specified file.
-filelist file_name
VCS exclude from coverage the source files listed in the specified file.

The usage of environment variable in the path is allowed for the above +/-file or
filelist statements. For example:
-file $PATH/common/abc.v
-file $PATH/common/xyz.vhd
The following statements (+library and -library) are not supported in the file you
submit to URG with the -hier command-line option.
+library library_name
VCS compiles for coverage all the Verilog modules and VHDL entities in the specified MX
work library. VCS excludes all other Verilog modules and VHDL entities from coverage.
-library library_name
VCS excludes from coverage all the Verilog modules and VHDL entities in the specified
MX work library. VCS includes all other Verilog modules and VHDL entities in coverage.
The +library and -library directives in a cm_hier file include or exclude MX
work libraries for coverage. The library_name is the name of a work library
that you assign when you analyze design source files with the -work option in
vlogan or vhdlan commands.
Do not confuse these directives with the following unrelated compile-time
options:
• The -v and -y VCS options, which specify Verilog library and include files
during compilation.
• The -cm_libs yv coverage option, which enables coverage for source files
in Verilog libraries.
The +/-library directives apply only to MX work libraries specified with -work
in vlogan or vhdlan.
+moduletree module_name [level_number]
VCS provides coverage metrics for all instances of the specified module and for all module
instances in the hierarchy below the specified module. In other words, each hierarchy tree
starting at each instance of the specified module will have coverage metrics provided. The
coverage metrics are only provided for the number of levels of hierarchy specified by the
optional level_number.
-moduletreemodule_name [level_number]
VCS excludes coverage metrics for all instances of the specified module and for all
module instances in the hierarchy below the specified module. In other words, each

hierarchy tree starting at each instance of the specified module will have coverage metrics
excluded. The coverage metrics are only excluded for the number of levels of hierarchy
specified by the optional level_number.
+/-node
Excludes or includes a signal in toggle coverage. For more information, see the topics
Excluding and Including Signals in the -cm_hier File.
You can use the * , ? and + wildcard characters in the configuration file to specify
definitions, instances, VHDL libraries, and file names.
You can add comments to this file using the convention for Verilog comments. Comments
are supported both at compile-time and at report time with URG.

Begin - End Blocks for Coverage Type Control
The keyword arguments to the -cm compile-time option (line, cond, fsm, tgl, branch,
and assert) specify the type of coverage for which VCS compile. These arguments
specify compiling the entire design for that type of coverage. With begin-end blocks in
the -cm_hier file, you can specify what parts of the design VCS compile for each type of
When you use this feature, the argument to the -cm compile-time option
enables the compilation of the type of coverage and the entries in the -cm_hier
file begin-end blocks specify where VCS compiles for that type of coverage.
Lines in the -cm_hier file that are not begin-end blocks must come before any
begin-end block lines.
The following are examples of the usage of begin-end blocks in the -cm_hier file:
Example 1
begin fsm+line +tree TOP.D1 end
This line specifies that VCS compile only the instances in the specified subhierarchy
(TOP.D1) for FSM coverage. This line only specifies where VCS compile for FSM

coverage. If other types of coverage are specified with other -cm compile-time option
arguments, VCS compile the entire design for those types of coverage.
VHDL hierarchical names can only contain uppercase letters. This requirement
is not true for Verilog.
Example 2
begin line+tgl+cond -module bdev end
This line specifies that VCS does not compile the instances of the module or design entity
named bdev for line, toggle, and condition coverage. To specify more than one type of
coverage, use the plus (+) delimiter.
Example 3
begin cond+line -library gate end
begin tgl -tree TOP.D1.L* end
The first begin-end block calls for excluding all instances of the entities in the MX work
library named gate (assigned with the -work option during analysis) from condition and
line coverage. The second begin-end block calls for excluding all subhierarchies where the
top instance has a hierarchical name beginning with TOP.D1.L (some of these uppercase
letters could be lowercase in the VHDL source code) from toggle coverage.
Example 4
+tree tb.dut1
begin line -module bdev end
The first line does not specify a type of coverage. It calls for VCS to compile the instances
in the subhierarchy with the top instance tb.dut for the types of coverage specified with
the -cm compile-time option (the hierarchical name has lowercase letters so it must be a
Verilog instance).
The second line is a begin-end block that tells VCS not to compile all instances of the
definition named bdev for line coverage.
Enhancements to the -cm_hier and -hier Switches
The
-cm_hier
-cm_hier and
urg -hier
urg -hier switches enable you to provide numerical ranges and
alternative lists. In addition, wildcards can be combined with numerical ranges and
alternative lists in the hierarchical paths of cm_hier and hier configuration file directives.
These enhancements reduce the number of entries in the cm_hier and hier configuration

files and avoid manual work that might lead to a risk of mistakes. For more details, see the
following sections:
• Supporting Numerical Ranges
• Providing Alternative Lists
• Related Notes
Note: Not all hier file directives support these new features. Only +/-node, +/-tree, +/-
moduletree, +/-module_node, and +/-module are supported.
Supporting Numerical Ranges
VCS Coverage allows you to specify a numerical range as part of the hierarchical path of
cm_hier and hier configuration file directives. You can define the initial and final values of
a numerical range in curly braces, with two dots ".." between the values. For example, to
exclude all signals whose names start with ''a'' in the instances numbered between 1 and
50, use the following syntax in the cm_hier and hier configuration files:
-node DUT{1..50}.inst{1..50}.a*
Providing Alternative Lists
VCS Coverage allows you to specify a list of alternate strings to be matched. The syntax
to allow a list of alternatives in the paths is as follows:
-node DUT1.inst1.b2.d7.{ab|mn|z}*
where
ab, mn, and z are examples of signal names that need to be excluded.
Related Notes
• Numerical ranges and alternative lists can be combined in the hierarchical path, as
shown in the following example:
-node DUT{1..50}.inst{1..50}.{ab|mn|z}*
• This feature applies to both VHDL and Verilog (and mixed) designs, where applicable
to the language in question.
• This feature also works with partition compile and pre-compiled IP flows to the extent
that the cm_hier/ hier files are already supported for those flows.

• This feature supports only integer values in numerical ranges. This feature does not
support other ranges (example, for ASCII characters).
• Numerical ranges cannot be used inside alternate lists, and alternate lists cannot be
used inside numerical ranges. Therefore, the following examples are not supported:
top.d1.{a|b|{1..50}} // NOT SUPPORTED
top.d1.{1..{50|60}} // NOT SUPPORTED
• Wildcards are not supported for the +/-file or +/-library directives.
• Alternate lists require at least two operands. For example: +module mod_{A|B}
• Nested numerical range operator, for example, {{1..4}..{3..5}} is not supported
• Excluding or including bit-select and part-select through numerical range and list of
alternatives is not supported for signals. For example:
-node top.arr_MDA[{3..1}][{3..1}]
-node top.arr[{0|2}]
-node top.arr[{3..0}]
Matching Hierarchical Nodes With Depth-Level Granularity
In cm_hier files, the * wildcard matches across hierarchies. For example, top.*.a
matches top.b.a, top.b.c.a, top.b.c.d.a, and so on. While its use can be powerful
and the right choice in some cases, using it unnecessarily can significantly increase
compile time.
-cm_hier-cm_hier[cm_hier]
This feature allows you to use the % wildcard character in cm_hier files. The % wildcard
matches hierarchical names without spanning across instance boundaries. You can pass
the hierarchical patterns in both the -cm_hier (compile-time) and -hier (report-time)
modes.
You can specify the cm_hier files as follows:
Compile Time
%vcs -full64 -sverilog <test.v> -cm tgl -cm_hier <hier/txt>
With assert commands:
%vcs -full64 -sverilog <test.v> -cm tgl+assert -cm_common_hier -cm_hier
<hier/txt>
Report Time

%vcs
urg -dir simv.vdb -hier <hier.txt>
Usage Example
Consider the following testcase:
Example 34 test.v
reg test_signal;
dut inst_dut0();
dut \inst_dut%0 ();
dut \inst_dut1%0 ();
dut \inst_dut@0 ();
end

module dut();
reg dut_signal;
A inst_a0();
A inst_a1();
end

module A;
reg signal_a0, signal_a1, signal_a2;
B inst_b0();
B inst_b1();
end

module B;
reg signal_b0, signal_b1, signal_b2;
C inst_c0();
C inst_c1();
end

module C;
reg signal_c0, signal_c1, signal_c2;
D inst_d0();
D inst_d1();

end

module D;
reg signal_d0, signal_d1, signal_d2;
E inst_e0();
E inst_e1();
end

module E;
reg signal_e0, signal_e1, signal_e2;
end
The % wildcard character is used in the following scenarios:
Scenario 1: Hierarchical rule with single %
node test.inst_dut0.%.signal_a1
In this scenario, the % wildcard limits only one level after inst_dut0 in the
node rule. For example, it matches test.inst_dut0.inst_a0.signal_a1
and test.inst_dut0.inst_a1.signal_a1. However, it does not match
test.inst_dut0.inst_a0.inst_b0.signal_a1.
Similarly, it limits only one level after inst_dut in the tree rule.
Scenario 2: Hierarchical rule with multiple %
node test.inst_dut0.%.%
In this scenario, the % wildcard goes down for two levels below test.inst_dut0 because
of two consecutive % in the node rule.
Scenario 3: Hierarchical rule with multiple % in different locations
node test.inst_dut0.%.inst_b0.%
In this scenario, it matches patterns such as
test.inst_dut0.inst_a0.inst_b0.signal_b0 and
test.inst_dut0.inst_a1.inst_b0.signal_b2
Scenario 4: Hierarchical rule with a combination of multiple wildcards
node test.inst_dut0.*.inst_b?.%
In this scenario, the wildcard * matches all the patterns up to any level in between
inst_dut0 and inst_b0.

Scenario 5: Hierarchical rule with tree/node/assert (cm_common_hier)
assert test.inst_dut0.%
The % wildcard supports assert patterns.
Scenario 6: Special cases with escape names
node test.\inst_dut%0.inst_a%.%
The % wildcard that is in the middle of the escape name also acts as a wildcard character
(same as *). Therefore, it matches all the characters between t and 0 only for one level.
Scenario 7: Hierarchical rule with -cm_tgl portsonly
The % wildcard works with the VCS command-line option, -cm_tgl portonly .
Scenario 8: Hierarchical rule that continues with *%
In this scenario, priority goes to the * wildcard, and it processes all the depth.
Module Tree Support for Verilog and VHDL
VCS provides support to include or exclude coverage metrics for all instances of a
specified Verilog module tree. A module tree specifies a subtree of a specific module,
everywhere it is instantiated.
VCS also provides support to include or exclude coverage metrics for all
instances of a specified VHDL module and for all module instances in the
hierarchy below the specified VHDL module. To enable this VHDL feature, use the
-cm_hier_enable_moduletree_vhdl switch with the -cm_hier option at compile time as
vcs TOP -cm_hier <hier_file> -cm_hier_enable_moduletree_vhdl
The content of the hier_file file is as follows:
+moduletree <module_name> [level_number]
-moduletree <module_name> [level_number]
where, [level_number] specifies the number of levels of hierarchy for which coverage
metrics for a module tree are included or excluded. If this number is specified as 0, the
entire hierarchy is included or excluded.
At report time, use the following URG command to generate reports:
urg -dir <dir_name> -format text

Consider the following example that shows the top module as TOP with a sub-module as
sub_top and its Verilog and VHDL instances:
For this example, consider the following content of the hier file:
+moduletree sub_top
The command includes the coverage metrics for all instances of sub_top and for all
module instances in the hierarchy below it. As the level number is not specified in this
command, the above command becomes the same as the following command:
+moduletree sub_top 0
Compile this example using the -cm_hier_enable_moduletree_vhdl switch with the
-cm_hier option. For this example, VCS generates the following URG report:
The report shows that all the coverage metrics for all instances of sub_top and for all
module instances in the hierarchy below it are computed for coverage calculation.

Now, consider the following content of the hier file:
-moduletree sub_top
The command excludes the coverage metrics for all instances of sub_top and for all
module instances in the hierarchy below it. When the URG report is generated, it shows
that coverage is computed only for the TOP module (see the figure below):
If the level number of the moduletree option is specified as 1, the following URG reports
are generated:
For +moduletree sub_top 1 :
The report shows that coverage is computed only for the sub-top module only.
For -moduletree sub_top 1:
The report shows that coverage computation is excluded only for the sub-top module. For
all other instances of the module and its top module, VCS computes their coverage.

If the level number of the moduletree option is specified as 2, the following URG reports
are generated:
For +moduletree sub_top 2 :
The report shows that coverage is computed only for VHD_SUB0 , sub0, and sub_top.
For -moduletree sub_top 2 :
The report shows that coverage computation is excluded for VHD_SUB0, sub0, and
sub_top. For all other instances of the module and its top module, coverage is computed.

Monitoring Coverage for Encrypted Designs
VCS enables monitoring of coverage for encrypted Verilog designs by default, as
explained here: :
• If a module is fully encrypted, VCS skips monitoring of coverage for the fully encrypted
modules and the hierarchies below them.
• If a module is partially encrypted,
◦ VCS skips monitoring of coverage for self-instances of the module.
◦ VCS monitors coverage on a module instance instantiated inside a partially
encrypted module if:
The definition of the instance is unencrypted.
The instantiation does not fall under encrypted regions of the partially encrypted module.
• The encrypted files should be generated using the +object_protect option.
• Monitoring of coverage for the encrypted VHDL designs is not enabled by default.
module top;//coverage not reported since it is partially encrypted module
mid m1();// Reports coverage
`protect
bot b1();// Does not report coverage
initial begin// Does not report coverage
………
end
`endprotect
module mid;
bot b2();// Reports coverage
bot b3();// Reports coverage
initial begin// Reports coverage
……..
end
module bot;
initial begin// Reports coverage
……
end
In this example, coverage is not monitored for module top as it is partially encrypted.

Disabling the Monitoring of Initial Blocks
The
-cm_report noinitial
-cm_report noinitial compile-time option can be used to disable the monitoring of
the contents of
initial blocksdisable
initial blocks for line, condition, and branch metrics.
In most of the cases, the initial blocks are completely covered, which might increase the
coverage percentage needlessly. Disabling the monitoring of the contents of these initial
blocks allows you to focus on the actual design coverage.
Using the -cm_report noinitial compile-time option does not affect toggle
coverage and FSM coverage.
To disable the monitoring of the contents of initial blocks, include the -cm_report
noinitial compile-time option in the vcs command-line.
module dut(a,b,c);
input a,b;
output c;
wire c;
assign c = a&&b;
module tb();
reg y,x,w;
reg clk;
wire z;
//The contents of this block are ignored for coverage
$monitor($time,"x=%b,y=%b,z=%b",x,y,z);
#1;
clk = 1'b0;
x = 1'b0;
y = 1'b0;
#1;
x = 1'b1;
y = 1'b1;
#1;
x = 1'b0;
y = 1'b0;
#1;
x = 1'b1;
y = 1'b1;
#1;
x = 1'b0;
y = 1'b0;
#1;
#50;
$finish;
end

//The contents of this block are ignored for coverage
if(x)
$display("In the if loop\n");
$display("In the else loop\n");
end
always #5
clk = !clk;
always@(posedge clk) begin
if(z)
$display("z = 1'b1\n");
$display("z = 1'b0\n");
end dut dut1(x,y,z);
To disable the monitoring of the contents of initial blocks in the example, execute the
% vcs test.v -cm line+branch+cond -cm_report noinitial

ignored for coverage.

number.

If the subhierarchy includes instances in the other HDL, VCS does not include these
instances.
-tree instance_name [level_number] VCS exclude this instance from coverage and
other instances under it. These instances can be Verilog module or VHDL entity instances.
VCS include all other instances in coverage.
A level number of 0 (or no level number) specifies the entire subhierarchy, 1 specifies only
this instance, 2 specifies this instance and those instances directly under this instance,
and so on.
If the subhierarchy includes instances in the other HDL, VCS does not exclude these
instances.
+module module_name | entity_name
VCS compiles all instances of the specified Verilog module or VHDL entity definition, and
excludes all other definitions under it, for coverage.
-module module_name | entity_name
VCS does not compile all instances of the specified Verilog module or VHDL entity
definition, and includes all other definitions under it, for coverage.
+file file_name
VCS compile for coverage only the code in this file. If the file is not in the current directory,
specify the path name of the file.
-file file_name
VCS excludes the code in this file from coverage. If the file is not in the current directory,
specify the path name of the file.
Limitation
The -/+file is supposed to work at the module and instance levels which are defined
in the file specified in the directive. They do not work on signals or even when part of a
module is inside the specified file. The starting line of the module definition should be in
the file for it to be considered for the -/+file directive for cm_hier. With -/+file, it is not
supported to reference a Verilog Include file that has just part of the internals of a Verilog
module.
+filelist file_name
VCS compile for coverage only the source files listed in the specified file.
-filelist file_name
VCS exclude from coverage the source files listed in the specified file.

The usage of environment variable in the path is allowed for the above +/-file or
filelist statements. For example:
-file $PATH/common/abc.v
-file $PATH/common/xyz.vhd
The following statements (+library and -library) are not supported in the file you
submit to URG with the -hier command-line option.
+library library_name
VCS compiles for coverage all the Verilog modules and VHDL entities in the specified MX
work library. VCS excludes all other Verilog modules and VHDL entities from coverage.
-library library_name
VCS excludes from coverage all the Verilog modules and VHDL entities in the specified
MX work library. VCS includes all other Verilog modules and VHDL entities in coverage.
The +library and -library directives in a cm_hier file include or exclude MX
work libraries for coverage. The library_name is the name of a work library
that you assign when you analyze design source files with the -work option in
vlogan or vhdlan commands.
Do not confuse these directives with the following unrelated compile-time
options:
• The -v and -y VCS options, which specify Verilog library and include files
during compilation.
• The -cm_libs yv coverage option, which enables coverage for source files
in Verilog libraries.
The +/-library directives apply only to MX work libraries specified with -work
in vlogan or vhdlan.
+moduletree module_name [level_number]
VCS provides coverage metrics for all instances of the specified module and for all module
instances in the hierarchy below the specified module. In other words, each hierarchy tree
starting at each instance of the specified module will have coverage metrics provided. The
coverage metrics are only provided for the number of levels of hierarchy specified by the
optional level_number.
-moduletreemodule_name [level_number]
VCS excludes coverage metrics for all instances of the specified module and for all
module instances in the hierarchy below the specified module. In other words, each

hierarchy tree starting at each instance of the specified module will have coverage metrics
excluded. The coverage metrics are only excluded for the number of levels of hierarchy
specified by the optional level_number.
+/-node
Excludes or includes a signal in toggle coverage. For more information, see the topics
Excluding and Including Signals in the -cm_hier File.
You can use the * , ? and + wildcard characters in the configuration file to specify
definitions, instances, VHDL libraries, and file names.
You can add comments to this file using the convention for Verilog comments. Comments
are supported both at compile-time and at report time with URG.
Type Used for
// comment The end of the line comment.
code /* comment */ code The inside of a line comment.
/* comment 1 comment 2comment3 */ Multiple line comments.
Begin - End Blocks for Coverage Type Control
The keyword arguments to the -cm compile-time option (line, cond, fsm, tgl, branch,
and assert) specify the type of coverage for which VCS compile. These arguments
specify compiling the entire design for that type of coverage. With begin-end blocks in
the -cm_hier file, you can specify what parts of the design VCS compile for each type of
When you use this feature, the argument to the -cm compile-time option
enables the compilation of the type of coverage and the entries in the -cm_hier
file begin-end blocks specify where VCS compiles for that type of coverage.
Lines in the -cm_hier file that are not begin-end blocks must come before any
begin-end block lines.
The following are examples of the usage of begin-end blocks in the -cm_hier file:
Example 1
begin fsm+line +tree TOP.D1 end
This line specifies that VCS compile only the instances in the specified subhierarchy
(TOP.D1) for FSM coverage. This line only specifies where VCS compile for FSM

coverage. If other types of coverage are specified with other -cm compile-time option
arguments, VCS compile the entire design for those types of coverage.

VHDL hierarchical names can only contain uppercase letters. This requirement
is not true for Verilog.
Example 2
begin line+tgl+cond -module bdev end
This line specifies that VCS does not compile the instances of the module or design entity
named bdev for line, toggle, and condition coverage. To specify more than one type of
coverage, use the plus (+) delimiter.
Example 3
begin cond+line -library gate end
begin tgl -tree TOP.D1.L* end
The first begin-end block calls for excluding all instances of the entities in the MX work
library named gate (assigned with the -work option during analysis) from condition and
line coverage. The second begin-end block calls for excluding all subhierarchies where the
top instance has a hierarchical name beginning with TOP.D1.L (some of these uppercase
letters could be lowercase in the VHDL source code) from toggle coverage.
Example 4
+tree tb.dut1
begin line -module bdev end
The first line does not specify a type of coverage. It calls for VCS to compile the instances
in the subhierarchy with the top instance tb.dut for the types of coverage specified with
the -cm compile-time option (the hierarchical name has lowercase letters so it must be a
Verilog instance).
The second line is a begin-end block that tells VCS not to compile all instances of the
definition named bdev for line coverage.
Enhancements to the -cm_hier and -hier Switches
The
-cm_hier
-cm_hier and
urg -hier
urg -hier switches enable you to provide numerical ranges and
alternative lists. In addition, wildcards can be combined with numerical ranges and
alternative lists in the hierarchical paths of cm_hier and hier configuration file directives.
These enhancements reduce the number of entries in the cm_hier and hier configuration

files and avoid manual work that might lead to a risk of mistakes. For more details, see the
following sections:
• Supporting Numerical Ranges
• Providing Alternative Lists
• Related Notes
Note: Not all hier file directives support these new features. Only +/-node, +/-tree, +/-
moduletree, +/-module_node, and +/-module are supported.
Supporting Numerical Ranges
VCS Coverage allows you to specify a numerical range as part of the hierarchical path of
cm_hier and hier configuration file directives. You can define the initial and final values of
a numerical range in curly braces, with two dots ".." between the values. For example, to
exclude all signals whose names start with ''a'' in the instances numbered between 1 and
50, use the following syntax in the cm_hier and hier configuration files:
-node DUT{1..50}.inst{1..50}.a*
Providing Alternative Lists
VCS Coverage allows you to specify a list of alternate strings to be matched. The syntax
to allow a list of alternatives in the paths is as follows:
-node DUT1.inst1.b2.d7.{ab|mn|z}*
where
ab, mn, and z are examples of signal names that need to be excluded.
Related Notes
• Numerical ranges and alternative lists can be combined in the hierarchical path, as
shown in the following example:
-node DUT{1..50}.inst{1..50}.{ab|mn|z}*
• This feature applies to both VHDL and Verilog (and mixed) designs, where applicable
to the language in question.
• This feature also works with partition compile and pre-compiled IP flows to the extent
that the cm_hier/ hier files are already supported for those flows.

• This feature supports only integer values in numerical ranges. This feature does not
support other ranges (example, for ASCII characters).
• Numerical ranges cannot be used inside alternate lists, and alternate lists cannot be
used inside numerical ranges. Therefore, the following examples are not supported:
top.d1.{a|b|{1..50}} // NOT SUPPORTED
top.d1.{1..{50|60}} // NOT SUPPORTED
• Wildcards are not supported for the +/-file or +/-library directives.
• Alternate lists require at least two operands. For example: +module mod_{A|B}
• Nested numerical range operator, for example, {{1..4}..{3..5}} is not supported
• Excluding or including bit-select and part-select through numerical range and list of
alternatives is not supported for signals. For example:
-node top.arr_MDA[{3..1}][{3..1}]
-node top.arr[{0|2}]
-node top.arr[{3..0}]
Matching Hierarchical Nodes With Depth-Level Granularity
In cm_hier files, the * wildcard matches across hierarchies. For example, top.*.a
matches top.b.a, top.b.c.a, top.b.c.d.a, and so on. While its use can be powerful
and the right choice in some cases, using it unnecessarily can significantly increase
compile time.
-cm_hier-cm_hier[cm_hier]
This feature allows you to use the % wildcard character in cm_hier files. The % wildcard
matches hierarchical names without spanning across instance boundaries. You can pass
the hierarchical patterns in both the -cm_hier (compile-time) and -hier (report-time)
modes.
You can specify the cm_hier files as follows:
Compile Time
%vcs -full64 -sverilog <test.v> -cm tgl -cm_hier <hier/txt>
With assert commands:
%vcs -full64 -sverilog <test.v> -cm tgl+assert -cm_common_hier -cm_hier
<hier/txt>
Report Time

%vcs
urg -dir simv.vdb -hier <hier.txt>

The % wildcard character is used in the following scenarios:
Scenario 1: Hierarchical rule with single %

The % wildcard character is used in the following scenarios:
Scenario 1: Hierarchical rule with single %
node test.inst_dut0.%.signal_a1
In this scenario, the % wildcard limits only one level after inst_dut0 in the
node rule. For example, it matches test.inst_dut0.inst_a0.signal_a1
and test.inst_dut0.inst_a1.signal_a1. However, it does not match
test.inst_dut0.inst_a0.inst_b0.signal_a1.
Similarly, it limits only one level after inst_dut in the tree rule.
Scenario 2: Hierarchical rule with multiple %
node test.inst_dut0.%.%
In this scenario, the % wildcard goes down for two levels below test.inst_dut0 because
of two consecutive % in the node rule.
Scenario 3: Hierarchical rule with multiple % in different locations
node test.inst_dut0.%.inst_b0.%
In this scenario, it matches patterns such as
test.inst_dut0.inst_a0.inst_b0.signal_b0 and
test.inst_dut0.inst_a1.inst_b0.signal_b2
Scenario 4: Hierarchical rule with a combination of multiple wildcards
node test.inst_dut0.*.inst_b?.%
In this scenario, the wildcard * matches all the patterns up to any level in between
inst_dut0 and inst_b0.

Scenario 5: Hierarchical rule with tree/node/assert (cm_common_hier)
assert test.inst_dut0.%
The % wildcard supports assert patterns.
Scenario 6: Special cases with escape names
node test.\inst_dut%0.inst_a%.%
The % wildcard that is in the middle of the escape name also acts as a wildcard character
(same as *). Therefore, it matches all the characters between t and 0 only for one level.
Scenario 7: Hierarchical rule with -cm_tgl portsonly
The % wildcard works with the VCS command-line option, -cm_tgl portonly .
Scenario 8: Hierarchical rule that continues with *%
In this scenario, priority goes to the * wildcard, and it processes all the depth.
Module Tree Support for Verilog and VHDL
VCS provides support to include or exclude coverage metrics for all instances of a
specified Verilog module tree. A module tree specifies a subtree of a specific module,
everywhere it is instantiated.
VCS also provides support to include or exclude coverage metrics for all
instances of a specified VHDL module and for all module instances in the
hierarchy below the specified VHDL module. To enable this VHDL feature, use the
-cm_hier_enable_moduletree_vhdl switch with the -cm_hier option at compile time as
vcs TOP -cm_hier <hier_file> -cm_hier_enable_moduletree_vhdl
The content of the hier_file file is as follows:
+moduletree <module_name> [level_number]
-moduletree <module_name> [level_number]
where, [level_number] specifies the number of levels of hierarchy for which coverage
metrics for a module tree are included or excluded. If this number is specified as 0, the
entire hierarchy is included or excluded.
At report time, use the following URG command to generate reports:
urg -dir <dir_name> -format text

Consider the following example that shows the top module as TOP with a sub-module as
sub_top and its Verilog and VHDL instances:
For this example, consider the following content of the hier file:
+moduletree sub_top
The command includes the coverage metrics for all instances of sub_top and for all
module instances in the hierarchy below it. As the level number is not specified in this
command, the above command becomes the same as the following command:
+moduletree sub_top 0
Compile this example using the -cm_hier_enable_moduletree_vhdl switch with the
-cm_hier option. For this example, VCS generates the following URG report:
The report shows that all the coverage metrics for all instances of sub_top and for all
module instances in the hierarchy below it are computed for coverage calculation.

Now, consider the following content of the hier file:
-moduletree sub_top
The command excludes the coverage metrics for all instances of sub_top and for all
module instances in the hierarchy below it. When the URG report is generated, it shows
that coverage is computed only for the TOP module (see the figure below):
If the level number of the moduletree option is specified as 1, the following URG reports
are generated:
For +moduletree sub_top 1 :
The report shows that coverage is computed only for the sub-top module only.
For -moduletree sub_top 1:
The report shows that coverage computation is excluded only for the sub-top module. For
all other instances of the module and its top module, VCS computes their coverage.

If the level number of the moduletree option is specified as 2, the following URG reports
are generated:
For +moduletree sub_top 2 :
The report shows that coverage is computed only for VHD_SUB0 , sub0, and sub_top.
For -moduletree sub_top 2 :
The report shows that coverage computation is excluded for VHD_SUB0, sub0, and
sub_top. For all other instances of the module and its top module, coverage is computed.

Monitoring Coverage for Encrypted Designs
VCS enables monitoring of coverage for encrypted Verilog designs by default, as
explained here: :
• If a module is fully encrypted, VCS skips monitoring of coverage for the fully encrypted
modules and the hierarchies below them.
• If a module is partially encrypted,
◦ VCS skips monitoring of coverage for self-instances of the module.
◦ VCS monitors coverage on a module instance instantiated inside a partially
encrypted module if:
The definition of the instance is unencrypted.
The instantiation does not fall under encrypted regions of the partially encrypted module.
• The encrypted files should be generated using the +object_protect option.
• Monitoring of coverage for the encrypted VHDL designs is not enabled by default.
module top;//coverage not reported since it is partially encrypted module
mid m1();// Reports coverage
`protect
bot b1();// Does not report coverage
initial begin// Does not report coverage
………
end
`endprotect
module mid;
bot b2();// Reports coverage
bot b3();// Reports coverage
initial begin// Reports coverage
……..
end

pragmas for coverage metrics
Pragmas are meta comments in your source code.
VCS have pragmas that allow you to specify that certain lines of Verilog code, Verilog
source files, specified signal, and all instances of certain module definitions are not to be
compiled for line, toggle, condition, FSM, or branch coverage. They work like compiler
directives.
These pragmas are as follows:
Pragma Description
//VCS coverage off pragma//VCS coverage off pragma[VCS coverage off]
//VCS coverage off Specifies disabling coverage for the block of
source code that follows.
//VCS coverage on pragma//VCS coverage on pragma[VCS coverage on]
//VCS coverage on Specifies re-enabling coverage for the
source code that follows when a previous
block of source code is disabled by the
//VCS coverage off pragma.
//VCS coverage exclude_file
//VCS exclude_file pragma//VCS exclude_file pragma[VCS exclude_file]
Specifies disabling coverage for the code
in the source file that contains this pragma.
Synopsys recommends entering this pragma
at the beginning of the source file, before any
module definitions.
//VCS exclude_module pragma//VCS exclude_module pragma[VCS exclude_module]
//VCS coverage exclude_module Specifies disabling coverage for all instances
of the module definition that contains this
pragma. Enter this pragma immediately after
the port declarations. This pragma does not
exclude from coverage the module instances
hierarchically under these instances. To do
this, see Controlling the Scope of Coverage
Compilation.
The HDL Compiler and Behavioral Compiler users can use the //synopsys
translate_off directive in place of the //VCS coverage off pragma and the
//synopsys translate_on directive in place of the //VCS coverage on pragma.

The //VCS coverage on pragma enables line coverage after a //synopsys
translate_off directive and a //synopsys translate_off directive disables line
coverage after a //VCS coverage on pragma.
Similarly, the //VCS coverage off pragma disables line coverage after a //synopsys
translate_on directive and a //synopsys translate_on directive enables line
coverage after a //VCS coverage off pragma.
Pragmas Inside 'protect
//VCS coverage on/off pragmas within `protect blocks are ignored. Therefore, these
pragmas within 'protect blocks do not enable or disable coverage computation. For
example, consider the following code snippet:
'protect
b1=0; c1=0;
#5 b1=1;
#5 c1=1;
end
'endprotect
In the example, the //VCS coverage off pragma exists outside the 'protect block.
This pragma disables coverage monitoring for the remaining code till the time it gets the
//VCS coverage on pragma. The //VCS coverage on pragma exists in the 'protect
block, therefore, it does not have any effect on coverage scores. Therefore, no coverage
is computed and reported even for the code that exists below the //VCS coverage on
pragma.
Using Pragmas to Limit Line Coverage
When you disable line coverage using pragmas, URG indicates this fact in its line
coverage report.
Pragmas do not exclude module instances. For example:
reg clk, a;
// synopsys translate_off
mod1 inst1(a,clk);
// synopsys translate_on
.
.
.

This example does not exclude test.inst1 from coverage.
Pragma pairs for disabling and re-enabling coverage cannot be used across module
boundaries or across blocks of code (such as begin-end or always blocks). Figure 20
illustrates this point.
Figure 20 Using Pragmas
always @(posedge CLK)
casex (Control_state_next)
3’b0: PC = PCmux;
3’b001: begin
IR = Iin;
end
3’b010: begin
RS_ALU = RSbus;
T_ALU = RTbus;
end
3’b011: begin
MAR = ALUout;
SMDR = RTbus;
end
default: begin
RS_ALU = RSbus;
SMDR = ALUout;
end
end
always @(Control_state_pres)
casex (Control_state_pres)
3’b100: Wrt_en = 1’b1;
default: Wrt_en = 1’b0;
end
The first pair is good
This pair straddles
begin-end boundaries
This pair straddles
always block
boundaries and is
and is therefore illegal
therefore illegal

Using Pragmas to Limit VHDL Lines From Coverage
VCS has pragmas that instruct VCS not to compile certain lines of VHDL sequential
statements or concurrent signal assignments for line and condition coverage. They
also instruct VCS not to compile certain signal declarations for toggle coverage. These
pragmas are as follows:--synopsys coverage_off pragma[-]--synopsys coverage_off pragma[synopsys coverage_off]
--synopsys coverage_off
Specifies disabling line and condition coverage for the sequential statements or concurrent
signal assignments that follow, for line and condition coverage. Specifies disabling toggle
coverage for the signal declarations that follow.--synopsys coverage_on pragma[-]--synopsys coverage_on pragma[synopsys coverage_on]
--synopsys coverage_on
Specifies re-enabling line and condition coverage for the sequential statements or
concurrent signal assignments that follow and also specifies re-enabling toggle coverage
for the signal declarations that follow, when a previous block of source code is disabled by
the --synopsys coverage_off pragma.
The following examples use these pragmas to disable and re-enable line and condition
coverage in a sequential code:
Example 1
architecture A of E is
.
.
.
p : process
--synopsys coverage_off
sig1 <= 0; -- not compiled for coverage
--synopsys coverage_on
if (x == '0') then
s <= y;
end if;
end process p;
end A;
VCS does not compile the signal assignment statement to signal sig1 for line coverage.
Example 2
package body mypack is
procedure vec_assn(
signal out: bit_vector(3 downto 0);
x : bit_vector(3 downto 0)
) is
--synopsys coverage_off

if (x == "000") then -- not compiled for coverage
sequential statements -- not compiled for coverage
.
.
.
end if;
--synopsys coverage_on
out <= x;
end vec_assn;
.
.
.
VCS does not compile the sequential statements controlled by the if statement in
procedure vec_assn for line or condition coverage.
Example 3
You can also use these pragmas around signal declarations to disable and re-enable
toggle coverage. For example:
architecture A of E is
signal clk : bit;
--synopsys coverage_off
signal flag1 : integer; --not compiled for toggle coverage
--synopsys coverage_on
signal flag2 : integer; --compiled for toggle coverage
.
.
.
end A;
VCS does not compile signal flag1 for toggle coverage; it does compile signal flag2 for
toggle coverage.
Pragmas to Limit Toggle Coverage
To disable toggle coverage for a variable or a net, enter the pragma before the variable or
net declaration. The allowed pragmas are:
// VCS coverage off
// VCS coverage on

All code between the off and on is excluded for all code coverage metrics. In the case of
toggle coverage, the pragmas should block out the reg / wire declaration and not the line
that updates the reg or wire. Example 35 shows how this works:
Example 35 Pragmas for Toggle Coverage
reg r1;
reg r2,r3;
wire w1;
wire w2,w3;
#1 r1=1; //pragmas
r2=1;
r3=1;
#1 r1=0;
r2=0;
r3=0;
#1 r1=1;
r2=1;
r3=1;
#1 r2=0;
#1 r2=1;
#100 $finish;
end
assign w1=r1; // pragmas
assign w2=r2;
assign w3=r3;
Example 35 contains pragmas before the reg r1 and wire w1 declarations, in order to
exclude them from the toggle coverage.
The toggle coverage report shows reg r2 and r3 and wire w2 and w3. It does not report reg
r1 or wire w1.
This feature works only with Verilog code.
If you enter any of these pragmas in your source code, but some time later want
VCS to ignore these pragmas, enter the
-cm_ignorepragmas-cm_ignorepragmas[-]
-cm_ignore_pragma compile-time
option.

Pragmas to Limit FSM Coverage
You can use pragmas to specify an FSM that VCS might not automatically extract.
Pragmas do not apply to VHDL.
With pragmas, you can inform VCS about the following FSM matter:
• The vector signal, part-select of a vector signal, or concatenation of signals that hold
the current state of the FSM.
• The vector signal that holds the next state of the FSM, unless the FSM does not use
a signal for the next state (in which case VCS displays a warning and assumes that
the current state and next state are in the same signal, part-select of a signal, or
concatenation of signals).
• The possible states of the FSM that are specified in a parameter declaration. When
using pragmas to specify an FSM, there must be a parameter declaration to specify the
possible states of the FSM.
Specifying the Signal That Holds the Current State
You use the following pragma to identify the vector signal that holds the current state of the
FSM:/* VCS state_vector signal_name */ pragma
/* VCS state_vector signal_name */
VCS and state_vector are required keywords. You must enter this pragma inside the
module definition where the signal is declared.
You also must use a pragma to specify an enumeration name for the FSM. This
enumeration name is also specified for the next state and the possible states, associating
them with each other as part of the same FSM. There are two ways you can do this:
• Use the same pragma:
/* VCS state_vector signal_name enum enumeration_name */
• Use a separate pragma in the signal’s declaration:
/* VCS state_vector signal_name */
reg [7:0]
/* VCS enum enumeration_name */ pragma
/* VCS enum enumeration_name */ signal_name;
In either case, enum is a required keyword. If using the separate pragma, VCS is also a
required keyword. Also, when using a separate pragma, enter the pragma immediately
after the bit range of the signal.

Specifying the Part-Select that Holds the Current State
You can specify that a part-select of a vector signal holds the current state of the FSM.
Normally, when URG displays or reports FSM coverage data, it names the FSM after the
signal that holds the current state. In your FSM, if a part-select holds the current state, you
must also specify a name for the FSM that URG can use. The FSM name is not the same
as the enumeration name.
You can specify the part-select with the following pragma:
/* VCS state_vector signal_name[n:n] FSM_name enum enumeration_name */
Specifying the Concatenation that Holds the Current State
Like specifying a part-select, you can specify a concatenation of signals to hold the current
state. When you do this, you also need to specify an FSM name and an enumeration
name:
/* VCS state_vector { signal_name, signal_name,} FSM_name
enum enumeration_name */
The concatenation is of the entire signals. You cannot include bit-selects or part-selects of
signals.
Specifying the Signal that Holds the Next State
You also specify the signal that holds the next state of the FSM with the pragma that
specifies the enumeration name:
reg [7:0] /* VCS enum enumeration_name */ signal_name
If, and only if, the FSM does not have a signal for the next state, you can omit this pragma.
Specifying the Current and Next State Signals in the Same
Declaration
If you use the pragma for specifying the enumeration name in a declaration of multiple
signals, VCS assumes that the first signal following the pragma holds the current state and
the next signal holds the next state. For example:
/* VCS state_vector cs */
reg [1:0] /* VCS enum myFSM */ cs, ns, nonstate;
In this example, VCS assumes that signal cs holds the current state and signal ns holds
the next state. It assumes nothing about signal nonstate.

Specifying the Possible States of the FSM
You can also specify the possible states of the FSM with the pragma that specifies the
enumeration name:
parameter /* VCS enum enumeration_name */
S0 = 0,
s1 = 1,
s2 = 2,
s3 = 3;
Enter this pragma immediately after the keyword parameter, unless you specify a bit
width for the parameters. If you do specify a bit width, enter the pragma immediately after
the bit width:
parameter [1:0] /* VCS enum enumeration_name */
S0 = 0,
s1 = 1,
s2 = 2,
s3 = 3;
Pragmas in One Line Comments
These pragmas work in both block comments, between the /* and */ character strings,
and in one line comments, following the // character string. For example:
parameter [1:0] // VCS enum enumeration_name
S0 = 0,
s1 = 1,
s2 = 2,
s3 = 3;

Specifying FSM With Pragmas - an Example
module m3;
reg[31:0] cs;
reg[31:0] /* VCS enum MY_FSM */ ns;
reg[31:0] clk;
reg[31:0] rst;
// VCS state_vector cs enum MY_FSM
parameter // VCS enum MY_FSM
p1=10,
p2=11,
p3=12;

endmodule // m3
Signal ns holds the next state
signal cs holds the current state
p1, p2, and p3 are possible
states of the FSM
Using Pragmas to Limit Branch Coverage
The //VCS coverage exclude_file and //VCS coverage exclude_module pragmas
exclude a source file or module definition from branch coverage.
Additionally, you can use the //VCS coverage off and //VCS coverage on pragmas to
exclude certain code from branch coverage.
When you use if-else statements as in Example 36:
Example 36 If Statements in a Design
always @ (r1 or r2 or r3)
if (r1)
$display("r1 is true");
r4=r1;
end
$display("r1 not true");
if (r2)
$display("r2 is true");

r5=r2;
end
$display("r2 not true");
if (r3)
$display("r3 is true");
r6=r3;
end
$display("r3 not true");
end
end
$display("no op");
end
URG reports a column for each conditional expression as in Example 37:
Example 37 Branch Coverage Report

Using Pragmas to Limit VHDL Lines From Coverage
VCS has pragmas that instruct VCS not to compile certain lines of VHDL sequential
statements or concurrent signal assignments for line and condition coverage. They
also instruct VCS not to compile certain signal declarations for toggle coverage. These
pragmas are as follows:--synopsys coverage_off pragma[-]--synopsys coverage_off pragma[synopsys coverage_off]
--synopsys coverage_off
Specifies disabling line and condition coverage for the sequential statements or concurrent
signal assignments that follow, for line and condition coverage. Specifies disabling toggle
coverage for the signal declarations that follow.--synopsys coverage_on pragma[-]--synopsys coverage_on pragma[synopsys coverage_on]
--synopsys coverage_on
Specifies re-enabling line and condition coverage for the sequential statements or
concurrent signal assignments that follow and also specifies re-enabling toggle coverage
for the signal declarations that follow, when a previous block of source code is disabled by
the --synopsys coverage_off pragma.
The following examples use these pragmas to disable and re-enable line and condition
coverage in a sequential code:
Example 1
architecture A of E is
.
.

--synopsys coverage_off
sig1 <= 0; -- not compiled for coverage
--synopsys coverage_on
if (x == '0') then
s <= y;
end if;
end process p;
end A;
VCS does not compile the signal assignment statement to signal sig1 for line coverage.
Example 2
package body mypack is
procedure vec_assn(
signal out: bit_vector(3 downto 0);
x : bit_vector(3 downto 0)
) is
--synopsys coverage_off

if (x == "000") then -- not compiled for coverage
sequential statements -- not compiled for coverage
.
.
.
end if;
--synopsys coverage_on
out <= x;
end vec_assn;
.
.
.
VCS does not compile the sequential statements controlled by the if statement in
procedure vec_assn for line or condition coverage.

Pragmas to Limit Toggle Coverage
To disable toggle coverage for a variable or a net, enter the pragma before the variable or
net declaration. The allowed pragmas are:
// VCS coverage off
// VCS coverage on

All code between the off and on is excluded for all code coverage metrics. In the case of
toggle coverage, the pragmas should block out the reg / wire declaration and not the line
that updates the reg or wire. Example 35 shows how this works:
Example 35 Pragmas for Toggle Coverage
reg r1;
reg r2,r3;
wire w1;
wire w2,w3;
#1 r1=1; //pragmas
r2=1;
r3=1;
#1 r1=0;
r2=0;
r3=0;
#1 r1=1;
r2=1;
r3=1;
#1 r2=0;
#1 r2=1;
#100 $finish;
end
assign w1=r1; // pragmas
assign w2=r2;
assign w3=r3;
Example 35 contains pragmas before the reg r1 and wire w1 declarations, in order to
exclude them from the toggle coverage.
The toggle coverage report shows reg r2 and r3 and wire w2 and w3. It does not report reg
r1 or wire w1.
This feature works only with Verilog code.
If you enter any of these pragmas in your source code, but some time later want
VCS to ignore these pragmas, enter the
-cm_ignorepragmas-cm_ignorepragmas[-]
-cm_ignore_pragma compile-time
option.

Pragmas to Limit FSM Coverage
You can use pragmas to specify an FSM that VCS might not automatically extract.
Pragmas do not apply to VHDL.
With pragmas, you can inform VCS about the following FSM matter:
• The vector signal, part-select of a vector signal, or concatenation of signals that hold
the current state of the FSM.
• The vector signal that holds the next state of the FSM, unless the FSM does not use
a signal for the next state (in which case VCS displays a warning and assumes that
the current state and next state are in the same signal, part-select of a signal, or
concatenation of signals).
• The possible states of the FSM that are specified in a parameter declaration. When
using pragmas to specify an FSM, there must be a parameter declaration to specify the
possible states of the FSM.
Specifying the Signal That Holds the Current State
You use the following pragma to identify the vector signal that holds the current state of the
FSM:/* VCS state_vector signal_name */ pragma
/* VCS state_vector signal_name */
VCS and state_vector are required keywords. You must enter this pragma inside the
module definition where the signal is declared.
You also must use a pragma to specify an enumeration name for the FSM. This
enumeration name is also specified for the next state and the possible states, associating
them with each other as part of the same FSM. There are two ways you can do this:
• Use the same pragma:
/* VCS state_vector signal_name enum enumeration_name */
• Use a separate pragma in the signal’s declaration:
/* VCS state_vector signal_name */
reg [7:0]
/* VCS enum enumeration_name */ pragma
/* VCS enum enumeration_name */ signal_name;
In either case, enum is a required keyword. If using the separate pragma, VCS is also a
required keyword. Also, when using a separate pragma, enter the pragma immediately
after the bit range of the signal.

Specifying the Part-Select that Holds the Current State
You can specify that a part-select of a vector signal holds the current state of the FSM.
Normally, when URG displays or reports FSM coverage data, it names the FSM after the
signal that holds the current state. In your FSM, if a part-select holds the current state, you
must also specify a name for the FSM that URG can use. The FSM name is not the same
as the enumeration name.
You can specify the part-select with the following pragma:
/* VCS state_vector signal_name[n:n] FSM_name enum enumeration_name */
Specifying the Concatenation that Holds the Current State
Like specifying a part-select, you can specify a concatenation of signals to hold the current
state. When you do this, you also need to specify an FSM name and an enumeration
name:
/* VCS state_vector { signal_name, signal_name,} FSM_name
enum enumeration_name */
The concatenation is of the entire signals. You cannot include bit-selects or part-selects of
signals.
Specifying the Signal that Holds the Next State
You also specify the signal that holds the next state of the FSM with the pragma that
specifies the enumeration name:
reg [7:0] /* VCS enum enumeration_name */ signal_name
If, and only if, the FSM does not have a signal for the next state, you can omit this pragma.
Specifying the Current and Next State Signals in the Same
Declaration
If you use the pragma for specifying the enumeration name in a declaration of multiple
signals, VCS assumes that the first signal following the pragma holds the current state and
the next signal holds the next state. For example:
/* VCS state_vector cs */
reg [1:0] /* VCS enum myFSM */ cs, ns, nonstate;
In this example, VCS assumes that signal cs holds the current state and signal ns holds
the next state. It assumes nothing about signal nonstate.

Specifying the Possible States of the FSM
You can also specify the possible states of the FSM with the pragma that specifies the
enumeration name:
parameter /* VCS enum enumeration_name */
S0 = 0,
s1 = 1,
s2 = 2,
s3 = 3;
Enter this pragma immediately after the keyword parameter, unless you specify a bit
width for the parameters. If you do specify a bit width, enter the pragma immediately after
the bit width:
parameter [1:0] /* VCS enum enumeration_name */
S0 = 0,
s1 = 1,
s2 = 2,
s3 = 3;

does not report, these ternary operators and their conditional expression for branch
coverage:
Example 47 Excluding All Conditional Operators for the Ternary Operator

If you enter any of these pragmas in your source code, and at later time, want VCS to
ignore these pragmas, enter the
-cm_ignorepragmas-cm_ignorepragmas[-]
-cm_ignorepragmas compile-time option.
Users can use pragmas in their source code to exclude coverage monitoring in under
specific conditions and signal values. This allows designers to specify unreachable or
uninteresting scenarios that might otherwise be automatically monitored for coverage, and
to do so in a way that is independent from the specific types or modes of coverage that are
used.
Today exclusions are done on an object-by-object basis for each coverage metric that
was collected, and the verification team must consult with the designers to ensure that
any excluded objects should actually be excluded. And, while VCS has powerful tools for
reusing exclusions as the code changes, some maintenance of these exclusions is still
required by the verification team. Furthermore, if the metrics or coverage options change,
the exclusions have to be reworked.
This section describes a feature that allows designers to communicate impossible or do
not-care conditions using pragmas in the HDL code itself that is based on the source
signal values.
• Usage

Usage
The pragmas described in this section are used for toggle, condition and line coverage.
They have no effect if none of those metrics are enabled. In addition, they are enabled
only when the new pragma command-line options are given at compile time.
To enable pragma exclusions at compile time, use the -cm_pragma advanced option with
the vcs command.
The default support for pragmas uses a "coverage off " pragma to indicate the start
of a region to exclude, and a "coverage on " pragma to resume coverage monitoring.
For example, the following code snippet contains pragmas before reg r1 and wire w1
declarations, and excludes them from coverage monitoring:

reg r1;
reg r2,r3;
wire w1;
wire w2,w3;

#1 r1=1; //pragmas
r2=1;
r3=1;
#1 r1=0;
r2=0;
r3=0;
#1 r1=1;
r2=1;
r3=1;
#1 r2=0;
#1 r2=1;
#100 $finish;
end

assign w1=r1; // pragmas
assign w2=r2;
assign w3=r3;
In the example, the toggle coverage report would show reg r2 and r3 and wire w2 and
w3. It does not report reg r1 or wire w1 .

The new pragmas use the same basic syntax, but with additional qualifying clauses.
For example, to exclude all coverable objects that require signal s to be equal to 1 to be
covered, start the exclusion section with the following:
//VCS coverage off when { s == 1'b1 }
The following sections describe each qualifying clause type and how it is used.
Once coverage objects are excluded with pragmas, they cannot be
"unexcluded" at simulation time. You can only modify compile-time exclusions
by modifying the pragmas in the source code.
• The for Clause
• The when Clause
The for Clause
The for clause in the VCS coverage off pragma is used to exclude signals and parts of
signals from toggle coverage. The syntax of the for clause in the pragma is as follows:
// VCS coverage off for {expr} (trans)
where,
• expr is a signal name, a bit- or part-select expression on a signal name, or a struct
or union field. Only one signal or bit- or part-select expression on a signal name may
be given in expr. To exclude multiple signals or parts of signals, you can use multiple
pragmas.
• trans is an optional bit transition, either 0 -> 1 or 1 -> 0 , to be excluded for all bits
specified in expr.
To exclude part of a signal for toggle coverage, use the left and right bounds in expr. For
example, to exclude part of the signal dsko, the pragma is as follows:
// VCS coverage off for { dsko[3:0]} (0 -> 1)
inout[7:0] dsko;
Assuming only dsko[7:6] are covered during simulation, URG creates the following
report for the pragma:

Note that only the 0->1 transitions are excluded because 0->1 is given at the end of the
pragma; the 1->0 transitions for these bits are still reported as not covered. Bounds of
expressions that can be evaluated as elaboration constant values can be used to specify
bounds. For example:
// VCS coverage off for { dsko[(SZ/2)-1:0] }
inout[SZ-1:0] dsko;
The when Clause
The when clause in the VCS coverage off pragma is used for line and condition
coverage. The syntax of the when clause in the pragma is as follows:
// VCS coverage off when {bexpr}
where,
• bexpr is a Boolean expression. Coverage objects that can only occur when bexpr
evaluates to true are excluded.
The when clause is used to exclude monitoring coverable objects that depend on a
particular combination of values. For example, coverage objects that can only happen
when the signal k is 1 and both y and x are 0 are as follows:
reg x, y, k;
always @(x,y) begin
//VCS coverage off when { k==1'b1 && (y||x)==1'b0 }

if( k==1'b1 && (y||x)==1'b0 )
$display("Excluded\n");
$display("Not excluded\n");
end
URG creates the following line and condition coverage reports:
Line Coverage:

Condition Coverage:
Exclusions with "when" conditions are limited to the scope in which they appear. The
supported scopes are begin/end blocks and single statements.
To apply the exclusion condition only to blocks of code within begin/end statements, the
pragma must appear inside that block. For example:
module m(…);
// VCS coverage off when { m == 1 }
if (m && n && q) begin
…
end
end

always@(posedge clk) begin
if (m == 1 && en)
…
end
…

You can use multiple VCS coverage off pragmas in a module. Each pragma
applies only to a region in which it is enclosed.
For a single-statement block such as initial or always, a pragma may be given after the
single statement in the block to limit the effect of the pragma to only that statement. For
example:
always@(*)
c <= w && y; // VCS coverage off when { w == 1'b1 }
For a continuous assignment, the pragma must be given on the same line as the
continuous assignment. For example:
assign c = b && d; // VCS coverage off when { b == 1'b1 }
Pragmas have the following limitations:
• General Limitations
• Limitations of the for Clause
• Limitations of the when Clause
General Limitations
1. Partition Compile (PC) flow is not supported. VCS ignores the -cm_pragma advanced
switch in PC flow and it does not give any warning that pragmas are ignored.
2. Pragmas cannot be used in VHDL code. VCS honors pragmas used in Verilog code.
3. Use of Cross-Module References (XMRs) in pragma expressions is not supported.

Limitations of the for Clause
1. Signals defined in interfaces, packages, and unit scopes are not supported for
exclusions.
2. Field selects on a packed structure variable are not supported. For example:

Limitations of the when Clause
1. The inside operator is not supported.
2. Pragma exclusions apply only when operands used in a pragma exactly match with the
operands given in a condition expression. For example:
wire k=1;
reg a;
//VCS coverage off when { a==k }
if(a==k)
if(a==1)

Here, the pragma applies only when a==k is given as a condition
expression of the if block. Therefore, the pragma does not exclude
the if block when a==1 is given as its condition expression.

or

VCS coverage off when { a==1 }
if(a==1)
if(a==k)

Here, the pragma applies only when a==1 is given as a condition
expression of the if block. Therefore, the pragma does not exclude
the if block when a==k is given as its condition expression.

3. The scope of the pragma is not applied inside the body of a task or a function that is
called within the pragma region. For example:
always @(posedge clock) begin
//VCS coverage off when { a && b}
my_function();
if( a && b) begin
$display("Pragma {a && b} applies in this block \n");
end
end

function void my_function;
if( a && b)
$display("Pragma {a && b} does not apply in the function block
\n");
end
endfunction
Here, the scope of the pragma is between initial begin-end. The pragma excludes the a
&& b condition within initial begin-end. However, the pragma does not exclude the a &&
b condition in the my_function function.
◦ Structure/union variables are not supported in pragma expressions.
4. VCS does not honor pragmas if there are delays present within pragmas. For example,
consider the following code snippet:
//VCS coverage off when {t && s}
#2 r=3;s=2;t=1;
#0;
r=s || t && s? s:t;
#2 $finish;
end

Subtopics cover line coverage suppression in always blocks, condition coverage filtering,

on Verilog designs. Available as a compile-time option and as a runtime override for toggle
coverage.glitch suppression
Signals often go through many oscillations before they settle down for an event. Such
transitions to a value for a short period of time, or the transition to a value and then to
another value during the same simulation time step can cause transitions or toggles on
other signals. These transitions and toggles cause some lines to execute, and perhaps
execute more than once during the same time step.
These oscillations, glitches, or narrow pulses can skew the coverage results in a line,
condition or toggle coverage by showing lines, conditions, or toggles that are covered only
when these glitches occur and not after these oscillating signals settle down.
You can suppress these glitches by using the
-cm_glitch-cm_glitch[-]
-cm_glitch compile-time option as follows:
vcs -cm line+cond+tgl -cm_glitch period
where, period indicates a non-negative integer.
When you use this switch for line coverage, VCS ignores the coverage in the first 'n' time
units even though there are no glitches. This is to ignore any glitches that may occur
during the initial few timestamps due to the design setup. This scenario is valid for a
Verilog design only.
You can use the -cm_glitch 0 option to remove the delta cycle glitches.

To disable glitch suppression on contassign, use the -cm_glitch
0+nolinecontassign compile-time option. Alternatively, you can use the
-cm_glitch nolinecontassign+0 compile-time option.
The simulation time that you specify is similar to the simulation time you specify in
a delay specification (#10, for example). It is scaled based on the time_unit and
time_precision arguments to the 'timescale compiler directive.

In this example, the conditional expression (input1 && input2) could be briefly true
during one of these glitches or narrow pulses, but after settling down the expression
is finally not true. If this happens, when VCS monitors instances of this module for
line coverage, it sees that the lines controlled by the if part and the else part of this
conditional expression, both assignment statements, are executed.

entire length of these glitches or narrow pulses, and in this example only, VCS sees the
execution of the second assignment statement in the final execution of the always block.

Toggle Coverage Glitch Suppression
The -cm_glitch positive_integer compile-time option specifies the simulation time
period of glitch suppression.
Unlike glitch suppression in line and condition coverage, glitch suppression in toggle
coverage is not focused on rapidly triggering always blocks. Glitch suppression in toggle
coverage indicates that VCS does not monitor or record any value change on a signal that
lasts fewer simulation time units than the simulation time specified with the -cm_glitch
compile-time option. It does not matter whether these short interval changes, or glitches,
are caused by statements in an always or initial block, continuous assignments, or
connections to a gate, primitive, or user-defined primitive (UDP).
Another difference between glitch suppression for toggle coverage and glitch suppression
for line or condition coverage, is that there is a -cm_glitch runtime option for toggle
coverage. This runtime option overrides the glitch period for toggle coverage specified at
compile-time. This runtime option does not work for either line or condition coverage.
Glitch suppression in toggle coverage is not necessary for zero time glitches, that is
transitions from 0 -> 1 and then 1 ->0, or from 1 -> 0 and then 0 ->1, during the same
simulation time step. VCS never monitors or records these transitions for toggle coverage.
This feature works only with Verilog code.
Condition Coverage Glitch Suppression
The -cm_glitch positive_integer compile-time option specifies the simulation time
period of glitch suppression.
In glitch suppression for condition coverage, like glitch suppression for line coverage,
VCS looks for fast triggering of always blocks, not initial blocks, and the glitch period is an
interval of simulation time in which there are one or more executions of the statements in
the always block.
When you use glitch suppression, VCS only monitors and records the results on the last
execution of the always block during the glitch period.
