The following examples show compilation and runtime options to generate one or more
metrics and invoking URG and Coverage GUI. You can view the coverage report in batch
mode using URG or in GUI mode using Verdi Coverage:
Example 1 Line Coverage Only
% vcs -cm line source.v
% simv -cm line
% urg -dir simv.vdb //to generate URG report
% verdi -cov -covdir simv.vdb //to view coverage report
//in the Verdi Coverage GUI
1. VCS compiles for line coverage.
2. During simulation, VCS looks for line coverage.
Example 2 Line, Condition and FSM Coverage
% vcs -cm line+cond+fsm source.v
% simv -cm line+cond+fsm
% urg -dir simv.vdb
% verdi -cov -covdir simv.vdb
1. VCS compiles for Line, Condition, and FSM coverage.
2. During simulation, VCS looks for Line, Condition, and FSM coverage.
Example 3 Line, Condition, FSM, Toggle, and Branch Coverage
% vcs -cm line+cond+fsm+tgl+branch -lca source.v
% simv -cm line+cond+fsm+tgl+branch
% urg -dir simv.vdb
% verdi -cov -covdir simv.vdb
1. VCS compiles for Line, Condition, FSM, Toggle, and Branch coverage.
2. During simulation, VCS keeps track of Line, Condition, FSM, Toggle, and Branch
coverage.
Example 4 Line, Condition, and Assertion Coverage
% vcs -cm line+cond+assert source.v
% simv -cm line+cond+assert
% urg -dir simv.vdb / verdi -cov -covdir simv.vdb

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
1. VCS compiles for Line, Condition, and Assertion coverage.
2. During simulation, VCS keeps track of Line, Condition, and Assertion coverage.
Example 5 Compiling for FSM, Toggle, and Branch Coverage while Simulating only
Branch Coverage
% vcs -cm fsm+tgl+branch source.v
% simv -cm branch
% urg -dir simv.vdb / verdi -cov -covdir simv.vdb
1. VCS compiles for FSM, Toggle, and Branch coverage.
2. You can choose to simulate VCS to track only few metrics than what you have
specified during the compilation stage, such as Branch coverage.
However, choosing fewer metrics for coverage compilation and choosing more during
simulation does not work.
Example 6 Specifying More Metrics at Compile-time and Runtime but Generating Reports for
Fewer Metrics
% vcs -cm line+fsm+branch+cond source.v
% simv -cm line+fsm+branch+cond
% urg -dir simv.vdb -metric line+fsm
% verdi -cov -covdir simv.vdb
1. VCS compiles for and simulates Line, FSM, Branch, and Condition coverage.
2. While generating reports, you can choose to generate reports for fewer metrics than
what you have specified during compilation and simulation and use URG to generate
only Line and FSM coverage.

Setting Up Coverage Metrics
This chapter describes how you can set up coverage metrics using various methods, as
discussed in the following sections:
• Overview of Coverage Metrics
• Code Coverage
• Functional Coverage
• Coverage Support for Inconsequential Code Reduction
• Support for Embedded Covergroup Inheritance
• Enabling Proper UVM Hierarchical Naming for Covergroup Instances
• Support for type_option.merge_instances and option.get_inst_coverage
• Support for Covergroup Mapping
• Writing and Configuring Test Run Metrics
• Discarding Test Records From Merged VDBs
• Preserving Paths of RTL Source Files
• Reporting Coverage on a Subset of a Design
Overview of Coverage Metrics
VCS monitors and evaluates coverage metrics of Verilog, VHDL, and mixed HDL designs
during simulation to determine which portions of the design have been exercised.
The results of the analysis are reported in a number of ways that allow you to see the
shortcomings in your testbench and improve tests as needed to obtain the complete
coverage. Functional coverage is the determination of how much functionality of the
design has been exercised by the verification environment.

title: Verification Continuum™
text:
VCS writes both code and functional coverage databases during simulation. Using VCS,
you can generate the following types of coverage databases:
• Code Coverage
You can obtain the following types of code coverage information:
◦ The control-flow coverage that tracks which lines and branches have taken the flow
of execution through the Verilog or VHDL code. Control-flow metrics that includes
line coverage and branch coverage.
◦ The value coverage that monitors what values the signals and expressions take
on during simulation. Value-coverage metrics include toggle coverage and FSM
coverage, that track the values (or value-transitions) of signals and variables.
• Functional Coverage
Functional coverage provides information about the testbench variable and signal
values and their state transitions. You can enable cross-coverage between variables
and signals. Cross coverage allows you to check the combinations of values between
two or more signals.
The VCS implementation of SystemVerilog supports the covergroup construct, which
you specify as the user. These constructs allow the system to monitor values and
transitions for variables and signals. They also enable cross-coverage between
variables and signals.
This section discusses the following types of code coverage metrics.
• Line Coverage
• Toggle Coverage
• Condition Coverage
• FSM Coverage
• Branch Coverage
• Monitoring Code Coverage for SystemVerilog Packages
• Coverage Options and Sub-Options

Enabling Line Coverage for Continuous Assignments
By default, line coverage does not include Verilog continuous assignments. You can
enable line coverage for continuous assignments with the
-cm_line contassign-cm_line contassign[-]
-cm_line contassign compile-
time option and keyword argument. For example:
% vcs -f design_files -cm line -cm_line contassign
When you include this compile-time option and keyword argument, URG shows the
continuous assignment statement, including any delay specification, as a block of code.
If a continuous assignment assigns a constant value to the signal or variable on the left
hand side of the continuous assignment operator, VCS does not compile or monitor it for
line coverage.
module dev;
wire w1,w2,w3;
reg r1,r2;
.
.
.
assign #5 w1=1;
assign #3 w2=r1;
assign #10 w3=r1 && r2;
VCS compiles and monitors the continuous assignments to w2 and w3 for line coverage,
but not to w1.
Line Coverage for VHDL
In line coverage, VCS tracks the following in the VHDL source code:
• Individual statements
• Statement blocks
• Statement block type
◦
blocksin line coverage
Statement blocks consist of a set of individual statements executed sequentially
and always executed together in the same time step.
◦ Concurrent signal assignments and component instantiations are not reported in the
coverage reports because they are always executed.
◦ Coverage information is not reported for execution lines in entity or configuration
declaration statements.

◦ VCS monitors line coverage inside for-generates blocks, but individual instances
of the generate loop are not monitored separately. Therefore, a line is reported as
covered if it is covered in any iteration of the loop, and a line is reported not covered
only if it is not covered in any iteration of the loop.
SystemVerilog Testbench Line Coverage
Line coverage shows which lines of code are exercised by the testbench during a
simulation run. VCS supports collection of line coverage for tasks and functions defined
in SystemVerilog
classes
classes and
program blocks
program blocks. This feature helps in improving coverage
closure by enabling you to identify coverage holes. The feature also supports exclusion of
coverable lines inside classes and program blocks.
To enable line coverage collection for tasks and functions in classes and program blocks,
use the
-cm_line svtb
-cm_line svtb compile-time option:
% vcs -cm line -cm_line svtb
The -cm_line svtb compile-time option works only in conjunction with the -cm
line option.
To monitor line coverage in SystemVerilog classes and program blocks, use the following
command at runtime:
./simv -cm line
To refer to line coverage in SystemVerilog classes from your HVP plan, a new source type,
class, is added in the HVP. The syntax of the class type in the HVP plan is as follows:
source = "class: <scope_name>[::]<class_name>";
For example, consider the following HVP plan, New_Plan, which shows the class type to
add line coverage information:
Example 9 New_Plan
plan New_Plan;
feature Feature_1;
measure Line, Cond, FSM, Toggle, Branch, SnpsAvg
Measure_1;
source = "class: xbus_tb_top::xbus_master_agent",
"class: xbus_tb_top::xbus_*";
endplan
To view this HVP plan in URG, use the following command:
urg -dir <coverage_database> -plan New_Plan.hvp

To view this HVP plan in Verdi, use the following command:
verdi -cov -covdir <coverage_database> -plan New_Plan.hvp

Toggle Coverage
Toggle coverage monitors value changes on signal bits in the design. When toggle
coverage reaches 100%, it means that every bit of every monitored signal has changed
its value from 0 to 1 and from 1 to 0. VCS generates metrics for the total coverage of nets
and registers that tell you how much activity is occurring on all the elements; thus giving
you a clear indication of how much testing is actually being performed at the gate level.
Missing transitions of values provide definitive conclusions about inactive elements and
portions of the design that are not exercised. The statistics produced for each module can
be examined to quickly determine areas of low coverage. This helps you to write tests to
address the missing activity.
By default, toggle coverage does not display or report 0 -> 1 and 1 -> 0
transitions where the signal returns to its original value during the same time
step that is, a glitch during which zero simulation time passes.
Example 17 Example For Toggle Coverage
module test;
reg r1;
reg [7:0] r2;
wire w1;

dut dut1 (w1,r1);

r1=0;
r2=8'b00000000;
#100 $finish;
end

always
#10 r1=~r1;

always
#25 r2=r2+1;

module dut (out,in);
output out;
input in;
reg dutr1;

always @ in
dutr1=in;

assign out=dutr1;
In Example 17, the top-level module, test, instantiates module dut. The top-level module,
test, contains two registers, r1 and r2, and one net, w1. The module instance dut1 of
module dut contains one register dutr1 and two nets, ports in and out.
In the top-level module, test, reg r1 have ten 0 -> 1 or 1 -> 0 transitions and vector reg r2
increments three times.
In module instance dut1, all the signals have ten 0 -> 1 or 1 -> 0 transitions.
A signal bit might transition from 0 to X and then to 1 over multiple time steps during
simulation. VCS records this transition as a 0 -> 1 transition, and value changes to X are
ignored for toggle coverage. Similarly, a transition from 1 to X and then to 0 over multiple
time steps is counted as toggling that bit from 1 -> 0. Transitions through Z are treated the
same way: 0 -> Z -> 1 counts as a 0 -> 1 toggle and 1 -> Z -> 0 counts as a 1 -> 0 toggle.
A signal that transitions 0 -> X -> 0 is not counted for toggle coverage as it is
unclear whether any real signal transition occurred. In other words, a signal
transitions from a known value (0) to an unknown value (X), and then back
to the same known value (0) is ignored for toggle coverage. If X is 0 then no
transition occurs.

Enabling Line Coverage for Continuous Assignments
By default, line coverage does not include Verilog continuous assignments. You can
enable line coverage for continuous assignments with the
-cm_line contassign-cm_line contassign[-]
-cm_line contassign compile-
time option and keyword argument. For example:
% vcs -f design_files -cm line -cm_line contassign
When you include this compile-time option and keyword argument, URG shows the
continuous assignment statement, including any delay specification, as a block of code.
If a continuous assignment assigns a constant value to the signal or variable on the left
hand side of the continuous assignment operator, VCS does not compile or monitor it for
line coverage.
module dev;
wire w1,w2,w3;
reg r1,r2;

assign #3 w2=r1;
assign #10 w3=r1 && r2;
VCS compiles and monitors the continuous assignments to w2 and w3 for line coverage,
but not to w1.
Line Coverage for VHDL
In line coverage, VCS tracks the following in the VHDL source code:
• Individual statements
• Statement blocks
• Statement block type
◦
blocksin line coverage
Statement blocks consist of a set of individual statements executed sequentially
and always executed together in the same time step.
◦ Concurrent signal assignments and component instantiations are not reported in the
coverage reports because they are always executed.
◦ Coverage information is not reported for execution lines in entity or configuration
declaration statements.

◦ VCS monitors line coverage inside for-generates blocks, but individual instances
of the generate loop are not monitored separately. Therefore, a line is reported as
covered if it is covered in any iteration of the loop, and a line is reported not covered
only if it is not covered in any iteration of the loop.

Line Coverage in Packages
VCS monitors testbench lines for class tasks and functions in the SystemVerilog packages
(other than OVM, UVM, and VMM) using the following switch:
% vcs -cm line
-cm_line svtb
-cm_line svtb
To monitor testbench lines for class tasks and functions in all SystemVerilog packages
including OVM, UVM, and VMM, use the following switch:
% vcs -cm line
-cm_line svtb+svtb_include_lib
-cm_line svtb+svtb_include_lib
The
-cm_line svtb_include_lib
-cm_line svtb_include_lib switch is a modifier for the -cm_line svtb switch.

Toggle Coverage
Toggle coverage monitors value changes on signal bits in the design. When toggle
coverage reaches 100%, it means that every bit of every monitored signal has changed
its value from 0 to 1 and from 1 to 0. VCS generates metrics for the total coverage of nets
and registers that tell you how much activity is occurring on all the elements; thus giving
you a clear indication of how much testing is actually being performed at the gate level.
Missing transitions of values provide definitive conclusions about inactive elements and
portions of the design that are not exercised. The statistics produced for each module can
be examined to quickly determine areas of low coverage. This helps you to write tests to
address the missing activity.
By default, toggle coverage does not display or report 0 -> 1 and 1 -> 0
transitions where the signal returns to its original value during the same time
step that is, a glitch during which zero simulation time passes.
Example 17 Example For Toggle Coverage
module test;
reg r1;
reg [7:0] r2;
wire w1;

In Example 17, the top-level module, test, instantiates module dut. The top-level module,
test, contains two registers, r1 and r2, and one net, w1. The module instance dut1 of
module dut contains one register dutr1 and two nets, ports in and out.
In the top-level module, test, reg r1 have ten 0 -> 1 or 1 -> 0 transitions and vector reg r2
increments three times.
In module instance dut1, all the signals have ten 0 -> 1 or 1 -> 0 transitions.
A signal bit might transition from 0 to X and then to 1 over multiple time steps during
simulation. VCS records this transition as a 0 -> 1 transition, and value changes to X are
ignored for toggle coverage. Similarly, a transition from 1 to X and then to 0 over multiple
time steps is counted as toggling that bit from 1 -> 0. Transitions through Z are treated the
same way: 0 -> Z -> 1 counts as a 0 -> 1 toggle and 1 -> Z -> 0 counts as a 1 -> 0 toggle.
A signal that transitions 0 -> X -> 0 is not counted for toggle coverage as it is
unclear whether any real signal transition occurred. In other words, a signal
transitions from a known value (0) to an unknown value (X), and then back
to the same known value (0) is ignored for toggle coverage. If X is 0 then no
transition occurs.

◦ In terminal connection lists in task-enabling statements:

◦ In PLI routine calls:

FSM Coverage
In hardware, a Finite State Machine (FSM) is implemented as sequential logic that outputs
a current state and combinational logic that outputs the next state. When VCS compiles
your design for FSM coverage, it identifies FSMs based on the analyzed data and control
flow and tracks the states and transitions that occur in the FSM during simulation.
The sequential logic is driven by the next state signal and by the clock and reset signals.
The combinational logic is driven by the current state signal and the inputs to the FSM.
Coverage extraction does not support FSMs that are implemented with VHDL variables.

VCS treats a signal as an FSM if the signal is assigned constant values, and where the
execution of those assignments depends on that signal's value. The values assigned
must be clearly identifiable as constants or parameters and there must be a dependency
between the current state and the next state. The following group of Verilog statements is
an FSM:
input in;
reg [3:0] current,next;

current=4'b0001;

always @ in
case (1'b1)
current [0] : next=4'b0010;
current [1] : next=4'b0100;
current [2] : next=4'b1000;
current [3] : next=4'b0001;
#2 current=next;
end

FSM Coverage for Verilog
In Verilog, a signal is treated as an FSM when:
• There are at least three constants or parameters ("states") assigned to that signal,
directly or indirectly.
• The execution of the assignments of those states depends on the current value of the
signal.
• The next value assigned to the signal is not computed from its current value (as in a
counter, for example).
Indirect assignments of a state to the FSM signal may go through multiple other signals, or
be passed through certain function/procedure calls or module subinstances.
Example 18 is a Verilog module definition that contains statements that function as an
FSM:
Example 18 Verilog Module Definition Containing an FSM
module dev (clk,in,state);
input clk,in;
output [1:0] state;

reg [1:0] state,next;
parameter idle = 2'b00,
first = 2'b01,
second = 2'b10,
third = 2'b11;

state=idle;
next=idle;
end

always @ in
next = state; // by default hold
case (state)
idle : if (in) next = first;
first : if (in) next = second;
second : if (in) next = third;
third : if (in) next = idle;
end

always @ (posedge clk)
state=next;

The FSM has four states: idle, first, second, and third. The possible transitions are idle-
>first, first->second, second->third, and third->idle.
The values that the statements in the group assign to a signal are the states of the FSM,
and must be of an identifiable set of parameters, numeric constants, enumerated type
values, declared (named) constants, or text macros (where the macro text that VCS
substitutes for the macro name is a numeric constant).
FSM Coverage for VHDL
This section describes how VCS extracts FSMs from the VHDL code when the
-cm_fsmopt vhdladveng switch is given on the VCS command line. You can still use the
old FSM engine by omitting this switch, but it has different (more restrictive) rules on how
FSMs are recognized and monitored and is not recommended. See the next section for
more about the FSM extraction engine.
VCS automatically extracts FSMs from VHDL code in the following scenarios:
• The state values are stored in enumerated, std_logic_vector, bit_vector, or
integer data types.
• The state values of the FSM are either an enumerated type, VHDL constant, generic,
or literal constant.
• The FSM control logic may be implemented using case statements, if-else
statements, conditional signal assignments, or combinations of these structures.
• The code for the FSM is entirely within a procedure or process or using one
combinational process to determine the next state of the FSM and a sequential process
to set the next state on the clock edge.
Example 19 illustrates a VHDL architecture that models an FSM:
Example 19 VHDL Architecture Modeling an FSM
architecture exfsmarch of exfsm is
type my_fsm_states is (idle, first, second, third);
signal curr_state : my_fsm_states := idle;
signal next_state : my_fsm_states := idle;
my_fsm : process(insig)
next_state <= curr_state;
case curr_state is
when idle => if (insig = '1') then next_state <= first; end if;
when first => if (insig = '1') then next_state <= second; end if;
when second => if (insig = '0') then next_state <= third; end if;
when third => if (insig = '1') then next_state <= idle; end if;
end case;

advance_fsm : process
wait until clk'event and clk = '1';
curr_state <= next_state;
end exfsmarch;
FSM Support for VHDL Generate Blocks
When the -cm_fsmopt vhdladveng switch is given on the command line, VCS
automatically extracts FSMs from inside VHDL generate blocks. Consider the following
example that shows the FSM code inside the generate block, INNERB:
INNERB: for J in 0 to 1 generate
b1: block is
signal state: bit_vector(2 downto 0);
signal nstate: bit_vector(2 downto 0);
process (clk2, rstn)
if (rstn = '0') then
state <= "000";
state <= nstate;

case(state) is
when "001" =>
nstate <= "010";
when "010" =>
nstate <= "100";
when others =>
nstate <= "101";
end case;
end block;
end generate INNERB;
When the -cm_fsmopt vhdladveng switch is given, VCS extracts the following two FSMs
from the generate block, INNERB:
INNERB(0).B1.STATE
INNERB(1).B1.STATE

The FSM Extraction Engine
The FSM recognition engine provides benefits such as accurate FSM extraction,
diagnostic messages, support for FSM reset filtering, and compile-time performance. The
engine improves the analysis of FSMs split across module boundaries. It also improves
the analysis of FSMs with code in functions.
The FSM engine identifies when there are multiple signals used to hold the next-state
value as it is being computed. There are some cases where signals are not considered to
be FSMs. If you see differences you do not understand, it is recommended that you use
the -diag fsm switch on the VCS command line at compile time. This produces messages
explaining why signals are or are not recognized as FSMs.
The FSM extraction engine finds some impossible state-to-state changes. Also, you can
see that the order, in which states and transitions is reported, helps in identifying the
source line numbers for states and transitions. Note that VCS uses a strict ordering for
both states and transitions.
The VHDL FSM extraction engine is enabled by default. This section discusses the
following features that are enabled by default in the VHDL FSM extraction engine to
enhance its quality, scalability, and performance:
• Integer-Type Generics for FSM States
• Variables
• Declared Constants for FSM States
• Part-Select FSMs
• FSMs Inside a Generate Block
• Part-Select FSM Code Inside a Generate Block
• Array of Enumerated Type

• FSMs From Arrays of Vectors
• Diagnostics
• Ignoring Reset-Only Transitions
• The FSM Configuration File
• Other Notes
Integer-Type Generics for FSM States
The FSM extraction engine supports generics for base type integer for states. For
example, consider the following code snippet:
Example 20 Integer-Type Generics
entity pci_target is
generic (
Idle : integer := 0;
B_Busy : integer := 1;
Backoff : integer := 2;
S_Data : integer := 3;
Turn_Ar : integer := 4 );
In this example, five states, Idle, B_Busy, Backoff, S_Data, and Turn_Ar are defined as
integer, which is supported by the FSM engine.
Variables
The FSM extraction engine recognizes variables that implement FSMs. For example,
consider the following code snippet:
Example 21 Variable That Implements FSMs
architecture arch1 of mymod is
signal cur : integer := 0;
signal reset : boolean;
p : process
variable nxt : integer;
if (reset) then nxt := 0;
elsif (0 = cur) then nxt := 1;
elsif (1 = cur) then nxt := 2;
else nxt := 0;
cur <= nxt;

Declared Constants for FSM States
The extraction engine enables you to use declared constants for FSM states. The
following example shows four constants, red, blue, green, and yellow of type integer
and their values:
Example 22 Declared Constants for FSM States
constant red : integer := 0;
constant blue : integer := 1;
constant green : integer := 2;
constant yellow : integer := 3;
Part-Select FSMs
The FSM extraction engine can identify when the design uses a part-select of a vector to
store the current state of an FSM.
Consider the following example that shows an FSM in the part-select expression cur(4
downto 0) :
Example 23 A Part-Select FSM
constant red : bit_vector(2 downto 0) := "000";
constant blue : bit_vector(2 downto 0) := "001";
constant green : bit_vector(2 downto 0) := "010";
constant yellow : bit_vector(2 downto 0) := "111";

signal cur : bit_vector(4 downto 0);
signal nxt : bit_vector(4 downto 0);
signal reset : boolean;
p : process
if (reset) then
nxt(4 downto 2) <= red;
elsif (red = cur(4 downto 2)) then
nxt(4 downto 2) <= blue;
elsif (blue = cur(4 downto 2)) then
nxt(4 downto 2) <= green;
nxt(4 downto 2) <= red;

cur(4 downto 2) <= nxt(4 downto 2);

wait for 5 ns;
VCS recognizes the following part-select FSM:
CUR(4 DOWNTO 2)

FSMs Inside a Generate Block
The extraction engine supports FSMs inside generate blocks. The following example
shows the FSM code inside the generate block, INNERB:
Example 24 FSMs Inside a Generate Block
INNERB: for J in 0 to 1 generate
b1: block is
signal state: bit_vector(2 downto 0);
signal nstate: bit_vector(2 downto 0);
process (clk2, rstn)
if (rstn = '0') then
state <= "000";
state <= nstate;

case(state) is
when "001" =>
nstate <= "010";
when "010" =>
nstate <= "100";
when others =>
nstate <= "101";
end case;
end block;
end generate INNERB;

INNERB(0).B1.STATE
INNERB(1).B1.STATE
Part-Select FSM Code Inside a Generate Block
The extraction engine supports part-select FSMs inside a generate block. For example,
the following code snippet shows a part-select FSM, state, with the generate block, GK:
Example 25 A Part-Select FSM Inside a Generate Block
signal state: bit_vector(3 downto 0);
signal nstate: bit_vector(3 downto 0);

GK: for K in 1 to 2 generate
b1: block is
signal dupname : bit;
process (clk2, rstn)

dupname <= '1';
if (rstn = '0') then
state((K*2)-1 downto (K*2)-2) <= "00";
state((K*2)-1 downto (K*2)-2) <=
nstate((K*2)-1 downto (K*2)-2);
if ((state((K*2)-1 downto (K*2)-2)) = "00") then
nstate((K*2)-1 downto (K*2)-2) <= "01";
elsif ((state((K*2)-1 downto (K*2)-2)) = "01") then
nstate((K*2)-1 downto (K*2)-2) <= "10";
nstate((K*2)-1 downto (K*2)-2) <= "11";
end block;

STATE(1 DOWNTO 0)

type State_type is array (0 to 3) of parallel_states;

when IDLE =>
if … then
NEXT(i) <= ACTIVE;
NEXT(i) <= IDLE;

when ACTIVE =>

NEXT(i) <= IDLE;

NEXT(i) <= ENABLED;

Diagnostics
VCS displays messages to understand how it attempts to detect FSMs in the source when
you give the -diag fsm switch. Consider the example below that checks the value of suit.
All the assignments are to n_suit but there is no assignment from n_suit to suit:
parameter [4:0] clubs = 2'b00, hearts = 2'b01, diamonds = 2'b11;
always @(suit) begin
if (suit == clubs) n_suit <= hearts;
else if (suit == hearts) n_suit <= 63;
else if (suit == 63) n_suit <= diamonds;
else n_suit <= clubs;
When the -diag fsm switch is given, suit is rejected as an FSM as it does not qualify the
criteria of having the minimum number of states as 3:
Note-[VCM-FSMRJST] FSM unrecognized
justmissed.v, 1
mifelse, "suit"
Signal "suit" was rejected as an FSM because VCS did not find enough
states for it to qualify. The minimum number of states is 3, but 0 were
found.
Also, n_suit is rejected as an FSM as none of its assigned states are controlled by
checking the value of n_suit.
Note-[VCM-FSMRJCK] FSM unrecognized
justmissed.v, 1
mifelse, "n_suit"
Signal "n_suit" was rejected as an FSM because VCS found 0 places where
it was compared to a possible state value, but 2 are required.
Ignoring Reset-Only Transitions
The FSM extraction engine enables you to specify that transitions that can only happen on
reset should be ignored. To ignore these transitions, you specify the design's resets using
the -cm_fsmresetfilter compile-time option. The reset filter specification file is passed on
the VCS command line as follows:
vcs -cm fsm -cm_fsmresetfilter <filename>
where <filename> is the FSM reset filter configuration file.

You can specify a global reset signal, a reset signal for specific modules, or reset signals
for specific modules and FSMs. An example of the global reset signal is as follows:
signal=reset case=FALSE
In this example, the FSM engine treats any test that compares a signal named reset to
false as being a check for reset. Thus, transitions caused by the assignment of the IDLE
state in the below example is ignored:
if (!reset) next_state <= IDLE;
A reset signal can also be specified for specific modules as follows:
module=mymod signal=reset case=FALSE
In this example, only transitions FSMs in the mymod module are filtered for reset == false
conditions.
The different styles can be combined in the reset filter file. The following example specifies
a global rule to apply (reset == TRUE) for any FSM signal named abc, and a separate rule
for abc in the mymod module, where the reset signal is named rst:
signal=reset case=TRUE fsm=abc
module=mymod signal=rst case=TRUE fsm=abc
VCS gives priority to a line with module name even if no FSM is specified. A
line with no module name or FSM name is the lowest priority.
The FSM extraction engine can detect reset tests even in complex conditions. For
example, consider the following code snippet that shows the complex condition, reset &&
dum:
n_suit <= ((reset && dum) ? clubs :
((suit == hearts) ? diamonds :
((suit == diamonds) ? spades :
((suit == spades) ? clubs :
hearts))));
The FSM Configuration File
The FSM configuration file provides the following features:
• Detection of Illegal States
The FSM configuration file allows you to specify the list of states for a given FSM signal.
If a one-hot FSM is being specified and an illegal state is specified, VCS gives a message
explaining that the state is illegal and why, and that it is being ignored.
• Keyword: AUTO

The AUTO keyword directs VCS to use the FSMs as specified in the configuration file for
those signals, but also allows VCS to automatically detect other signals as FSMs. This
allows you to tweak the FSM extraction of a module without having to become responsible
for all FSMs in that module. The keyword is used with the FSMS directive in place of the
RESTRICT and EXCLUDE keywords:
FSMS = AUTO
• Support for Concatenation Expressions
Concatenations of signals can be specified in the FSM configuration file. For example:
CURRENT={s1,s2,s3}
This allows you to specify concatenations as FSMs without modifying the source code.
Paired with the AUTO keyword, you can add a concatenation FSM to a module without
affecting other FSMs in that module.
Other Notes
To reuse existing exclusions, you can use the -excl_bypass_checks switch while
generating a report. However, the recommended way to reuse exclusions is to load elfiles
into Verdi, bypass checks, and then save them to a new file.
The FSM extraction engine has the following limitations:
• Recognition of FSMs across instance hierarchy barriers is not supported.
• Pragmas in the HDL source code to modify FSMs are not supported.
• FSMs implemented across entity/architecture boundaries are not supported.
• Part-selects with computed bounds, which cannot be resolved at elaboration time, are
not supported.
• Generics of non-integer types, such as bit_vector, are not supported.
• FSMs with multidimensional array indices, such as cur(k)(P), are not supported. For
example, consider the following code snippet that shows nested generate for the if-
elsif type FSM with generics and constants as state type:
Example 27 Multidimensional Array Indices are Not Supported
GEN1: for k in 1 to 2 generate
GEN2: for P in 1 to 2 generate
b1 : block is
p1 : process
variable nxt : integer;

if (reset) then nxt := red;
elsif (red = cur(k)(P)) then nxt := blue;
elsif (blue = cur(k)(P)) then nxt := green;
else nxt := red;

cur(k)(P) <= nxt;

wait for 5 ns;
end block;
end generate GEN2;
end generate GEN1;
In this example, the cur(k)(P) expression is not handled by the VHDL FSM extraction
engine and therefore, it does not identify that cur(k)(P)is associated with the nxt
variable.
Recognition of FSMs With All Possible Transitions
By default, VCS recognizes a signal as an FSM if it finds a constant value that is assigned
to a next-state signal and this assignment is guarded by a comparison to a constant value.
This analysis is used to determine which transitions are possible in the FSM. For example,
if an assignment nextstate <= S2 is guarded by a check if (curstate == S1) , VCS
knows to monitor for the transition S1 -> S2 .
By default, when VCS finds state comparisons and assignments but cannot determine the
set of possible transitions, it does not monitor the FSM for coverage.
When the -cm_fsmopt full compile-time option is given, VCS extracts FSMs even when
a subset of possible transitions could not be found. In these cases, every transition from
each state to every other state is part of the FSM coverage model.
Consider the following code snippet that shows part of an FSM in which BUSY and IDLE
are constant values, curst is a current-state signal, and nxtst is a next-state signal:
if (curst == IDLE)
nxtst <= BUSY;
In this example, a constant BUSY is assigned to nxtst and this assignment is guarded by
the if statement that compares curst to a constant value, IDLE. By default, VCS can
determine that IDLE -> BUSY is a valid FSM transition, and it adds this transition to the
FSM coverage model.

Now, consider the following code snippet that shows part of an FSM in which curstate
and nxtstate are signals, and RDY and WORK are constant values:
if (curstate == RDY)
nxtstate <= somesig;
nxtstate = WORK;
In this example, the assignment of somesig to nxtstate is guarded by a state check
of curstate == RDY , but VCS cannot extract any specific transitions as the value of
somesig at this location could be any FSM state. The assignment of WORK to nxtstate is a
state assignment, but does not limit the FSM to a specific transition.
If the rest of the FSM coding is similar, and VCS cannot limit the total transitions to
anything other than every state to every other state, by default, VCS does not monitor this
as an FSM. Using the -cm_fsmopt full option, however, VCS extracts FSMs like this.
• Coverage databases that are created using the -cm_fsmopt full compile-time option
cannot be merged with the coverage databases that are created without using this
option.
FSM Support for Inside Range Expressions
VCS treats all values in 'inside' expressions as possible FSM states and transitions when
the following command is used at compile time:
vcs -cm fsm
When an FSM is extracted, VCS ensures every value in the range is treated as a state for
coverage and all its transitions are tracked and reported.
Example 28 shows a range expression [b:o] in a 'case inside' statement. Any state value
in the range b, g, y, and o is matched by the [b:o] case item.
Example 28 Range Expression, [b:o]
module m1 (input wire reset,clk);
enum integer { v=1, i=2, b=3, g=4, y=5, o=6, r=7 } e2;
reg [15:0]cs; reg [15:0]ns;

always @(clk, reset) begin
if(reset)
cs <= v;
else begin
case(cs) inside
v, i: begin
cs <= b;
end
[b:o]: begin
cs <= r;
end
r: begin
cs <= v;
end
end
end
In this example, the values corresponding to g and y are considered for FSM analysis.

The URG report of Example 28 is as follows:
Figure 10 URG Report
The highlighted states and transitions in the report represent g and y of Example 28. Note
that the values are inferred from the range, therefore, they are shown as integer literals
rather than the enumerated type names, g and y.

This feature has the following limitations:
1. FSMs that use state values greater than 64-bits are not supported for finding states
and transitions from 'inside' expressions.
2. Range expressions that use an arithmetic operation in one or both endpoints are not
supported. For example, the following FSMs are not supported:
case(state)

P3-2: next_state <=

case(state) inside

[P0:P0+2]: next_state =
Ignoring FSM Transitions for Unguarded State Assignments
By default, VCS FSM coverage creates FSM transitions in the coverage model wherever
it sees a state assigned to the FSM signal. It tries to determine which possible states the
FSM could be in when that assignment happens, and creates a transition from each of
those states to the assigned state.
When VCS cannot determine which states the FSM must be in when a new state is
assigned, by default it creates a transition from every known state of the FSM to the
new state. However, when the -cm_fsmopt ignoreOpenAssigns compile-time switch
is specified, VCS does not create any transitions for the FSM when it cannot determine
the possible state values at the location where the new state is assigned. The purpose
of this switch is to limit the transitions in the FSM model only to those that are identified
as controlled by the current value, as opposed to creating transitions due to other
assignments such as initialization and resets.
For more information, see the following sections:
• Examples
• Notes
• Reports
This section gives examples of the effect of the -cm_fsmopt ignoreOpenAssigns switch.

Example 29
Consider the following code snippet that shows a state assignment guarded by a check on
the current value of the FSM signal:
if (cur == S0 || cur == S1) nxt <= S2;

or

case(cur)
S0, S1: nxt <= S2;
VCS creates the following two FSM transitions for this FSM:
S0 à S2
S1 à S2
Now, consider the following example where the state assignment of a state S3 is not
guarded by any check on the value of the FSM signal, cur.
if (cur) nxt <= S3;
By default, VCS creates a transition from every possible state of cur to S3 for this
assignment. If the states of the FSM are S0, S1, S2, S3 and S4, then the following
transitions are created:
S0->S3
S1->S3
S2->S3
S4->S3
But if the -cm_fsmopt ignoreOpenAssigns switch is given, and these transitions are not
found anywhere else in the code for the FSM, they are excluded from coverage score
computation. Depending on the reporting tool and compile-time options, they are shown as
Ignored in URG reports or as compile-time excluded in Verdi. For details, see the Reports
section.
Example 30
Consider the following code snippet that shows four states, S0, S1, S2, and S3 of
current_state:
case(current_state)
S0 : if (en) next_state <= S1; else next_state <= S3;
S1 : next_state<= S2;
default: next_state=S0;
In this example, there is no difference with or without the -cm_fsmopt
ignoreOpenAssigns switch, because VCS is able to determine that the assignment in
case S0 is guarded by a check to see if current_state == S0 . The switch also does not

affect the default clause, as VCS can detect that the default clause is only reached
when current_state is not S0 and not S1.
Notes
While using this feature, keep the following guidelines in mind:
• The coverage databases generated using this switch can be merged with the coverage
databases generated without this switch, but which database is used as the base
database affects the results. If a coverage database compiled with this switch is used
as a base design, transitions related to unguarded state assignments are reported as
Ignored. Alternatively, if a coverage database compiled without this switch is used as a
base design, no transitions are reported as Ignored.
• The -cm_fsmopt ignoreOpenAssigns switch does not intend to precisely identify
and ignore reset-only transitions. It decides whether transitions should be created
based only on whether the state assignment is guarded by a check on the value of
the FSM signal. For precise control of ignoring transitions that explicitly depend on
reset, VCS provides the -cm_fsmresetfilter compile-time option. For more details
on -cm_fsmresetfilter, see the Ignoring Reset-Only Transitions section.
• Transitions that are marked as ignored are reported as Ignored whether they are
covered or not covered.
• If after extracting transitions and applying the filtering rule specified by -cm_fsmopt
ignoreOpenAssigns, it turns out that all transitions to a given state would be ignored,
then all states that were detected that go to the state would instead be monitored.
This prevents cases where due to the coding style, a state is assigned without a guard
check that may stay in effect - for example, as with an assignment used as a default
that may be overridden by later assignments.
• If all of a given state's transitions are marked as Ignored by -cm_fsmopt
ignoreOpenAssigns, because all detected assignments are not guarded by any state
check, VCS leaves them as-is and does not mark them as Ignored to ensure that these
states are counted in the report and any issue with the encoding can be analyzed.
Reports
Transitions suppressed by the -cm_fsmopt ignoreOpenAssigns switch are not included
in FSM coverage score computation. URG and Verdi present these transitions differently,
and neither tool marks them as Unreachable. At a casual glance, compile-time excluded
transitions in Verdi can look similar to uncovered transitions, so it is important to
understand how each tool reports them.

URG Reports
By default, URG does not list suppressed transitions in the FSM state and transition detail
tables. Instead, URG prints the following message in the FSM coverage section when any
transitions were suppressed:
Some transitions were marked Ignored because the
-cm_fsmopt ignoreOpenAssigns switch was given at compile time.
When you compile with -cm_fsmopt ignoreOpenAssigns and also specify -diag
noconst, URG lists the suppressed transitions in the FSM transition detail table with a
status of Ignored. These transitions are shown whether or not they were exercised in
simulation, and they do not count toward the FSM coverage score. The following figure
shows an example URG FSM transition detail report:
Figure 11 URG FSM Transition Detail Report Showing Ignored Transitions
In this example, transitions such as S1->S0 and S2->S0 correspond to an unguarded
state assignment and are reported as Ignored. Transition S3->S0 is not ignored because it
corresponds to a default case item that only some FSM states can reach.
When -diag noconst is specified, VCS also reports a Note message for each ignored
unguarded state assignment at compile time. For example:
Note-[VCM-FSMOTIG] Unguarded state assignment ignored
file.v, 14
VCS will not monitor the transitions associated with the state
assignment of "S0" to signal "curst" on this line because the
"-cm_fsmopt ignoreOpenAssigns" switch was given, and no check
on the value of "curst" could be detected guarding the assignment.
Transitions associated with this assignment will be shown as
Ignored in coverage reports.

Verdi Reports
In Verdi Coverage, transitions suppressed by -cm_fsmopt ignoreOpenAssigns are
marked as compile-time excluded in the FSM transition matrix. They appear as gray
cells with an excluded indicator rather than as red uncovered cells or as unreachable
transitions. These transitions are removed from the coverage model at compile time and
do not affect the FSM coverage score.
The following figure compares the same FSM transition matrix without and with
-cm_fsmopt ignoreOpenAssigns . Without the switch, transitions created from unguarded
state assignments appear as uncovered (red). With the switch, those same transitions
appear as compile-time excluded (gray).
Figure 12 Verdi FSM Transition Matrix Without and With ignoreOpenAssigns
In the lower matrix, transitions such as fiftn->idle, fiftn->ten, five->idle, and
five->ten were created from unguarded default assignments and are shown as compile-
time excluded rather than as uncovered transitions to be exercised.

Compile-time excluded transitions shown for ignoreOpenAssigns are not
the same as unreachable transitions. Unreachable transitions are filtered
by constant analysis or other compile-time optimizations and are reported
separately. If you see transitions disappear or change status after enabling
ignoreOpenAssigns, verify that the affected transitions correspond to
unguarded state assignments rather than to unreachable logic.
• This feature does not guarantee that VCS will detect reset-only transitions. It is
recommended to follow the coding style as shown in the examples above to ensure
that the transitions are extracted as expected.
FSM Compile Times
VCS Coverage allows you to specify a maximum width for any signal or expression to be
considered as a possible FSM. Any expression wider than that number is ignored for FSM
analysis. This feature helps to speed up FSM analysis.
This section consists of the following sub-sections:
• Specifying FSM Maximum Width
• Analyzing FSM Module Times
Specifying FSM Maximum Width
To specify the maximum FSM width, use the -cm_fsm_limit switch as follows:
% vcs -cm fsm -cm_fsm_limit maxwidth=N -diag fsm
For example, to set the maximum FSM width to 32, use the following command:
% vcs -cm fsm -cm_fsm_limit maxwidth=32 -diag fsm
The FSM configuration file does not support specifying arrays of FSMs or part-select
FSMs. Therefore, re-including excluded arrays of FSMs or part-select FSMs in the
configuration file is not supported in the FSM configuration file.
Analyzing FSM Module Times
VCS Coverage provides additional diagnostics to see the time spent in analyzing each
module for FSMs. This feature is provided under the -diag fsm+times switch. The
following is the syntax:
% vcs -cm fsm -diag fsm+times …

Once this switch is used at compile time, the time spent for every module’s FSM analysis
is printed if the time is over a certain level.
If a module does not have an FSM, it can be excluded from analysis using a begin/end
block in the -cm_hier file as follows:
begin fsm
-module <module_name>
end
If any module’s FSM analysis time exceeds a set value, the following message is issued:
Note-[VCM-FSMMXT] High FSM analysis time for module
big_test_mod.v, 1
FSM analysis for the module 'bit_testbench' is taking a longer time than
normal, 34 minutes so far. The size or complexity of this module may be
incompatible with full FSM analysis.
You can tell VCS to skip this module for FSM coverage using a cm_hier
file and the "begin fsm" syntax or by adding pragmas to the code. See
the VCS User Guide for more information on these features.
It is not possible to change the analysis time at which the message can be printed.
However, you can suppress the printing of this message using the -suppress option as
% vcs -suppress=VCM-FSMMXT -cm fsm …
Excluding High Compile-Time Modules
To re-include an FSM that is excluded due to its width, specify its name in an FSM
configuration file. Once the FSM is included in the configuration file, VCS analyzes it as an
FSM even when it crosses its threshold limit. For example, to ensure that the signal cur
is analyzed as an FSM in the module m, include the following lines in the configuration file
passed to the -cm_fsmcfg switch:
MODULE=m
CURRENT=cur
Once the signal cur is specified in the configuration file, VCS analyzes the signal normally
even when its width is greater than the limit.
Branch Coveragebranch coverage
Branch coverage monitors the execution of
conditional statements
conditional statements such as if/else
statements, case statements, and the
ternary operator
ternary operator "?:" in a design. By default, Branch
coverage analyzes which alternative of these conditional statements is covered during
simulation. It can also monitor and report the values computed by a
ternary expression
ternary expression.

To compile and simulate the design for VHDL branch coverage, use the
following commands: % vcs [vcs_options] -cm branch top_cfg/entity/
module % simv [simv_options] -cm branch
Consider the code in Example 31:
Example 31 Branch Coverage Code Example
case (r1)
1'b1 : if (r2 && r3)
r4 = (r5 && r6) ? 1'b0 : 1'b1;
1'b0 : if (r7 && r8)
r9 = (r10 && r11) ? 1'b0 : 1'b1;
default : $display("no op");
In this block of code, there are procedural assignment statements where the value
assigned is controlled by the ternary operator (?:). These statements in turn are controlled
by if statements and the if statements are controlled by a case statement.
In this block of code, the possible vectors of signal or expression values that result in
simulation events or prevent simulation events are as follows:
r1 (r2 && r3) (r5 && r6) (r7 && r8) (r10 && r11)

text:
The FSM has four states: idle, first, second, and third. The possible transitions are idle-
>first, first->second, second->third, and third->idle.
The values that the statements in the group assign to a signal are the states of the FSM,
and must be of an identifiable set of parameters, numeric constants, enumerated type
values, declared (named) constants, or text macros (where the macro text that VCS
substitutes for the macro name is a numeric constant).
FSM Coverage for VHDL
This section describes how VCS extracts FSMs from the VHDL code when the
-cm_fsmopt vhdladveng switch is given on the VCS command line. You can still use the
old FSM engine by omitting this switch, but it has different (more restrictive) rules on how
FSMs are recognized and monitored and is not recommended. See the next section for
more about the FSM extraction engine.
VCS automatically extracts FSMs from VHDL code in the following scenarios:
• The state values are stored in enumerated, std_logic_vector, bit_vector, or
integer data types.
• The state values of the FSM are either an enumerated type, VHDL constant, generic,
or literal constant.
• The FSM control logic may be implemented using case statements, if-else
statements, conditional signal assignments, or combinations of these structures.
• The code for the FSM is entirely within a procedure or process or using one
combinational process to determine the next state of the FSM and a sequential process
to set the next state on the clock edge.
Example 19 illustrates a VHDL architecture that models an FSM:
Example 19 VHDL Architecture Modeling an FSM
architecture exfsmarch of exfsm is
type my_fsm_states is (idle, first, second, third);
signal curr_state : my_fsm_states := idle;
signal next_state : my_fsm_states := idle;
my_fsm : process(insig)
next_state <= curr_state;
case curr_state is
when idle => if (insig = '1') then next_state <= first; end if;
when first => if (insig = '1') then next_state <= second; end if;
when second => if (insig = '0') then next_state <= third; end if;
when third => if (insig = '1') then next_state <= idle; end if;
end case;

Diagnostics
VCS displays messages to understand how it attempts to detect FSMs in the source when
you give the -diag fsm switch. Consider the example below that checks the value of suit.
All the assignments are to n_suit but there is no assignment from n_suit to suit:
parameter [4:0] clubs = 2'b00, hearts = 2'b01, diamonds = 2'b11;
always @(suit) begin
if (suit == clubs) n_suit <= hearts;
else if (suit == hearts) n_suit <= 63;
else if (suit == 63) n_suit <= diamonds;
else n_suit <= clubs;
When the -diag fsm switch is given, suit is rejected as an FSM as it does not qualify the
criteria of having the minimum number of states as 3:
Note-[VCM-FSMRJST] FSM unrecognized
justmissed.v, 1
mifelse, "suit"
Signal "suit" was rejected as an FSM because VCS did not find enough
states for it to qualify. The minimum number of states is 3, but 0 were
found.
Also, n_suit is rejected as an FSM as none of its assigned states are controlled by
checking the value of n_suit.
Note-[VCM-FSMRJCK] FSM unrecognized
justmissed.v, 1
mifelse, "n_suit"
Signal "n_suit" was rejected as an FSM because VCS found 0 places where
it was compared to a possible state value, but 2 are required.
Ignoring Reset-Only Transitions
The FSM extraction engine enables you to specify that transitions that can only happen on
reset should be ignored. To ignore these transitions, you specify the design's resets using
the -cm_fsmresetfilter compile-time option. The reset filter specification file is passed on
the VCS command line as follows:
vcs -cm fsm -cm_fsmresetfilter <filename>
where <filename> is the FSM reset filter configuration file.

text:
You can specify a global reset signal, a reset signal for specific modules, or reset signals
for specific modules and FSMs. An example of the global reset signal is as follows:
signal=reset case=FALSE
In this example, the FSM engine treats any test that compares a signal named reset to
false as being a check for reset. Thus, transitions caused by the assignment of the IDLE
state in the below example is ignored:
if (!reset) next_state <= IDLE;
A reset signal can also be specified for specific modules as follows:
module=mymod signal=reset case=FALSE
In this example, only transitions FSMs in the mymod module are filtered for reset == false
conditions.
The different styles can be combined in the reset filter file. The following example specifies
a global rule to apply (reset == TRUE) for any FSM signal named abc, and a separate rule
for abc in the mymod module, where the reset signal is named rst:
signal=reset case=TRUE fsm=abc
module=mymod signal=rst case=TRUE fsm=abc
VCS gives priority to a line with module name even if no FSM is specified. A
line with no module name or FSM name is the lowest priority.
The FSM extraction engine can detect reset tests even in complex conditions. For
example, consider the following code snippet that shows the complex condition, reset &&
dum:
n_suit <= ((reset && dum) ? clubs :
((suit == hearts) ? diamonds :
((suit == diamonds) ? spades :
((suit == spades) ? clubs :
hearts))));
The FSM Configuration File
The FSM configuration file provides the following features:
• Detection of Illegal States
The FSM configuration file allows you to specify the list of states for a given FSM signal.
If a one-hot FSM is being specified and an illegal state is specified, VCS gives a message
explaining that the state is illegal and why, and that it is being ignored.
• Keyword: AUTO

The AUTO keyword directs VCS to use the FSMs as specified in the configuration file for
those signals, but also allows VCS to automatically detect other signals as FSMs. This
allows you to tweak the FSM extraction of a module without having to become responsible
for all FSMs in that module. The keyword is used with the FSMS directive in place of the
RESTRICT and EXCLUDE keywords:
FSMS = AUTO
• Support for Concatenation Expressions
Concatenations of signals can be specified in the FSM configuration file. For example:
CURRENT={s1,s2,s3}
This allows you to specify concatenations as FSMs without modifying the source code.
Paired with the AUTO keyword, you can add a concatenation FSM to a module without
affecting other FSMs in that module.
Other Notes
To reuse existing exclusions, you can use the -excl_bypass_checks switch while
generating a report. However, the recommended way to reuse exclusions is to load elfiles
into Verdi, bypass checks, and then save them to a new file.
The FSM extraction engine has the following limitations:
• Recognition of FSMs across instance hierarchy barriers is not supported.
• Pragmas in the HDL source code to modify FSMs are not supported.
• FSMs implemented across entity/architecture boundaries are not supported.
• Part-selects with computed bounds, which cannot be resolved at elaboration time, are
not supported.
• Generics of non-integer types, such as bit_vector, are not supported.
• FSMs with multidimensional array indices, such as cur(k)(P), are not supported. For
example, consider the following code snippet that shows nested generate for the if-
elsif type FSM with generics and constants as state type:
Example 27 Multidimensional Array Indices are Not Supported
GEN1: for k in 1 to 2 generate
GEN2: for P in 1 to 2 generate
b1 : block is
p1 : process
variable nxt : integer;

if (reset) then nxt := red;
elsif (red = cur(k)(P)) then nxt := blue;
elsif (blue = cur(k)(P)) then nxt := green;
else nxt := red;

cur(k)(P) <= nxt;

Recognition of FSMs With All Possible Transitions
By default, VCS recognizes a signal as an FSM if it finds a constant value that is assigned
to a next-state signal and this assignment is guarded by a comparison to a constant value.
This analysis is used to determine which transitions are possible in the FSM. For example,
if an assignment nextstate <= S2 is guarded by a check if (curstate == S1) , VCS
knows to monitor for the transition S1 -> S2 .
By default, when VCS finds state comparisons and assignments but cannot determine the
set of possible transitions, it does not monitor the FSM for coverage.
When the -cm_fsmopt full compile-time option is given, VCS extracts FSMs even when
a subset of possible transitions could not be found. In these cases, every transition from
each state to every other state is part of the FSM coverage model.
Consider the following code snippet that shows part of an FSM in which BUSY and IDLE
are constant values, curst is a current-state signal, and nxtst is a next-state signal:
if (curst == IDLE)
nxtst <= BUSY;
In this example, a constant BUSY is assigned to nxtst and this assignment is guarded by
the if statement that compares curst to a constant value, IDLE. By default, VCS can
determine that IDLE -> BUSY is a valid FSM transition, and it adds this transition to the
FSM coverage model.

Now, consider the following code snippet that shows part of an FSM in which curstate
and nxtstate are signals, and RDY and WORK are constant values:
if (curstate == RDY)
nxtstate <= somesig;
nxtstate = WORK;
In this example, the assignment of somesig to nxtstate is guarded by a state check
of curstate == RDY , but VCS cannot extract any specific transitions as the value of
somesig at this location could be any FSM state. The assignment of WORK to nxtstate is a
state assignment, but does not limit the FSM to a specific transition.
If the rest of the FSM coding is similar, and VCS cannot limit the total transitions to
anything other than every state to every other state, by default, VCS does not monitor this
as an FSM. Using the -cm_fsmopt full option, however, VCS extracts FSMs like this.
• Coverage databases that are created using the -cm_fsmopt full compile-time option
cannot be merged with the coverage databases that are created without using this
option.
FSM Support for Inside Range Expressions
VCS treats all values in 'inside' expressions as possible FSM states and transitions when
the following command is used at compile time:
vcs -cm fsm
When an FSM is extracted, VCS ensures every value in the range is treated as a state for
coverage and all its transitions are tracked and reported.
Example 28 shows a range expression [b:o] in a 'case inside' statement. Any state value
in the range b, g, y, and o is matched by the [b:o] case item.
Example 28 Range Expression, [b:o]
module m1 (input wire reset,clk);
enum integer { v=1, i=2, b=3, g=4, y=5, o=6, r=7 } e2;
reg [15:0]cs; reg [15:0]ns;

always @(clk, reset) begin
if(reset)
cs <= v;
else begin
case(cs) inside
v, i: begin
cs <= b;
end
[b:o]: begin
cs <= r;
end
r: begin
cs <= v;
end
end
end
In this example, the values corresponding to g and y are considered for FSM analysis.

The URG report of Example 28 is as follows:
Figure 10 URG Report
The highlighted states and transitions in the report represent g and y of Example 28. Note
that the values are inferred from the range, therefore, they are shown as integer literals
rather than the enumerated type names, g and y.

This feature has the following limitations:
1. FSMs that use state values greater than 64-bits are not supported for finding states
and transitions from 'inside' expressions.
2. Range expressions that use an arithmetic operation in one or both endpoints are not
supported. For example, the following FSMs are not supported:
case(state)

P3-2: next_state <=

case(state) inside

[P0:P0+2]: next_state =
Ignoring FSM Transitions for Unguarded State Assignments
By default, VCS FSM coverage creates FSM transitions in the coverage model wherever
it sees a state assigned to the FSM signal. It tries to determine which possible states the
FSM could be in when that assignment happens, and creates a transition from each of
those states to the assigned state.
When VCS cannot determine which states the FSM must be in when a new state is
assigned, by default it creates a transition from every known state of the FSM to the
new state. However, when the -cm_fsmopt ignoreOpenAssigns compile-time switch
is specified, VCS does not create any transitions for the FSM when it cannot determine
the possible state values at the location where the new state is assigned. The purpose
of this switch is to limit the transitions in the FSM model only to those that are identified
as controlled by the current value, as opposed to creating transitions due to other
assignments such as initialization and resets.
For more information, see the following sections:
• Examples
• Notes
• Reports
This section gives examples of the effect of the -cm_fsmopt ignoreOpenAssigns switch.

Notes
While using this feature, keep the following guidelines in mind:
• The coverage databases generated using this switch can be merged with the coverage
databases generated without this switch, but which database is used as the base
database affects the results. If a coverage database compiled with this switch is used
as a base design, transitions related to unguarded state assignments are reported as
Ignored. Alternatively, if a coverage database compiled without this switch is used as a
base design, no transitions are reported as Ignored.
• The -cm_fsmopt ignoreOpenAssigns switch does not intend to precisely identify
and ignore reset-only transitions. It decides whether transitions should be created
based only on whether the state assignment is guarded by a check on the value of
the FSM signal. For precise control of ignoring transitions that explicitly depend on
reset, VCS provides the -cm_fsmresetfilter compile-time option. For more details
on -cm_fsmresetfilter, see the Ignoring Reset-Only Transitions section.
• Transitions that are marked as ignored are reported as Ignored whether they are
covered or not covered.
• If after extracting transitions and applying the filtering rule specified by -cm_fsmopt
ignoreOpenAssigns, it turns out that all transitions to a given state would be ignored,
then all states that were detected that go to the state would instead be monitored.
This prevents cases where due to the coding style, a state is assigned without a guard
check that may stay in effect - for example, as with an assignment used as a default
that may be overridden by later assignments.
• If all of a given state's transitions are marked as Ignored by -cm_fsmopt
ignoreOpenAssigns, because all detected assignments are not guarded by any state
check, VCS leaves them as-is and does not mark them as Ignored to ensure that these
states are counted in the report and any issue with the encoding can be analyzed.
Reports
Transitions suppressed by the -cm_fsmopt ignoreOpenAssigns switch are not included
in FSM coverage score computation. URG and Verdi present these transitions differently,
and neither tool marks them as Unreachable. At a casual glance, compile-time excluded
transitions in Verdi can look similar to uncovered transitions, so it is important to
understand how each tool reports them.

URG Reports
By default, URG does not list suppressed transitions in the FSM state and transition detail
tables. Instead, URG prints the following message in the FSM coverage section when any
transitions were suppressed:
Some transitions were marked Ignored because the
-cm_fsmopt ignoreOpenAssigns switch was given at compile time.
When you compile with -cm_fsmopt ignoreOpenAssigns and also specify -diag
noconst, URG lists the suppressed transitions in the FSM transition detail table with a
status of Ignored. These transitions are shown whether or not they were exercised in
simulation, and they do not count toward the FSM coverage score. The following figure
shows an example URG FSM transition detail report:
Figure 11 URG FSM Transition Detail Report Showing Ignored Transitions
In this example, transitions such as S1->S0 and S2->S0 correspond to an unguarded
state assignment and are reported as Ignored. Transition S3->S0 is not ignored because it
corresponds to a default case item that only some FSM states can reach.
When -diag noconst is specified, VCS also reports a Note message for each ignored
unguarded state assignment at compile time. For example:
Note-[VCM-FSMOTIG] Unguarded state assignment ignored
file.v, 14
VCS will not monitor the transitions associated with the state
assignment of "S0" to signal "curst" on this line because the
"-cm_fsmopt ignoreOpenAssigns" switch was given, and no check
on the value of "curst" could be detected guarding the assignment.
Transitions associated with this assignment will be shown as
Ignored in coverage reports.

Verdi Reports
In Verdi Coverage, transitions suppressed by -cm_fsmopt ignoreOpenAssigns are
marked as compile-time excluded in the FSM transition matrix. They appear as gray
cells with an excluded indicator rather than as red uncovered cells or as unreachable
transitions. These transitions are removed from the coverage model at compile time and
do not affect the FSM coverage score.
The following figure compares the same FSM transition matrix without and with
-cm_fsmopt ignoreOpenAssigns . Without the switch, transitions created from unguarded
state assignments appear as uncovered (red). With the switch, those same transitions
appear as compile-time excluded (gray).
Figure 12 Verdi FSM Transition Matrix Without and With ignoreOpenAssigns
In the lower matrix, transitions such as fiftn->idle, fiftn->ten, five->idle, and
five->ten were created from unguarded default assignments and are shown as compile-
time excluded rather than as uncovered transitions to be exercised.

the same as unreachable transitions. Unreachable transitions are filtered
by constant analysis or other compile-time optimizations and are reported
separately. If you see transitions disappear or change status after enabling
ignoreOpenAssigns, verify that the affected transitions correspond to
unguarded state assignments rather than to unreachable logic.
• This feature does not guarantee that VCS will detect reset-only transitions. It is
recommended to follow the coding style as shown in the examples above to ensure
that the transitions are extracted as expected.
FSM Compile Times
VCS Coverage allows you to specify a maximum width for any signal or expression to be
considered as a possible FSM. Any expression wider than that number is ignored for FSM
analysis. This feature helps to speed up FSM analysis.
This section consists of the following sub-sections:
• Specifying FSM Maximum Width
• Analyzing FSM Module Times
Specifying FSM Maximum Width
To specify the maximum FSM width, use the -cm_fsm_limit switch as follows:
% vcs -cm fsm -cm_fsm_limit maxwidth=N -diag fsm
For example, to set the maximum FSM width to 32, use the following command:
% vcs -cm fsm -cm_fsm_limit maxwidth=32 -diag fsm
The FSM configuration file does not support specifying arrays of FSMs or part-select
FSMs. Therefore, re-including excluded arrays of FSMs or part-select FSMs in the
configuration file is not supported in the FSM configuration file.
Analyzing FSM Module Times
VCS Coverage provides additional diagnostics to see the time spent in analyzing each
module for FSMs. This feature is provided under the -diag fsm+times switch. The
following is the syntax:
% vcs -cm fsm -diag fsm+times …

Once this switch is used at compile time, the time spent for every module’s FSM analysis
is printed if the time is over a certain level.
If a module does not have an FSM, it can be excluded from analysis using a begin/end
block in the -cm_hier file as follows:
begin fsm
-module <module_name>
end
If any module’s FSM analysis time exceeds a set value, the following message is issued:
Note-[VCM-FSMMXT] High FSM analysis time for module
big_test_mod.v, 1
FSM analysis for the module 'bit_testbench' is taking a longer time than
normal, 34 minutes so far. The size or complexity of this module may be
incompatible with full FSM analysis.
You can tell VCS to skip this module for FSM coverage using a cm_hier
file and the "begin fsm" syntax or by adding pragmas to the code. See
the VCS User Guide for more information on these features.
It is not possible to change the analysis time at which the message can be printed.
However, you can suppress the printing of this message using the -suppress option as
% vcs -suppress=VCM-FSMMXT -cm fsm …
Excluding High Compile-Time Modules
To re-include an FSM that is excluded due to its width, specify its name in an FSM
configuration file. Once the FSM is included in the configuration file, VCS analyzes it as an
FSM even when it crosses its threshold limit. For example, to ensure that the signal cur
is analyzed as an FSM in the module m, include the following lines in the configuration file
passed to the -cm_fsmcfg switch:
MODULE=m
CURRENT=cur
Once the signal cur is specified in the configuration file, VCS analyzes the signal normally
even when its width is greater than the limit.

Branch coverage monitors the execution of
conditional statements
conditional statements such as if/else
statements, case statements, and the
ternary operator
ternary operator "?:" in a design. By default, Branch
coverage analyzes which alternative of these conditional statements is covered during

ternary expression.

To compile and simulate the design for VHDL branch coverage, use the
following commands: % vcs [vcs_options] -cm branch top_cfg/entity/
module % simv [simv_options] -cm branch
Consider the code in Example 31:
Example 31 Branch Coverage Code Example
case (r1)
1'b1 : if (r2 && r3)
r4 = (r5 && r6) ? 1'b0 : 1'b1;
1'b0 : if (r7 && r8)
r9 = (r10 && r11) ? 1'b0 : 1'b1;
default : $display("no op");
In this block of code, there are procedural assignment statements where the value
assigned is controlled by the ternary operator (?:). These statements in turn are controlled
by if statements and the if statements are controlled by a case statement.
In this block of code, the possible vectors of signal or expression values that result in
simulation events or prevent simulation events are as follows:
r1 (r2 && r3) (r5 && r6) (r7 && r8) (r10 && r11)

default - - - -
For example, in the first vector, r1 is 1'b1 and the expression (r2 && r3 ) is true,
therefore, the value of r4 depends on the value of (r5 && r6 ). The values of (r7 && r8 )
and (r10 && r11 ) do not matter.
Consider an another example where r1 is 1'b1, but the expression (r2 && r3 ) is false,
and the values of the other expressions are not applicable, therefore the scenario is not
simulated.
Branch coverage displays these vectors and indicates whether these vectors ever
occurred during simulation, in other words, whether they were covered.
By default, VCS does not monitor branch coverage for if and case statements and
ternary operator(?:) if they are in user-defined tasks or functions or in code that executes
as a result of a for loop. You can, however, enable branch coverage in this code.

For more information, see, Section "For Loops and User-defined Tasks and Functions" in
the Coverage Technology Reference Manual.
Branch Coverage With Unknown and High Impedance Values
If the conditional expression in an if statement evaluates to X or Z, branch coverage
treats this as a false value and reports that 0 value for the expression is covered.
If the case expression in a case statement evaluates to X or Z, VCS executes the default
case item. When this occurs, branch coverage reports that the vector for the default case
item is covered. If there is no default case item, branch coverage reports a vector for the
missing default case item and reports it as covered.
When the conditional expression for a ternary operator evaluates to X or Z, the vector for
the expression is not covered.

following expression:

The branch value coverage feature has the following limitations:
• Zero and non-zero values are covered; x and z values are not covered. For example:
assign out = ((din & {512 {1'bx}})? din :((~din) &
dout_temp) |(din & {512 {1'bx}})));
assign y = x & 3'bx; // this is not extracted in
// branch coverage
• Branch coverage for code inside functions and expressions that are function calls
cannot be extracted.
• VCS does not report if it is a condition of if/while/case, for example:
if (a ? b : c)
case(a ? b : c)
while(a ? b : c)
assign a = a || (a ? b : c)
• Branch values are not monitored for leaf nodes that have
unpacked dimensions
unpacked dimensions.
module test
reg a;
reg z[6:0];
reg b[6:0];
reg c[6:0];
z = a? b : c;
//Coverage should not create z = a? (b? b :b) : (c? c: c); //and
hence, the branch values are not monitored for the
//leaf nodes b and c.
end
• Branch values are not monitored for the nodes with
streaming operators
streaming operators [>> and <<].
• Branch value coverage ignores ternary expressions inside
generate
generate statements. For
genvar i;
generate for (i=0; i<4;i++ )
begin: inst
always @(posedge clk)
e[i] <= ((c[i] && d[i]) ? ((c[i]!=1'b0)?
c[i]: ~c[i]) : d[i]);
end
endgenerate
Branch coverage shows the following warning in the URG report:
e[i] <= ((c[i] && d[i]) ? ((c[i]!=1'b0)? c[i]: ~c[i]) : d[i]);
Warning: the following expressions cannot be annotated

-1- ((c[1] && d[1])) ? ;
-2- ((c[1] != 1'b0)) ? ;
Enhancing Branch Coverage for Fully-Defined Case Statements
Case statements are not required to have “default” clauses in Verilog. However, for
coverage purposes, in its default flow VCS implicitly includes a default statement in a
case statement that does not define one, even if the case statement is fully defined
with case items for all possible values. The implicit inclusion of default in a fully-defined
case statement reduces coverage scores as such a default is unreachable for coverage
computation.
To direct VCS to detect fully-defined case statements and to skip including a default
statement in them , use the compile-time switch -cm_branch ignoreMissingDefault as
vcs -sverilog test.v -cm branch -cm_branch ignoreMissingDefault
No additional switch is required to enable this feature at runtime and report time.
Consider the following code snippet:
reg [1:0] state;

case (state)
2'b00: state = 2'b01;
2'b01: state = 2'b10;
2'b10: state = 2'b11;
2'b11: state = 2'b00;
end
end

In this example, the reg [1:0] state signal can accept four values, that is, 2'b00, 2'b01,
2'b10, and 2'b11. The case statement, case (state), consists of four case items. It is a
fully-defined case statement as it covers the complete range of state, therefore, there is
no need for a default statement in this case statement.

Case expressions whose width is greater than 16 are still have a case default
monitored whether they are fully specified or not.
When you specify the -cm_branch ignoreMissingDefault switch at compile time,
VCS detects that case (state) is fully defined and does not include a default statement.
Therefore, the switch provides 100% coverage as shown in Figure 14. The figure
also displays the URG report that is generated without using the compile-time switch,
-cm_branch ignoreMissingDefault , and shows coverage as 83.33%.
Figure 14 URG Reports

• x and z values of a case statement are ignored and the case statement is not
considered as fully defined. For example, in the following code snippets, the case items
with x and z values are ignored:
Figure 15 Example for x and z Values

To monitor code coverage for SystemVerilog packages, use the
-cm_report svpackages
-cm_report svpackages
compile-time option.
Example 32 illustrates the code coverage for a SystemVerilog package.
Example 32 Code Coverage for a SystemVerilog Package
'timescale 1ns/1ps

package fun;
logic temp, temp2,temp3;

function reg [3:0] myfunction;
input reg a, b, c, w, x, y, z, rst;

if (a && b && ~w)
myfunction = 3'b000;
if (c && a)
myfunction = 3'b001;
else begin
if (a && w)
myfunction= 3'b000;
myfunction = 3'b 011;
end
end
endpackage

module function_calling;

logic a, b,c, w, x, z, y, rst ;
logic [2:0] t;

import fun::*;

assign t = myfunction (c,a,b,w,x,z,y,rst);
assign temp = temp2 && temp3;

a = 0; b=0; c=0; w=0; x=0; y=0; w=0; z=0;
#5 a=1; x=1;
#5 b=1; y=1;
#5 c=1; z=1;
#5 w=1;
#5 temp3 = 1; temp2=1;
#100 $finish;
end
To monitor the SystemVerilog package in Example 32, execute the following VCS
command:
% vcs -sverilog -cm line+tgl+cond+branch -cm_cond tf+full \ -cm_report
svpackages pack_fun.sv -R

This command monitors code coverage for the following:
• Line coverage for functions and tasks defined in the SystemVerilog package.
• Toggle coverage for the signals declared in the SystemVerilog package.
• Condition and branch coverage for functions and tasks defined in the SystemVerilog
package.
-cm_cond tf and -cm_cond scalarbitwise options are ON by default. The
-cm_cond old compile-time option allows you to reverse the behavior of these
two switches.
Line Coverage
To monitor line coverage for functions and tasks defined in the SystemVerilog package
in Example 32, use the -cm_report svpackages compile-time option along with the -cm
line compile-time option. However, if a function or a task defined in a package is not
invoked in any portion of the design, it is not monitored.

FSM Coverage
This enhancement has no impact on the finite state machine (FSM) coverage. If a function
defined inside a package is imported into a module, VCS considers the imported package
function’s group of statements in the FSM extraction. Thus, there is no impact on the FSM
coverage.
The following are the limitations of the -cm_report svpackages compile-time option:
• Path coverage is not monitored within a SystemVerilog package.
• Only user-defined packages are monitored with this option. The following packages are
not monitored with this option:
◦ SVA packages
◦ VMM packages
◦ VIP packages
◦ DPI packages
◦ OVM/UVM packages
Coverage Options and Sub-Options
VCS Coverage provides options and sub-options that help you customize the generation
of coverage data for your design.
Mandatory Options for Generating Coverage Metrics
To generate coverage metrics, use the following commands during compile-time and
runtime:
-cm <cov_metrics_name>
The arguments to the -cm option are as follows:
line argument to the -cm option
line
Specifies line coveragecond argument to the -cm optioncondition coveragespecifying
cond
Specifies condition coverage

tgl argument to the -cm optiontoggle coveragespecifying
tgl
Specifies toggle coveragefsm argument to the -cm optionFSM coveragespecifying
fsm
Specifies FSM coveragebranch argument to the -cm option
branch
branch coveragespecifying
Specifies branch coverageassertion argument to the -cm optionassertion coveragespecifying
assert
Specifies assertion coverage
You can include more than one argument using a plus (+) as a delimiter between
arguments.
% vcs source.v -cm line+tgl+branch
VCS provides a capability to gather functional coverage metrics during simulation runs. If
your design has assertions or covergroups defined, VCS collects the coverage data and
generates the coverage database (simv.vdb). After simv.vdb is generated, you can:
• Use Unified Report Generator (URG) to generate text or HTML reports
• Use the Verdi Coverage GUI (Cov GUI) to view your assertion or covergroup reports
• Use custom coverage API to view the reports
The width of the coverpoint expression must not exceed 65535, otherwise,
VCS Coverage gives the following error:
Error-[FCCWETL] Coverpoint Width Exceeded The Limit
